Why full-fledged quantum computers might always be five years away

New Scientist July 31, 2026

What is a quantum computer? The question feels deceptively simple. It is a computer that uses quantum effects to run calculations – or at least, that is what I have been saying to friends and acquaintances for years. Because I report about the latest advances in quantum computing nearly constantly, I have felt confident in this answer. Recently, however, I have had to re-examine that confidence. A more detailed question makes clear why: though I can name many different components and functions of a quantum computer, could I identify exactly when they all become a quantum computer? One recent philosophical study suggests that this is at the root of the difficulty of forecasting the future of quantum computing.

Quantum computers are starting to become useful as scientific tools

For Christophe Jurczak at investment firm Quantonation, it all started at a conference that had nothing to do with quantum computing. Researchers were discussing a different emerging technology, and Jurczak realised that he had first heard about it 30 years ago. Back then, everyone was saying that it was only “five years away”. Déjà vu. Then, a worry set in – could quantum computers also be such a “perpetual five-year technology” (PFYT)? This drove him to do a year-long deep dive into philosophical literature. The paper I read was its outcome.

In it, he argues that, right now, quantum computers are firmly in the PFYT category. All attempts to forecast when quantum computers will truly arrive are misguided so long as they presuppose that we already know what quantum computers are, he writes. “If the identity of a quantum computer is still being settled as the machine develops, that presupposition fails.”

Advertisement

As someone who thinks about quantum computing an awful lot, I wanted to know what exactly brought Jurczak to this somewhat alarming conclusion. In the nearly five years that I have spent writing about quantum computers for New Scientist, they have certainly made measurable progress. Several firms have presented road maps for the future of their devices, including goals for their overall size and the performance of some of their components, and then they met those goals.

Quantum computers are also much closer to being useful devices than they were just a handful of years ago. Sure, they haven’t yet changed the world by aiding the discovery of some groundbreaking drug or battery redesign, but you could access a quantum computer through the cloud right now and use it as a scientific tool if you happen to be a chemist or a material scientist.

Jurczak doesn’t deny this. He even tells me that he recently ran an experiment remotely on a quantum computer made from extremely cold atoms that was housed in a lab in Canada while he was on his couch in Texas. But this doesn’t mean that the question of quantum computing is settled, he says. One way to see this is to note the diversity of approaches for building a quantum computer, as well as the many, many metrics that are important for capturing how well one might work.

The basic components of quantum computers are called qubits, and they can be built in many different ways, from using extremely cold atoms to tiny superconducting circuits or particles of light. Then, there are the things you may want to measure about your quantum computer: how many qubits it has, how well connected they are, how reliably they can be used for different parts of a computation, how quickly they can be controlled and so on. Perfecting one or even a few of these metrics typically doesn’t guarantee that all the others will become excellent too.

Having spoken to many researchers and executives within the field, I have come to recognise a certain mix of excitement and anxiety in how they often speak: celebrating all the components of a truly powerful machine having been proven to work by themselves, while trying to keep at bay the worry about what may happen when they are all put together.

Free newsletter

In his paper, Jurczak, together with Brooke Abeles at ENS Paris-Saclay in France, collected data about some of these metrics across the industry and inferred a clear trend – once a threshold is crossed for one metric, such as guaranteeing that a single qubit makes errors less often than once in a thousand times, the five-year horizon doesn’t collapse. Instead, it resets. This is a consequence of discovering what a quantum computer is as it is being built.

This was distinctly not the case during the development of conventional computers. Jurczak says sometimes researchers like to compare today’s quantum computers to ENIAC, the world’s first programmable general-purpose electronic computer, but building that room-sized digital behemoth was much more of an engineering challenge. “[Classical computing] was a very much more mature ecosystem at the time when it started,” says Jurczak. While he was digging through philosophical literature, he found that an idea more relevant for quantum computers from the philosopher of technology Gilbert Simondon.

His theory of “technical individuation” says a shifting assembly of elements becomes a coherent “individual” through a process that includes a whole ecosystem, which consists of infrastructure, knowledge and practices maturing through iterative steps of trial and error. A collection of qubits and the devices that control and house them, for example, becomes a quantum computer only through interconnected developments in, for instance, laser and cryogenics systems, the building of special chip foundries, the growth of a specialised quantum workforce and basic research in quantum physics and computer science. Really, the list goes on; the ecosystem is large and complex.

As we talked, I found myself increasingly won over to Jurczak’s view of what has happened with quantum computing. The fact that we don’t have a fully useful quantum computer yet isn’t a failure of prediction, nor a failure of the market, but rather reflects the groundbreaking, paradigm-shifting nature of trying to corral the denizens of the quantum world into doing computational work for us. The technology is still too close to scientific discovery to be easily wrangled, easily scaled, easily accelerated by the usual tricks of the economy. “Don’t despair,” Jurczak puts a positive spin on it, “this is highly nonlinear, it takes time.”

Currently, the quantum computing industry has its sights on reaching “fault tolerance”, or building a quantum computer that is so good at catching its own errors that it can reliably run unprecedentedly complex computations. Once this goal is reached – and many firms are projecting they will do so by the end of the decade – will quantum computers have arrived? Will we know which type of qubit won the quantum-computing race? And what will be the next milestone?

Though Jurczak says that his framework isn’t predictive, it does begin to unravel some of these questions. Almost certainly the horizon will shift again, and not all the machines will be fully individuated. He says he is excited about the possibility of a really heterogenous quantum-computing system – no specific qubit design will win, they will just, through their own process of individuation, find applications they are well suited for. The question of what a quantum computer is won’t be answered by just one device. “The people who will build and use these machines should have more of an open mind about what a quantum computer is as a technical individual and how it concretises and how it’s going to be used as well,” says Jurczak.

Quantum computers won’t remain PFYTs forever, but he speaks about them currently being in that category with excitement. When he says that the constantly resetting horizon represents possibility, I can’t help but find that compelling. But what should quantum-computing firms do with this philosophical insight, I asked him. Certainly, they will still have to put out road maps and announce their goals. It’s important to have strategies for the next five years, he conceded. “We all want that and that’s needed, but think beyond and have a little bit of imagination as well, would be my take,” says Jurczak.

Can video games help us better understand quantum mechanics?

One way to achieve that may be to start working with people outside physics, maybe even philosophers themselves. The ecosystem for a quantum computer ought to be interdisciplinary. AI companies are already hiring across not just the sciences, but also the humanities, and it ought to happen with quantum-computing firms as well, he says. Jurczak believes AI agents themselves may also help accelerate some of that interdisciplinary work, as they aren’t trained in the specialised ways that human researchers are. He and several researchers at quantum-computing company Pasqal, which he co-founded, have already tested several examples of how such agents could help quantum-computing novices run computations on real quantum hardware. “If you ask me in five years what failure would really be, [it would be] that we still have these silos,” he says.

My own physics education was definitely siloed, and I was never asked to take a class in philosophy or the history of technology. Because a reporter’s job is to take both the broad view and the long view, I have, at times, felt the lack of that training rather sharply. The sheer amount of research in quantum computing is both impressive and overwhelming, and making sense of it has required a different skill set than merely being literate in the mathematics of quantum theory and somewhat conversant in materials science.

To be fair, the next time someone asks me what a quantum computer is, I will almost definitely not be telling them that it is a technical individual in an ever-evolving state of becoming. For anyone who isn’t actively trying to shape the fast-growing quantum computing industry, that won’t be very helpful. But the next time a paper reporting some narrow yet impressive advance crosses my desk, I will file it away as part of this evolution, reset my personal expectations clock and get at least a little excited about the quantum-computing horizon having just shifted.

A leading sociologist says New Zealand First’s policy to pay parents for having children is addressing a real issue but will not have a tangible effect.

The party announced its policy to create a “Kiwi Kids Grant” for parents, one of whom must be a New Zealand citizen, for their first three children.

The tax-free annual grant would be worth $5000 per child for each of their first three years, meaning families could receive up to $45,000 in total.

Massey University Professor Paul Spoonley said data from other countries with similar policies, like Sweden, show a temporary “blip” in births which does not last.

The drop in fertility rates is a global concern, but governments’ attempts to make a difference have been ineffective, Spoonley told Newstalk ZB’s Mike Hosking.

“The international evidence, and there’s a lot of it, shows that it’s very difficult to provide financial incentives which actually change that fertility decline.”

He acknowledged New Zealand First for drawing attention to the topic.

“This is a major issue that we need to talk about and decide what we’re going to do about it.”

The amount of money will make more of a difference to some than it will to others, Spoonley said, but it will not increase the birthrate.

“Is it going to reverse fertility decline in New Zealand? No, I don’t think so. I think we’re going to see [a] continuing drop.”

New Zealand First leader Winston Peters told Ryan Bridge TODAY that other countries’ policies have not worked because they started too late, and he has “a lot of confidence” his party’s will be successful.

“We want to go back to a policy where we actually help people in the most difficult, high-cost time of having children.”

The grant would be administered as a monthly payment through Inland Revenue, although the first-year grant for the first child could be taken as an upfront sum. The party costed the policy at $400 million per year once fully implemented.

Peters said the money would come “from the same pot of money that the National Party and Labour Party and other parties’ promises are coming from”.

“The only difference is when we get to run the economy after the next election, there will be real money in the economy, not hand to mouth as we’ve been at the moment.”

Parenting expert Nathan Wallis told Newstalk ZB that while cost is a factor in people’s decision to have children, many other elements come into it.

The first three years of a child’s life were “vital”, he said.

Ngāi Tahu Farming chosen to operate New Zealand’s largest farm, Molesworth Station

New Zealand Herald August 02, 2026

Molesworth Station. Photo / RNZ, Sally Round

By RNZ

Ngāi Tahu Farming has been chosen by the Department of Conservation to operate the country’s largest farm.

Molesworth Station, an iconic 180,000ha high-country farm that spanned Marlborough and North Canterbury, was run as a cattle farm by the state-owned Pāmu (formerly Landcorp).

The area, known formally as the Rangitahi/Molesworth Recreation Reserve, covers land owned by the Crown and administered by DoC.

The department announced on Friday afternoon that it would invite Ngāi Tahu Farming – a subsidiary of Te Rūnanga o Ngāi Tahu Group – to apply for a concession to manage the land.

Four other bids, including one by former farm manager Jim Ward, were unsuccessful.

DoC deputy director-general regional operations Henry Weston said farming would remain the core commercial activity at Molesworth, but it was also a nationally important drylands ecosystem with significant biodiversity, heritage, recreational and cultural values.

“This decision ultimately came down to Ngāi Tahu Farming, a wholly owned subsidiary of Te Rūnanga o Ngāi Tahu Group, having the strongest experience of farming at scale in the high country of those who applied,” Weston said.

“They have strong financial and business foundations offering long-term security for the Crown, making them the best applicant for the opportunity to negotiate the concession.

“Ngāi Tahu Farming currently farms three high country stations, spanning 36,000ha, as part of the 100,000ha of farming and forestry land it manages across the South Island.

“Final details of the farming operations will be determined through the concession process and will need to deliver on our high expectations regarding public access and weed and pest control.

“DoC ran a thorough process, weighed up a range of expert advice and materials, and made a decision in the best interest of Molesworth, one of New Zealand’s truly special places.”

DoC expected public access and weed and pest control would be maintained or improved and details would emerge during the concession process.

Ward told RNZ he was informed of the decision during a short phone call about an hour and a half before the announcement was made publicly on Friday afternoon.

“I’m absolutely gutted,” he said.

“The last 12 months have been a huge body of work getting it in front of people.

“We are all a bit deflated at the minute, to be honest.

“My wife and I put 24 years into Molesworth plus this last year.

“It was looking to the future, looking to cement Molesworth as a place for mum and dad and the kids of New Zealand, to build on what we had started.

“It was a totally different concept – a station for the nation – making it into a charitable trust.

“It was quite a bold concept, but it was the right thing to do.”

DoC had not told him why his bid was not successful.

“I’m still pretty numb, but the decision’s been made, and I’ll just have to go find myself something else to do,” Ward said.

Te Rūnanga o Ngāi Tahu welcomed the news.

Chief executive Ben Bateman said DoC’s decision reflected the iwi’s proven capability in farming, conservation and commercial management.

“We are committed to making sure the terms of any concession we negotiate are good for all New Zealanders,” Bateman said.

“Public access, biodiversity and ecological stewardship are central to how we would manage Rangitahi Molesworth.

“For us, Rangitahi is not simply a farming opportunity.

“It is an ancestral landscape woven into the whakapapa of Ngāi Tahu, Ngāti Kurī, Ngāti Māmoe and Waitaha.

“To be entrusted with its stewardship is a responsibility we approach with humility and determination.”

Te Rūnanga o Kaikōura chairwoman Hariata Kahu said it was an important milestone for her hapū, Ngāti Kurī.

“For many generations we have longed to play a more active role in protecting Rangitahi Molesworth,” she said.

“Growing up, we learn the pūrākau of Rangitahi and the journeys our people made through this landscape.

“The Awatere and Waiautoa rivers are part of those stories, and even the name Rangitahi speaks to the coming together of those waters.

“To know that if we are granted a concession we would have the opportunity to help care for this whenua is incredibly significant.

“For Ngāti Kurī, this is about ensuring future generations can experience Rangitahi, much like our ancestors did, with its landscapes and stories protected.”

The iwi would now work through the details of its concession application.

Federated Farmers president Colin Hurst said he welcomed the clarity DoC’s decision provided.

“The Department of Conservation has run a really robust, competitive and fair process to get to this point,” Hurst said.

“We congratulate Ngāi Tahu Farming on putting forward a strong business case and being selected as the preferred operator to negotiate for the lease.

“Molesworth is an incredibly special property for all New Zealanders, owned by all New Zealanders, so it’s important whoever takes on the lease is well set up to succeed.”

Ngāi Tahu Farming had the experience and financial resilience to farm a property like Molesworth Station, Hurst said.

“Ngāi Tahu Farming has a strong balance sheet that would allow them to keep farming through tough years with drought or poor commodity prices.

“It’s also well placed to run an integrated system with existing finishing farms around North Canterbury – so the decision makes sense from that perspective.

“There also needs to be clear expectations set that public access to Molesworth is protected and that there is a commitment to active weed and pest management.”

- RNZ

Hauraki Gulf shellfish harvesting ban extended until 2028

New Zealand Herald August 02, 2026

Kina in the waters of Hauraki Gulf. Photo / Shaun Lee

By RNZ

A ban on harvesting certain shellfish in parts of the Hauraki Gulf has been extended for another two years.

The fisheries closures ban mussels, pāua, and packhorse rock lobster from being taken within one nautical mile of Waiheke Island.

Cockles cannot be picked at Umupuia Beach in East Auckland, and in Coromandel, Te Mātā and Waipatukahu are closed to the taking of cockles, mussels, oysters, and pipi.

Oceans and Fisheries Minister Shane Jones said the move follows a request by Ngāi Tai Ki Tamaki, Ngāti Tamaterā Treaty Settlement Trust, and Ngāti Pāoa Iwi Trust, to help replenish local shellfish populations.

The applicants are members of the Pou Rāhui Research Project, incorporating mātauranga Māori and scientific tools to restore identified marine taonga species within the areas.

“Extending these temporary closures is a practical step for the benefit of current and future generations,” Jones said.

“The group’s work involves training whānau in traditional skills and data collection to strengthen mātauranga, to support evidence-based decision-making, and to ensure the long-term sustainability of customary fisheries.”

The closures are part of a broader effort to restore shellfish populations across the upper North Island.

Earlier this year, separate two-year bans came into force at beaches around Whangaparāoa Peninsula, Kawau Bay and Ōmaha Bay, where the collection of shellfish, seaweed and other rockpool species is also prohibited to allow marine ecosystems to recover.

At the time, Fisheries New Zealand said education would be key to the success of the measures, with officers initially focusing on informing beachgoers about the new rules rather than issuing fines.

Conservation groups also stressed that the closures were only one part of protecting marine ecosystems, alongside public education about sustainable harvesting.

The extended closures come into effect on August 7. Information, including maps, is available on MPI’s website.

Fisheries New Zealand also has a wider, ongoing review of recreational shellfish harvesting in the Auckland Coromandel area.

Earlier this year, it warned the public to check local site regulations, including daily limits per species and other restrictions.

It’s been a shaky weekend for New Zealand, with GeoNet recording three magnitude 5-plus earthquakes in separate parts of the country.

A magnitude 5.7 quake struck 10km south of Te Araroa on North Island’s East Coast at 8.35pm last night.

According to GeoNet, the quake had a depth of 40km and more than 5000 people reported feeling the shaking, which was classified as “strong”.

Two smaller aftershocks followed soon after the main tremor - a magnitude 3 quake was recorded in the area at 8.40pm, followed by a magnitude 3.1 aftershock at 9.07pm.

Both were centred in Te Araroa at depths of 38km.

One person in Kawerau told the Herald the quake went on for some time.

“My partner and I watched the nightshade swaying around and around as we felt the movement.”

Another local in Whakatāne said their house shook lightly for about four seconds, followed by a “sharper shake” that lasted six or seven more.

“Cat leapt up but did not run for the door!” they said.

Social media users reported feeling the quake across the eastern and central North Island, including Hawke’s Bay, Rotorua, Ōpōtiki, Ruatōria, Matatā and the Coromandel.

Residents in South Taranaki reported hearing a rumble before feeling the shaking, while people in New Plymouth described “just a quick jolt”.

One person in Gisborne described it only as a “gentle roll”, yet another local detailed the opposite, saying they experienced a “brief shake” that suddenly jumped “to a quick shudder” and rattled their house.

Contact the NZ Herald newsroom

GeoNet took to social media last night “after a bit of a shaky weekend” to remind Kiwis of New Zealand’s continuous seismic unrest.

“In our beautiful country earthquakes can occur anywhere at anytime,” it wrote.

“Remember, drop, cover and hold is the right action to take during an earthquake.

“If you’re near the coast and the shaking is long or strong, then get gone.”

At the same time, NZ Civil Defence said the quake was the latest in “a shaky few days across the motu”.

“It’s a reminder that our beautiful landscapes were formed by massive forces at work below the surface, and living alongside them means staying prepared,” NZ Civil Defence wrote on Facebook.

A magnitude 5.2 quake struck at about 35km northwest of Te Anau on Saturday afternoon, with nearly 1500 people throughout the lower South Island reporting the “light” tremor to GeoNet.

The night before, a magnitude 4.6 earthquake struck off New Zealand’s coast at 11.09pm.

With its epicentre about 30km northwest of Porirua at a depth of 38km, GeoNet received reports from nearly 9000 people between Auckland and Christchurch.

Many described hearing the quake before feeling it, with a Kāpiti man noting the “phone alert went off same time as I heard [the earthquake].”

“Started with an audible bang before the shaking started,” one woman wrote on Facebook.

“Heard that one coming,” wrote another on X.

He said the “vast majority” of Kiwis wanted to “get out there and make things happen”.

Luxon said he had been trying to communicate - “maybe poorly” - that the economy was moving in the right direction, although he acknowledged there were pockets where families and businesses were still struggling.

Coercion, control and high demands: How cults squash their members’ identities

Sydney Morning Herald August 03, 2026

A 15-month parliamentary inquiry has defined what a “high-control” organisation is and proposed that their leaders be subject to criminal charges. How it might work is another question.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

When Laura McConnell was kicked out of her family and the religious cult they raised her in, she went to Centrelink so she could feed herself, a counsellor to work through her issues, and a doctor for a check-up.

None of them understood what she was telling them.

“They just didn’t have the vocabulary,” McConnell says. She was a teenager, so Centrelink wanted a form signed by a parent or guardian – which was impossible. The GP said, “All the women in your religion are depressed – I don’t know what to do for you.”

The counsellor gave McConnell the number of a priest, but her group relied on lay preachers, so she “grew up thinking that, to speak to a priest is to speak to the devil”.

“I just shut down and didn’t talk to a counsellor for years because I thought that’s where I’d be sent … I found myself in a world I didn’t know anything about, with no language to describe what had happened to me.”

All this happened 27 years ago, but McConnell said she helped people leaving the group today who still struggled with the same problems.

McConnell was born and raised in an ultra-strict Christian sect known as Two-by-Twos – but ignorance about the practices of such “high-control groups” is almost universal.

Last week, a Victorian parliamentary committee tried to find a language to combat that ignorance. It defined the features of groups sometimes known as cults, and recommended better training for police and child protection workers.

It also recommended the Law Reform Commission formulate a new criminal offence for “group-based coercion” to prosecute the leaders of such groups.

Patrick McIvor, a former member of a high-control organisation and a counsellor and policy consultant, said “the development of shared language that we haven’t had before” was the committee’s most significant finding.

“People have talked about this experience of not being able to know or name what they’ve been through, especially kids who have grown up in this environment,” McIvor said. “They have felt they’ve had to try to translate themselves into existing categories or terms that people understand.”

It’s unclear how many people are part of high-control groups, but the committee chair, Labor MP Ella George, said her 15-month inquiry had received more than 600 submissions and responses to questions from Victorians, and “to me that speaks to the size of the issue”.

George said she had found the evidence she’d heard “heartbreaking and devastating”.

Her report says the beliefs of these groups are almost immaterial – they can be “religious, commercial enterprise, therapeutic or wellness communities, or any other type of group structure”. What makes them a problem are their practices.

The committee found the coercive control these groups exercise over their members – whether they are born into them or are recruited – suppresses their capacity to act, think or live independently. The groups demand ideological or religious purity, they surveil and monitor their members’ activities and patrol their thoughts. They also foster an “us versus them” mindset towards the broader community.

The threat of public humiliation or excommunication fosters fear and keeps people under the thumb.

Cumulatively, it means members rely on the group for their identity, self-worth, morality, and decision-making – while questioning and critical thinking are punished.

The committee found these practices caused life-long psychological damage. People live in a state of threat, anxiety and hypervigilance, often even well after they have left the group. The erosion of individual autonomy and self‑trust means people often struggle to form or maintain their identity.

Children, such as McConnell, who were born into such groups were even more vulnerable than those who were recruited.

“Their entire sense of self, relationships, and worldview are constructed by the group before they have the capacity to question it,” the committee found. Children schooled at home or by the group are worse off because of severely constrained access to “safe adults” outside the group.

Healthy groups, by contrast, were transparent and gave their members choice and the freedom to question or refuse, and the ability to leave the group without fear of punishment, the report found.

“People also have the right to be free from religion,” McIvor said.

Cassie Davies, who was born into the Plymouth Brethren Christian Church, said the church’s practices had suppressed her identity, and, as a woman, had “boxed me in” to a framework of what was acceptable and not acceptable.

“The suppression of any sort of sexual exploration, the complete taboo of the subject, all of that is completely emotionally abusive of children,” she added.

Establishing who to blame, though, was complex, Davies said. “Who’s the perpetrator? My mum is – but that’s because she believes that’s right, and that’s how her identity has been formed.”

Davies did not give evidence to the Victorian parliamentary inquiry. A Plymouth Brethren Christian Church spokesman said the church had not been approached by the committee, and “its report and findings have nothing at all to do with our church”. Asked about coercive practices, the spokesman said “none of this describes life in our church. This report is not about us.”

Among the committee’s recommendations are that the charities regulator, ACNC, abolish the category of “basic religious charity”, under which a number of high-control organisations are exempt from key governance and reporting obligations.

The committee said its proposed new criminal offence would be similar to coercive control offences for family violence that have been introduced in some jurisdictions and promised in Victoria, but different in crucial ways.

It said criminal culpability should focus on leaders – “those who create, maintain and benefit from systems of control”. The “apparent consent or compliance” of a victim should not be a defence if it was produced by coercion.

Victoria Police said any legal change was up to the government.

In 1996, a federal committee considered if the harm caused by “cults and obsessive small religious groups” should be included in the definition of harm under criminal law. Nothing came of it – one of a number of similar recommendations over the years that have gone nowhere.

“This report looks great, it looks promising,” Davies said. “But it’s government. What are we going to see? Twenty years from now we might see a change.”

Rupert Lowe urges Nigel Farage to work with Restore Britain

The Guardian Sun, 02 Aug 2026 21:05:52 GMT

The leader of Restore Britain, Rupert Lowe, has extended an olive branch to Nigel Farage, saying the two should put “personalities and our past disagreements aside for the good of the country”.

Lowe told the Reform UK leader that if he was “prepared to work together around serious policies, serious reform and serious government, then so are we”.

In a video posted on X, Lowe said: “I truly believe there could be sufficient common ground for our two movements to cooperate collectively, destroy the looming leftwing alliance that will finish off what hope remains for this country.

“In my view, failing to even try because of our own personal difficulties is simply not an option. Now is the time to put our differences aside and cooperate for the good of the country that we all love.”

The offer comes after Restore Britain placed fourth in the Greater Manchester mayoral byelection, where its candidate, Marlon West, took 8.7% of the vote. Reform’s Sian Astley came second on 21%, behind Labour’s Andy Burnham’s successor, Bev Craig.

Lowe was among five Reform MPs who entered parliament for the first time in the 2024 general election, representing the constituency of Great Yarmouth.

The leader of Restore Britain was suspended in March 2025, when accusations emerged that he had bullied staff and threatened chair Zia Yusuf, claims Lowe denied.

Lowe founded Restore Britain in February with backing from Elon Musk.

Lowe asked Farage to put “personalities and our past disagreements aside” and set five conditions for cooperation: mass deportation of illegal migrants “including women and children”, tougher rules on legal migration, a ban on halal and kosher slaughter, the burqa, cousin marriage and Sharia courts, a referendum on the death penalty, welfare cuts to fund “self-sufficiency” and the exclusion of former Tory ministers from any future cabinet.

“Mass deportations must become a political inevitability,” he said. “They must all go.”

He cited Reform and Restore’s cooperation on Norfolk county council as proof cross-party working can succeed nationally.

Farage framed the next election as “an existential fight to save the country” and said Reform would need support beyond its own ranks to win.

“I understand Reform UK will need the support of people from other parties, as well as millions who have never voted before,” he wrote in a post on X. “That is the broad coalition I am building.”

He added that Reform has “always been open to anyone” who shares its aims on borders, the economy and democracy, but added: “I will never turn my back on my team.”

Farage is fighting a byelection after resigning his seat of Clacton. All other mainstream parties have declined to stand a candidate against him, though there are 34 independents on the ballot paper, including novelty candidates such as Count Binface.

Kuwaki wins Women’s Open after Henseleit’s unlucky break off marshal’s leg in playoff

The Guardian Sun, 02 Aug 2026 20:41:22 GMT

Japanese 23-year-old wins her first major championship

England’s Charley Hull and Lottie Woad finish tied sixth

It was no surprise that an extraordinary Sunday at the Women’s Open ended in such circumstances. Has the ankle of a marshal ever before played a crucial role in the outcome of a major championship? A competition that looked for so long as if no one wanted to win rumbled on at Royal Lytham & St Annes until fate played its hand.

Glory for Shiho Kuwaki, pain for Esther Henseleit. That barely explains the half of it. Henseleit had forced a playoff with a stunning birdie from 45ft on the final hole of regulation play. On the first visit back to the 18th, Kuwaki played a glorious approach to secure her four and the extension of the tournament.

What happened next was beyond anyone’s comprehension. Kuwaki found the fairway with a perfect drive. Henseleit cut her tee shot to the right, where it looked in enough bother before hitting the lower leg of a volunteer. The ball ricocheted to the bottom of a gorse bush. Henseleit did exceptionally well to advance the ball up the fairway but the clear advantage was with Kuwaki. Her four secured the trophy. Henseleit has legitimate cause to bemoan horrible fortune.

Earlier, this was a tournament where the nerves associated with the pursuit of a major championship were writ large across the faces of those looking to win the Women’s Open’s 50th edition.

Kuwaki’s is the most unlikely of triumphs. Perhaps her lack of experience in this domain actually helped the 23-year-old as those around her wilted. Kuwaki had played in only one Women’s Open before, missing the cut at Royal Porthcawl last year. Lytham provided such a contrasting storyline and Japan now has back-to-back Women’s Open victories.

Henseleit needed a birdie three at the last to halt Kuwaki. She sat 45ft from the hole in two, with the odds firmly stacked against her. The ball was 5ft from the hole when Henseleit knew its destination. Kuwaki surely feared the worst but she need not have worried.

Henseleit earlier offered a snapshot of what played out on this major Sunday. The German tied Kuwaki’s minus five with a tap-in birdie at the 15th. From the very next tee, Henseleit hooked a three wood into long grass. A bogey ensued. It was as if anyone who earned a proper view of the Women’s Open trophy was immediately blinded by the light.

Yealimi Noh held a three-shot lead after 54 holes. She even increased that advantage by one before wobbles started at the 4th. Noh posted a 74 before admitting it “stung” to fall short in this manner. She was one shy of the playoff mark of five under.

On the final hole, in the final group, Henseleit and Noh had the opportunity to force Kuwaki into extra time. Both missed the fairway, with approaches leaving only the remote chances of birdies. Noh left her attempt short, moments after her playing partner had stunned the crowd.

Ryu Hae-ran, seeking a third major win in as many starts, carded a three over par 74. Jeeno Thitikul? 73. Nelly Korda closed in the manner of a world No 1 with a 68 – the lowest round among the top 13 names on the leaderboard – catapulting her into a share of fourth.

Charley Hull and Lottie Woad never seriously looked like delivering a British winner for the third time in a row at Lytham. Hull’s 72 left her at minus one. Woad’s putter was colder than a winter’s morning in Siberia during her 73, which meant the same aggregate. Neither undertook media duties, which given their standing here was less than impressive. Tied sixth is hardly the stuff of disaster.

Anna Nordqvist signed off with a 68 before admitting the stresses and strains associated with her European Solheim Cup captaincy. Nordqvist will name her four captain’s selections on Monday for the clash against the United States, which takes place in the Netherlands in September. Intrigue surrounds whether Ireland’s Leona Maguire will keep her place in team Europe despite indifferent form. Nordqvist made some calls to players during Women’s Open week, which she conceded affected her own performance at Lytham.

“I think it’s hard to put it in words how hard it has been,” Nordqvist said. “I felt like as soon as I came off the course, it was just so much stuff about Solheim Cup, which has been hard because I really wanted to go and enjoy this week.

“I felt really off the first day but managed to battle through. I played really well the second day and then yesterday, I didn’t really play that badly, but mentally I was just exhausted. I think it [the size of the job] has been a lot more than I expected. There has been a lot more practical stuff to deal with. Maybe looking back, it was going to be a tough task to do both [play and be a captain], but I’m very proud of myself for how I’ve done it.”

The Guardian Sun, 02 Aug 2026 20:16:50 GMT

Donald Trump has said he cancelled planned military strikes against Iran on the basis of “rapidly” reaching a deal on its nuclear programme and the full reopening of the strait of Hormuz.

The US president paused the strikes in expectation of a breakthrough and in response to requests from Iran and other countries in the region, he claimed on his Truth Social platform on Saturday.

“Based on this request, I have agreed, for the future benefit of the WORLD and, likewise, the survival of a successful and prosperous Iran, to cancel the attack, subject to being able to rapidly make a DEAL.”

The deal would include the immediate and complete reopening of the strait and “an end to Iran’s nuclear threat”, he posted. It marked the latest climbdown from extravagant threats to pound the Islamic Republic in the months-long conflict.

However, hopes of a breakthrough faded on Sunday when Iran’s Mehr news agency said Trump’s claim that Tehran had requested a pause “was nothing but a new lie” and that the Iranian armed forces were “on high alert and ready for any eventuality”.

Another Iranian news agency, Fars, citing a source close to Iranian negotiators, said that as long as the US “maintains its hostile actions” the strait would remain closed.

Iran’s acting defence minister, Majid Ebn-e-Reza, said Trump had backed down “within the context of psychological operations and a war of calculations”. Iran’s forces would remain on alert, the minister said on X. “We will neither be taken by surprise nor will we be passive.”

Mediation efforts were continuing amid the standoff. Hassan Ghashghavi, a spokesperson for the Iranian parliament’s national security commission, said in a video interview that mediators were trying to revive an agreement brokered by Pakistan in June, Agence France-Presse reported.

The decision to halt fresh strikes came after the Saudi crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman, called Trump on Saturday to express concerns, it was reported. Trump’s reversal also followed Iranian threats to retaliate decisively against its neighbours in the event of US strikes, while Kuwait reported being hit by Iranian drones on Saturday and two ships were attacked off Oman in the strait of Hormuz.

One source described as having knowledge of the Trump-Prince Mohammed call told Axios that the Saudi crown prince had “urged Trump to de-escalate and refrain from launching the strikes”.

The Associated Press (AP) also reported the conversation, citing its own source. It said the Saudis were concerned that if the US targeted Iran’s energy infrastructure or carried out massive strikes on other key infrastructure, Tehran could respond by carrying out similar attacks on the kingdom and other Gulf countries.

The crown prince during Saturday’s call sought clarity from Trump on what potential new action he was weighing to take against Iran, AP reported.

A White House official, who was not authorised to comment publicly and requested anonymity, confirmed to AP that Trump and Prince Mohammed spoke on Saturday, but did not offer any detail about the substance of their conversation.

Saudi Arabia earlier this week joined the US in striking logistics and weapons sites used by Iranian-backed militias in Iraq, but has been urging the US and Iran to return to the negotiating table.

CBS News reported that the US and Israel were planning joint strikes, possibly throughout the weekend, with oil refineries and power plants among possible targets.

Eli Cohen, Israel’s energy minister and a member of prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s security cabinet, said there was close security and intelligence coordination between Israel and the US on everything happening in the region, while adding: “With or without an agreement, and regardless of any external commitments, if Iran attempts to renew its nuclear programme or advance its ballistic missile industries, we will be there. We will take action, and we will strike.”

The Israeli military, meanwhile, launched airstrikes on Sunday that hit Gaza for a second straight day, killing at least 18 Palestinians, medics said, despite Trump’s announcement of a breakthrough in efforts to implement last year’s ceasefire.

Israeli warplanes hit Gaza City in the north, the central ⁠city of Deir al-Balah and the ⁠southern area of Khan Younis, causing the biggest ​daily death toll in weeks, according to Palestinian health officials.

Trump’s assertion that Hamas militants had agreed to disarm had raised hopes of a turning point.

But on Sunday Cohen said Israel would give Hamas the opportunity to disarm but he was “very sceptical” that would happen.

Tehran warned this weekend against any “adventurous action” by the US and said it ⁠would retaliate decisively. The comments by Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, in separate phone calls on Saturday with senior Turkish, Pakistani and Saudi officials came just hours after Kuwait’s army said it had destroyed hostile ⁠drones launched by Iran against several vital facilities.

A government facility in northern Kuwait and civilian property belonging to a company ​on Bubiyan Island were hit, with falling ​shrapnel causing material damage but no casualties, the Kuwaiti ​army said.

Araghchi told regional counterparts that any attacks by the US and ​Israel or participation by regional countries in such actions would be ‌met with a “proportionate response”. Nournews, a ‌media outlet affiliated with Iran’s top security body, said on Saturday that US attacks on Iranian energy infrastructure would prompt Iranian strikes on oilfields in Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, as well as the gasfields of Qatar and Israel.

The developments appeared to have given Trump pause for thought, as he posted on Saturday night in characteristically grandiose language that “the USA is locked and loaded” to strike Iran with “military terror, strength, and power not seen since World War II”.

Richard E Grant’s Very Modern Odyssey review – far more thrilling than the Christopher Nolan borefest

The Guardian Sun, 02 Aug 2026 20:00:30 GMT

The actor gobbles up food, roars with glee and finds himself deeply moved in this four-part travelogue inspired by the journey of Homer’s hero. It’s a real success of a show

Here comes Richard E Grant, pounding towards us in his tiny leather jacket as he gesticulates wildly at his cobbled surrounds. “Wow,” he gasps. “Look at that.” We look at that. It’s Malta. Specifically, Malta’s Grand Harbour: a sobbingly beautiful gateway to the Mediterranean and the sun-blessed starting line for Richard E Grant’s Very Modern Odyssey, a four-part travelogue “inspired by Homer’s hero” in which the veteran actor traces Odysseus’s “incredible journey” while wearing a succession of increasingly voluminous linen trousers.

Said tracing is not, however, an exact science. This is not one of those awful celebrity things in which our noble hero arms himself with set squares and a scholastic scowl before setting sail on a “voyage” to uncover “the truth”.

Nor is it an attempt to contribute to the seemingly interminable Odyssey discourse – the ongoing hoo-ha over the historical accuracy of the Christopher Nolan blockbuster that already feels as if it’s lasted longer than the Trojan war.

Instead, it’s a loose-limbed, easygoing thing that attempts to separate Homeric myth from reality but appears equally “chill” with the fact that much of it remains fundamentally unknowable. “Essentially,” says Grant, grinning hugely, “we’re dealing with an act of the imagination.”

So here we are in the Maltese capital of Valletta, which doesn’t appear to have featured on Odysseus’s itinerary, but does have a Michelin-starred restaurant that serves butter-basted pigeon with sage and rosemary. Grant is cock-a-hoop. “Mmm,” he shouts while frantically licking his plate, much as the Greeks “licked” the Trojans after the siege of Troy.

This is followed by a brief stop at the luxurious Phoenecia hotel for a lime mocktail and some wistful reminiscing about Malta’s colonial past (“this was Queen Elizabeth’s favourite hangout!”), before it’s off for a gander at Valletta’s perfectly extraordinary St John’s Co-Cathedral.

“I’ve never seen anything like this in my life,” splutters our host, drifting through the nave open-mouthed as he takes in its baroque tumult of golden whorls and thunderstruck cherubim. “Honestly, it out-Sistines the Sistine Chapel.” And it does. Built by the Order of St John in the 16th century, it’s a frantic masterpiece of death and glory, its ornate marble floor housing the tombs of 400 “warrior knights”.

“In Homer’s world,” says Grant, “heroes make a sacrifice to the gods every time they sail into danger. Here, the ritual was different, but the idea was the same: ask for help before you do something terrifying.”

The actor is moved. “I’m not a religious man,” he tells us later, chin smushed into his enormous brown neckerchief. “But going inside that jewel of a church was one of the most beautiful experiences I’ve ever had.”

Here, there are epiphanies around every corner. Valletta’s Lurpak-coloured stonework is “a revelation”. The cave on the Maltese island of Gozo that may or may not have been the inspiration for the home of the saucy nymph Calypso leaves him “nearly in tears”.

“I’m utterly bewitched by every detail,” he roars at one point. He is a one-man brass section of patrician glee.

These days, we note, there is a slight fuzziness to Grant’s barrel-aged boom, as if his vowels had rolled under a chaise longue and been left to gather a fine layer of fluff. When he reads extracts from Homer’s poem in the ruins of an amphitheatre, he sounds both wearily thrilled and knackered, like a kindly oak tree completing a particularly taxing parkrun.

The opening episode concludes with a visit to the bronze age ruins of Troy. This was “almost certainly” the site of “a real, bloody war”.

More vagueness. But it’s all to the good. Homer’s gargantuan tale of Mediterranean aggro remains powerfully relevant, says a local historian. “Refugees, climate change, political crisis – all of these things you find in The Odyssey.”

Another huge grin from Grant. “It seems Homer blurred fact and fiction into a story that has lasted over two and a half thousand years,” he trumpets. “A success by any measure.” As, indeed, is Grant’s own Very Modern Odyssey.

Lime mocktails all round.

Richard E Grant’s Very Modern Odyssey is on Channel 4 now.

Pressure on Gianni Infantino increases as Uefa members prepare to oppose re-election

The Guardian Sun, 02 Aug 2026 19:36:26 GMT

European nations to withdraw letters of support for Fifa president

Appetite to ensure Infantino is quickly removed from post

European countries are planning to increase the pressure on Gianni Infantino with a mass withdrawal of letters supporting his re-election as Fifa president.

Infantino’s reign is in severe peril after the collapse of his privately backed scheme to sell off chunks of the World Cup, which was largely scuppered when Uefa member associations threatened to boycott future Fifa competitions. The mood remains febrile and there is a widespread appetite around Europe to ensure that he is quickly removed from his post.

Now a groundswell of national governing bodies are discussing the formal withdrawal of their support for Infantino in a bid to hasten his resignation, with announcements likely in the coming days. Before last week’s crisis unfolded all of Uefa’s 55 members apart from Germany, Romania and Norway had written letters to endorse Infantino’s candidature next March, with a fourth term for the Swiss viewed as a fait accompli.

A simultaneous withdrawal has been mooted but there is also the possibility member associations could remove their backing one by one. Doing so would effectively amount to a vote of no confidence and increase the pressure on Infantino to resign. Fifa must be notified by any country wishing to recall their letter.

Discussions continue with countries in other confederations. Despite the failure of his Fifa Forward Enterprise proposal, a number of countries in the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) publicly backed Infantino over the weekend. Sources within European football have questioned whether those federations have been made fully aware of the level of ­dissent facing Infantino.

After the financial powerhouse of Qatar backed Infantino on Saturday, smaller Asian associations Sri Lanka and Kuwait offered their public ­support on Sunday. The AFC rarely votes en masse however, and it is possible that some associations unhappy with Infantino could rally to the European cause.

As the Guardian revealed in July, more than 200 of Fifa’s 211 members have provided letters of endorsement for Infantino. Fifa is understood to have applied heavy pressure upon those wavering even though his tenure did not appear endangered at the time. Many backed him despite privately offering misgivings about his presidency but, in Europe and beyond, patience has run out.

Efforts to identify a candidate to replace Infantino are being stepped up. Anyone put forward for the election would require significant levels of support outside Europe, particularly from the AFC and the North and Central American and Caribbean confederation, Concacaf. Gathering quickly around a suitable contender could be key to persuading Infantino that his position is untenable.

The Guardian Sun, 02 Aug 2026 19:06:21 GMT

Australia dominate Games with 171 medals, 70 gold

The Welsh cyclist Emma Finucane wrote her name into the history books on the final day of the Commonwealth Games, but Glasgow 2026 will be remembered most for Australia’s dominance.

Before the Games, the Australia swimmer Sam Short had told reporters: “I’m so pumped – I can’t wait to go over there and smash those Pommies up.” And the whole Australia team seemed to get the memo as they finished with 171 medals, of them 70 gold. That put them a staggering 61 clear of England, who won 110 medals, with Canada third after winning 62.

Despite the medal gap to Australia, Team England chef de mission, Jonathon Riall, issued a bullish assessment of the performance. “To finish the Games with 110 medals and second place on the medal table is an incredible achievement, one that every athlete, coach, support staff member and national governing body should be immensely proud of,” he said.

“For Team England, success is about more than medals. It can mean achieving a lifetime best, overcoming adversity simply to reach the start line, or standing on the podium with a medal around your neck. We have seen all those different ways of winning throughout these Games.

“We won medals across nine sports, saw established champions deliver once again on the biggest stage and watched a new generation announce themselves on the Commonwealth stage. This team has embodied everything Team England stands for, and it has been an immense privilege to lead them.”

Finucane will certainly go down as one of the athletes of the Games after becoming the first sprint cyclist to win four track gold medals at the same Commonwealth Games.

The Welsh cyclist added to the golds she had already won in the team and individual sprints and 1,000m time trial, with a bravuro victory in the keirin.

Finucane, who won Olympic gold as part of the Great Britain sprint team at Paris 2024, moved to the front with two laps to go, daring others to get past her. None of them could as she won by half a bike length ahead of the Olympic champion, Ellesse Andrews of New Zealand.

“I was convinced they would come round me,” admitted Finucane. “Honestly it is hard to put into words. I could have easily gone out in the semis.

“After Paris, everything was a huge learning curve for me emotionally,” she added. “That week was really tough, and what I came away with was hard to process. But going into these Games I’ve learned to handle pressure better and regulate my emotions more.”

Finucane now plans to take a holiday with her sister before shifting her focus towards the track world championships in Shanghai in October.

“I definitely did feel the pressure but throughout the week I just rode my own race,” she added. “The team sprint was a big aim. The last time we rode it was four years ago and we got a bronze medal.

“To come back as the same team and win gold was iconic. Singing on the podium with the team was insane. I just rode each race as it came. I went out there and left everything on the track. To stand here and have four golds, I have no words.

She added: “I don’t think I’ll ever believe that I’ve made history here. I can’t believe little me has done this. Ten-year-old Emma is screaming inside, like, ‘What is going on?’ I hope I’ve inspired the nation to get on to a bike and get into a velodrome. I can’t believe I found this sport and this sport found me.”

Earlier on the last day, Leigh Hoffman became the first Australian cyclist to win four medals at one Games by winning the 1km men’s time trial, ensuring he took home three gold and one silver.

And there was more success for Australia in the para bowls as 76-year-old Louise Hoskins became the oldest athlete to win gold in Glasgow.

Hoskins and her partner, Serena Bonnell, secured a 6-3, 4-4 win, leaving Hoskins delighted. “It is incredible. I’m still pinching myself,” she said. “I never thought I’d ever get gold at my age. Get out there and have a go, and never give up.”

Elsewhere Jamaica fell short of pulling off another epic Commonwealth Games upset as they went down 56-48 to New Zealand in the women’s netball final. However England missed out on bronze after being thrashed 68-50 by Australia, who recovered from a shock one-point defeat to Jamaica on Saturday.

“Fourth place is agonising,” admitted the England captain, Fran Williams. “It’s the position nobody really wants to finish in when you’re just outside the medals. We just weren’t clinical enough today, and credit has to go to the Diamonds.

The normal hours [of testing] are not in the night,” said the head of cycling’s governing body.

“However, we support the ITA if they have to do some specific test, because we know that, with micro-dosing EPO, that’s something you can’t detect six or seven hours after. So, for the riders to know that the ITA may come, that’s always a fear.

“We always have suspicion in cycling, due to our past. I know what has been done to fight against doping. Night testing is a tool in this fight, but it is not a tool to use every day. You must use it very exceptionally. It’s not suspicion about any rider, but it’s a global message to the bunch.”

Lappartient is an International Olympic Committee member alongside the besieged Fifa president, Gianni Infantino, and was re-elected UCI president unopposed for a third term in September last year. He believes involving stakeholders is key to successful reform of sports governance. “I will not interfere in Fifa’s matters, but I can tell you that in the UCI transparency is important,” Lappartient said.

“When we want to make a reform of professional cycling, we will first make a presentation to the teams, the riders and the organisers. We have consultation with the stakeholders.

“I will not give advice to Fifa, but I think it’s important to work with this kind of transparency.”

Ross, who had strong links with the charity sector in Greece, is the daughter of a prominent lawyer in Edinburgh, where she also lived.

She was reported to have friends in Kypseli, where her body was discovered on 18 July by a homeless man in what had once been a car park. Wrapped in cloth, it had been placed in a suitcase left in a decrepit, rubbish-strewn building at the site.

Sources told the Guardian that the suspect’s alleged use of credit cards that belonged to Ross had contributed to police identifying him.

Police had described text messages sent to her father and other members of her family as deliberately misleading. The messages had spoken of her “need to be alone”.

“As confirmed, the victim arrived in the country on June 26 and stayed at the home of friends until July 10, from where she departed to an unknown [address],” the police statement said.

The homicide division said it had made the announcement after amassing evidence that proved the Afghan had “placed the body in the case and carried it to the abandoned car park” in Kypseli.

Analysis of CCTV footage had played a role.

“The subsequent preliminary investigation … using investigative material and digital analysis of video footage, proved the involvement of the 26-year-old foreign national in the incident. [He] was brought in [for questioning] on 30 July and confessed to his actions,” the statement said.

It remains unknown how Ross died. Media reports quoted the suspect as telling police that when he visited the flat in Exarchia he had discovered her lifeless body in the bathroom.

The Dutch sprinter Lorena Wiebes took her second win in this year’s Tour de France Femmes in Geneva, further extending her overall lead in the nine-day race. Wiebes is proving untouchable in the sprint finishes and her turn of speed in the final 250 metres, on the lakeside finish of the Quai du Mont-Blanc, reduced her rivals to onlookers.

But as the kilometres clicked down, the peloton clawed its way back, eclipsing Markus in the last 500 metres, before Wiebes made her inevitable surge to take yet another sprint win.

“The girls were chasing full gas to bring back Riejanne,” Wiebes said of her teammates. “It’s even more beautiful to finish it off in yellow.” She now leads the Tour overall by 14 seconds from Kim Le Court and by 16 seconds from the 2023 winner, Demi Vollering.

There is no indication that either Wiebes or her SD Worx Protime team intend to back down from their threat of legal action over what they consider to be a flawed weighing process, conducted in a gusting wind.

After her stage win in Lausanne on the opening day, Wiebes’ team manager, Erwin Janssen, made sure there was no repeat of the Giro debacle.

“I wanted to see how it all worked, how they actually did it,” he told the media at the start of stage two in Aigle. “I took some videos of the process. There was a four-person jury, and the whole setup was fairly enclosed. It took place in a tent, so there was no wind, and the installation looked solid. One of the four was someone who had handled the weigh-ins at the Giro. I think even he was feeling a bit nervous.”

Wiebes’ bike, Janssen said, came in within the rules at “a solid seven kilos”. “I could really sense a certain tension among the jury. I got the impression they were thinking, ‘I hope everything goes smoothly.’ Everything was recorded, and then you get a brief report,” he said. “If you agree with it, you have to sign it.”

But Janssen said that neither he nor any of his staff had signed ­paperwork at the Giro. “Our lawyers are currently exchanging questions with the other side, including questions about the procedure. We’ve received answers, but they’re too vague. There will be further developments on that front in the coming months.”

Janssen insisted that Wiebes was “unfairly expelled from the Giro” and that the Tour de France leader suffered both financial and reputational losses. “The stakes are incredibly high. Lorena could have secured three, perhaps even four, [stage] victories there. We are looking into whether we can be compensated for this. We have sponsorship contracts stipulating financial bonuses for achieving specific results – bonuses we missed out on because of this incident.”

Janssen insisted that the issue will be resolved, but through “a court case or arbitration” and added that “we expect that to happen”.

Last Wednesday was the busiest day for small boat crossings across the Channel so far this year, with 752 people arriving in the UK. I want them to change their mind about whether they get on the boat in the first place.”

She rejected calls to copy Spain’s response to the influx into Ceuta, in which tens of thousands of people have been returned to Morocco without processing any asylum claims. That was possible because Morocco and Spain share a land border and have an agreement in place. Mahmood said people smuggling and the shared waters of the Channel made things “trickier in many ways”.

Two firefighting helicopters have collided west of Athens, killing the two-person crew of one of the aircraft, as efforts to control a massive wildfire barrelling towards the outskirts of the Greek capital intensified.

Footage showed one of the helicopters losing control in the face of gale-force winds that have pushed flames towards settlements on Athens’ western fringes.

“The pilots … were taken unconscious to hospital, where their death was confirmed,” said the fire department’s director of communications, Vassilis Vathrakogiannis.

The Greek prime minister, Kyriakos Mitsotakis said the two dead were a Dane and a Greek. The two crew members of the second helicopter were rescued.

The helicopters had been leased from Australia’s McDermott Aviation, part of a fleet of 15. The company has said it has supported operations in Greece for the past seven years.

As Europe’s wildfire crisis fractured along different routes, and in further proof of the destructive force of climate-driven wildfires across the continent, the blazes ripped through Greece’s tinder-dry landscape, up mountain slopes and down to the sea, before encroaching on the capital.

Warning of “extremely difficult” days ahead, Mitsotakis underlined the threat posed by gusts that in recent days have exceeded 78mph (125km/h).

“When the winds blow with such force, even the dozens of aircraft we have at our disposal cannot operate safely,” he wrote on social media.

More than 100 homes were destroyed overnight in fires that broke out around the popular coastal village of Porto Germeno, about 45 miles (70km) north-west of Athens. By Sunday, more than 500 firefighters and forest commandos had been dispatched to keep the flames at bay.

The eastern Mediterranean, no stranger to wildfires, has had a relatively calm summer to date, leaving Greeks to watch in horror as the blazes have hit farther west.

As the advance of wildfires in Spain was finally curbed and officials in France announced that a mega-fire – four times the size of Paris – had begun to be contained, the blazes in Greece have prompted mass evacuations and devastated huge swathes of land from Crete to the southern Peloponnese, the Ionian isle of Cephalonia and islands across the Aegean.

Last week three Greek firefighters died from injuries sustained while they fought blazes.

Extreme winds have been a blessing – in bringing down summer temperatures – but also a curse, with their-gale force strength obstructing firefighting efforts.

Greece’s civil protection minister, Evangelos Tournas, a retired air force general, said at the weekend that the fire department had been “pushed to its limits”. He said high winds had created “extremely difficult conditions resulting in many cases where aircraft either cannot draw water or cannot carry out drops due to extreme turbulence”.

France’s largest wildfire remained contained after 224,000 people were forced to flee in what may have been the largest peacetime evacuation in French history. But active pockets still burned across 160 sq miles (420 sq km) of devastated forest.

Thousands remained unable to return home, and nearly 3,000 firefighters were deployed against the Gironde mega-fire and a second blaze in Provence that had stopped advancing but remained uncontained.

“The fire is now fixed, which does not mean that the fire is extinguished,” the Gironde prefecture said on Sunday, using the French firefighting term for a blaze whose advance has been stopped and whose perimeter has been contained.

The region remained under France’s highest red forest fire alert. Dry conditions and soaring temperatures around Bordeaux, combined with afternoon winds, created a continued risk of renewed flames.

Additional firefighters from Ukraine, Lithuania and French Polynesia were expected on Sunday and Monday to reinforce the operation.

Firefighting aircraft supported crews working to keep the flames away from villages among the vineyards, olive groves and wooded hills of the region known as Green Provence. About 2,500 people were evacuated as the fire threatened communities.

The blaze was the fourth major fire to strike the central Var since 19 July. A separate, smaller fire near Brignoles earlier in the week forced the Hollywood actor George Clooney and his family, along with about 700 other residents, to evacuate before it was brought under control.

The prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, said France’s wildfires were generally under control but cautioned that conditions remained highly changeable.

He announced that a national coordinator attached to the prime minister’s office would oversee reconstruction in fire-ravaged areas. More than 450 sq miles have burned across France since the beginning of the year.

Fires in France and Spain alone have driven roughly a third of a million people from homes and holiday sites, emptied communities at the height of the summer and stretched firefighters, aircraft and emergency services across simultaneous disasters.

The crisis is unfolding on the world’s fastest-warming continent. Europe has heated at more than twice the global average since the 1980s, according to the EU’s Copernicus Climate Change Service.

Higher temperatures and prolonged drought leave forests and scrubland drier and more combustible, allowing fires to spread faster and burn more intensely. Human-caused climate breakdown doubled the likelihood of the extreme fire conditions that fuelled the French blazes, scientists at World Weather Attribution calculated in a rapid analysis on Thursday while the fires were still burning.

A 35-year-old stuntwoman is one of the great unsung heroes of Christopher Nolan’s new blockbuster The Odyssey – standing in for Matt Damon and displaying what the actor called “the greatest arms I’ve ever seen”.

Canadian Devyn Dalton was the Hollywood star’s stunt double in a pivotal scene in the film where Odysseus (Damon) and his men are confronted by the Laestrygonians, giant armoured cannibals.

In order to make Damon and his crew appear dwarfed by the group of goliaths, the actors doing stunts needed to be small. Dalton is 4ft 6in (137cm) and her rippling, muscular arms were perfect to represent Damon’s own biceps.

Dalton has “the greatest arms I’ve ever seen”, said Damon, speaking to podcaster Josh Horowitz on his show Happy Sad Confused.

“Knowing my arms impressed Matt was honestly pretty special,” Dalton told the Guardian. “His shoutout in the press completely caught me by surprise … I’ll always appreciate that he did.”

Dalton said she had known she wanted to tell stories since she was a child, inventing characters and costumes and putting on shows for her family.

She started out acting professionally at nine years old, which gradually led her into stunt performing – a different way of telling those tales: through the body, through her own strength.

“We celebrate men who build careers around being powerful … so why shouldn’t women be celebrated for that too?” she said.

After Damon made the comments in his press tour for The Odyssey, the big-screen depiction of Homer’s epic Greek poem that has become a huge hit for Nolan and sparked endless media coverage, Dalton said her phone “absolutely exploded”.

She is currently filming a project in New Zealand and was not expecting to receive global attention.

“Apparently my biceps have their own fanclub right now, which definitely wasn’t on my 2026 prediction,” she said.

She said she was cast in the role through the network of professional representatives and stunt coordinators rather than any open casting call.

“When I found out I booked it, I was genuinely so excited and incredibly grateful. It’s one of those moments where years of hard work and persistence suddenly feels worthwhile,” she said.

Dalton flew to Scotland to film and she said it was a continuous reminder of just how many people it takes to put together a production like The Odyssey. “What audiences see for a few minutes often represents months of preparation,” she said.

“Those other countries around the world that we currently rely on to produce our food and vegetables, their climates are changing as well,” he said. “It does feel like there is going be some shortages of [food] products.”

Climate breakdown is exacerbating extreme weather conditions such as droughts. This summer the Met Office has reported that England had just 8% of its average rainfall for July and it is likely to be confirmed as the driest July on record.

About 23 million people across England and Wales are under a hosepipe ban. The dry weather has fuelled devastating wildfires across the country, most recently in Suffolk.

UKHSA has issued amber heat health alerts for the East Midlands, the east of England, the south-east and London regions from 9am on Monday to 9am on Wednesday. The north-west, Yorkshire and the Humber, West Midlands and the south-west regions will be under a yellow alert during the same period.

Bradshaw said: “Let’s draw a line in the sand and make sure we prioritise domestic food production to deliver growth across the UK.”

Cereals such as wheat and barley have been particularly affected, the Agriculture and Horticulture Development Board (AHDB) said.

Its first harvest report of 2026 said the hot weather had resulted in the earliest harvest since records began in 2006, with many farmers across the south and east of England completing harvest two to three weeks ahead of the long-term average.

Anthony Hopkins, the AHDB’s director of cereals and oilseeds, said: “Across much of the UK, combines have been rolling earlier than usual this year, with many farmers working through the night to avoid the most extreme daytime temperatures. Cereal yields have generally been below the 10-year average so far, with some farms experiencing significant reductions. Following successive years of difficult weather and rising costs, the financial pressures are becoming increasingly acute for those businesses hardest hit.”

Anthony Speight, a senior analyst at the AHDB, said: “At this stage, the emerging picture points to disappointing cereal yields in many areas, but we’ll gain a clearer understanding as harvest continues.”

Farming is becoming unprofitable as the government removes the EU-derived subsidies that once kept the industry afloat and the climate crisis causes extreme weather that can wipe out any profits from crops. A recent report found a third of British farmers were making a loss or only breaking even.

Gavin Lane, the president of the Country, Land and Business Association, warned that for many farmers this could be their last harvest.

He said: “Farmers are telling us this is the worst harvest in years. A sodden winter followed by drought has left wheat at half its usual height and some crops not worth harvesting.

“This is the third drought in five years. What was once extraordinary is becoming part of farming in Britain, and government must start planning for it. We know that proper government investment in resilient farming systems, from reservoirs to wildfire prevention, could help farmers cope with these new extremes.

“Farmers have shown again and again that they can adapt and deliver solutions, but resilience has limits. If we want them to keep feeding the country, they need proper support. Otherwise, this harvest could be their last.”

Polly Ashmore, an acting consultant in public health at the UKHSA, said periods of hot weather could result in serious health outcomes, especially for older adults, and it was therefore important that everyone took sensible precautions while enjoying the sun.

“We are urging health and social care services in affected regions to ensure they are prepared, and reminding people to look out for elderly relatives, neighbours and those with underlying health conditions, making sure they are aware of the forecast and following the necessary advice,” she said.

“Simple steps such as staying hydrated, avoiding the sun during the hottest part of the day and keeping your home cool are some of the key ways to help keep yourself and others safe during periods of hot weather.”

The Guardian view on drought: hot, dry conditions make inequality starker

The Guardian Sun, 02 Aug 2026 16:30:25 GMT

Water is a vital shared resource, and privatisation has made a just transition harder

Compared with rising heat-related deaths, and devastating wildfires in the Cairngorms and Suffolk, the announcement that the Royal Horticultural Society (RHS) is considering moving its hydrangea collection from Surrey to Greater Manchester and North Yorkshire might seem unimportant. But it points to geographical differences in exposure to global heating that have arguably never been more evident than this summer, with last month the driest on record. Seven areas of south and east England are officially in drought, along with the whole of Wales.

A drought is less easily measured than a heatwave, which is declared by the Met Office when the maximum temperature exceeds a set threshold on three consecutive days. But the fact that drought is harder to quantify does not make it less damaging. Water shortages are exposing specific vulnerabilities and inequalities, as well as the UK’s lack of preparedness for climate change overall.

Some of the unfairnesses revealed in recent weeks are shocking in their predictability. Exemptions that allow golf courses and schools with large sports grounds to water lawns, when councils and householders are banned from doing so, have led to justifiable anger. But while the insulation of elites from hardship is nothing new, the heightened impact of such patterns in extreme weather requires attention. Privileges such as guaranteed water for golf courses cannot survive a drought. People whose housing, jobs or health make them vulnerable must be shielded.

Andy Burnham has yet to set out his plans for greater public control of water companies. Nationalisation of Thames Water remains a welcome possibility. But it is vital that this industry’s role in exacerbating scarcity and injustice is addressed. Its bosses and shareholders are not solely to blame. The decision to privatise the water industry was taken by a Conservative government, while regulators bear responsibility for chronically weak oversight, particularly of Thames Water, which has been staving off collapse for years. But the extraction of billions of pounds of profits by businesses set up as regional monopolies, while infrastructure including wastewater treatment and storage was neglected, and debts piled up, has been a disgraceful failure. Drought conditions reveal how dangerous this is, since when people are asked to make sacrifices, it is vital that they have a sense of shared responsibility towards a common good.

At least new reservoirs, which store water gathered in winter for use in the summer, are on the way. After three decades during which no major ones were added, the industry has pledged to build 10, with two in the dry east of England given priority status. But questions remain over the viability of plans to build thousands of new homes in drought-prone areas, and the difficulties faced by farmers, who want it to be made easier to build reservoirs specifically for use on their crops. Water recycling and conservation efforts are also far behind where they should be, with household water use in England and Wales among the highest in Europe.

With the climate in the south of England increasingly resembling that of the Mediterranean, those able to move may increasingly look north – following the RHS’s hydrangeas. Global heating will reinforce old patterns of inequality, but it will also create new ones. Societies and governments must prepare for both. This summer’s drought makes it clear how urgent this is.
