The Guardian view on global corporate tax: a $500bn prize that states must seize

The Guardian Sun, 02 Aug 2026 16:25:25 GMT

Donald Trump may reject the negotiations, but he cannot veto a global effort to make multinational companies answer to governments

Governments are told that public services must shrink because money is tight. Yet a new Tax Justice Network report says that countries could capture an extra $500bn a year without raising corporate tax rates. The answer is to tax multinational profits where real economic activity happens – known as unitary taxation. No new profit is created. Revenue simply shifts from tax havens where profits are “booked” to the countries where workers produce and customers spend.

Making that principle a global tax standard depends on UN talks opening in New York on Monday. Modelled on the UN climate regime, a fiscal framework convention would create the governing body and procedures, with protocols providing detailed rules. The UN wants agreement by late 2027. Donald Trump’s US walked out last year and urged others to follow. None did.

Rich countries gain most when firms pay tax where people work, not where profits vanish in havens, because their economies are the largest. Britain would collect about £13bn extra a year in tax receipts – two‑thirds of the cost of an NHS-style social care system. EU governments could raise enough to quadruple climate-adaptation spending. Poorer countries also benefit. The report calculates that the global south would receive $156bn in one year – more than the International Monetary Fund has outstanding in loans to those nations.

For the first time in decades, multinationals could be taxed where they actually do business. Rules built for the corporate world of the 1920s – when national industrial giants dominated – would finally confront today’s companies organised around intangible assets and global supply chains, as well as profits of an altogether different scale. In 1929, General Motors made the equivalent of $4.7bn. Apple’s profit last year was $112bn. What the report calls “diversified” tax havens such as Switzerland and the Netherlands could offset losses by raising rates. Pure booking centres such as the Cayman Islands could not.

The talks suggest states are beginning to reclaim powers surrendered under globalisation to corporate lawyers and private tribunals. One protocol would let countries tax digital and other cross-border services without waiting for firms to establish domestic offices, blunting Mr Trump’s trade threats. A second could go further, shifting tax disputes from secretive investor-state arbitration into a more open, publicly accountable UN-led system.

The direction is unmistakable. Ireland, which is facing an estimated $11bn annual tax loss, has already begun putting aside part of its “windfall corporate tax receipts” in a new fund – an admission that the revenue won’t last. India and Nigeria have legislated so that companies profiting from their economies should not escape the tax net just because they operate across borders.

Britain has belatedly backed a UN-led shift towards taxing real activity. Defending rules entwined with its offshore network was politically indefensible and economically perverse. The US can sit out the negotiations, but it cannot shield American companies from others’ rules. The success of these talks has largely been down to African nations insisting on consensus where possible and majority rule where necessary. That denies the US and any rich-country bloc an effective veto. Backed by India, Brazil and other developing powers, an African-led coalition can now press a simple claim: countries should be free to tax value created within their economies. Britain should help them prevail.

India’s gen Z have discovered the power of collective action

The Guardian Sun, 02 Aug 2026 16:12:41 GMT

The recent Cockroach Janta party protests had widespread support, says Bhaskar Mani. Plus a letter from Nand Lal Rathore

A crucial point that your editorial on India’s gen Z protests (28 July) missed out was that the protests the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) launched in Delhi, hunger strikes and all, were not just supported by young, restless or unemployed people. It was wholeheartedly supported by their parents and grandparents, the old and the middle-aged, even well-off young adults with good jobs and little children. And this was not just in Delhi, but across the country in the huge metropolises of Mumbai, Kolkata, Chennai and Bengaluru, as well as smaller towns. And it was all peaceful, for which credit goes to the ethos of the protests and the CJP.

All of this was suppressed in the mainstream media, print and TV, and even distorted to suggest that it was violent in parts. This reflects not just the overwhelming angst and fear of young graduates facing poor prospects, but the significant grievances of a people who are seeing and experiencing their democracy fading away. Bhaskar ManiBengaluru, India

Your editorial captures an important truth: movements that begin with a single grievance often evolve into broader demands for justice, accountability and democratic reform. India’s gen Z protests are not simply about leaked exam papers; they reflect a generation’s frustration with institutions that have failed to protect merit and opportunity.

I could not help thinking about Pakistan. Here, too, students, jobseekers and marginalised communities have long expressed concerns about governance and access to justice. Yet these struggles rarely transform into sustained, nationwide civic movements. Local protests often remain isolated and receive limited attention or fail to generate the solidarity required for lasting institutional reform.

Whether in India or Pakistan, young people deserve institutions they can trust, exams they can believe in and public systems that reward merit rather than connections. The significance of India’s movement lies not only in political consequences but in the emergence of a generation that has discovered the power of peaceful collective action. Its long-term impact will depend on whether that energy strengthens democratic institutions rather than deepening divisions.

Nand Lal RathoreChachro, Sindh province, Pakistan

The monthly scourge of ‘period poop’ is real. Here’s why your gut acts up

The Guardian Sun, 02 Aug 2026 16:00:25 GMT

Menstrual and digestive discomfort often coincide, and a researcher who has been looking in to it for a decade tells us what she learned

Every period, right on schedule: the cramps arrive, and right behind them, the urgent need to poop.

If this is your experience, you’re in good company: in one study, 73% of healthy premenopausal women reported at least one significant gastrointestinal symptom in the days before or during their period. Abdominal pain and diarrhea were the most common complaints, but women reported nausea and constipation too.

Menstrual and digestive discomfort often coincide: “If you ask women about ‘period poops’ they’ll tell you they’re having menstrual cramps and those GI cramps at the same time,” said Taylor Judkins, a nutrition researcher at the University of Florida who has spent more than a decade studying the phenomenon.

Period-related GI symptoms are common enough to have their own moniker. The science, however, has barely kept up. Judkins has personal experience with the phenomenon; when she first went looking for research on the phenomenon as a university student, she found almost nothing. A decade later, she says, there’s still a lot to learn.

It all starts with the uterus. As your period approaches, levels of estrogen and progesterone fall sharply. That’s the signal for your body to start breaking down the uterine lining, which you start shedding on day one of your period.

At the same time, cells in the uterus start making hormone-like compounds called prostaglandins. These cause contractions in the type of muscle cells that make up most of your uterus and digestive tract, among other effects.

It’s unclear exactly what happens next. But the leading theory, said Judkins, is that some prostaglandins enter the bloodstream from the uterus and stimulate similar contractions in the neighboring gut. This would explain the intestinal cramping and diarrhea many experience alongside menstrual cramping, especially on the first day or two of their periods.

One other theory relates to the vagus nerve, which runs signals between the gut and the brain. This neural pathway is highly sensitive to stress signals and inflammation. When activated, it provokes fluid release within the gut and increased contractions of its muscles, leading to diarrhea. This is why some experts believe many people get an upset stomach when they’re anxious. Judkins theorizes that menstruation may also trigger the pathway.

Many women also note constipation one to two weeks before their periods start, says Judkins, which may be a consequence of high progesterone levels. However, the evidence is less clear on the prevalence and timing of that symptom.

People with irritable bowel syndrome and inflammatory bowel disease tend to have significantly worse symptoms around their periods, and those with endometriosis typically carry a higher burden of GI symptoms overall. But you don’t need an underlying diagnosis to have period poops.

“It’s very common, and some will tell you that it’s normal,” she says, “but it doesn’t mean you should have to live with this drastic decrease in your quality of life.”

Options exist, but none are a clear fix.

Judkins and her team ran the only randomized trial to date testing the effects of probiotics on menstrual GI symptoms. Probiotics improved indigestion – but not diarrhea, the symptom most people are actually trying to solve.

Sign up to Well Actually

Practical advice, expert insights and answers to your questions about how to live a good life

after newsletter promotion

Some experts recommend oral contraceptives on a theoretical basis: they reduce the amount of endometrial tissue your body makes, which should lead to less prostaglandin production when that tissue gets shed. However, there’s no good evidence suggesting they are effective for GI symptoms; one of Judkins’ studies that exclusively enrolled women taking oral contraceptives found they also reported period poops.

Anti-inflammatory drugs such as ibuprofen and naproxen reduce prostaglandin production, which can ease both uterine and digestive-tract cramps. The catch: they can irritate the gut lining and actually cause diarrhea, and for anyone with Crohn’s disease or ulcerative colitis, they can worsen symptoms and should generally be avoided.

For now, diet is your most practical starting point. Judkins recommends staying hydrated and eating more fiber – fruit, vegetables, whole grains, legumes — and less greasy comfort foods, which tend to worsen diarrhea. Exercise helps some people; the data aren’t robust, but the risk is low. And if symptoms are severe enough to affect work or daily life, that’s worth raising with a doctor.

Judkins began studying period gut over a decade ago. “When you search these keywords, it’s my name that comes up,” she says.

That’s not a triumphant statement. It reflects a research culture that has treated menstrual health as a niche concern rather than an important issue affecting roughly half the population.

When researchers don’t study something, clinicians are less likely to treat it. Patients are also less likely to raise it, because nobody has signaled that it’s worth mentioning or that anything can be done. Judkins hopes that changes. “Funding for women’s health research is ultimately a gain for everybody,” she says.

Instead, they are relegated to a “stifling” basement space with broken furniture, continuing problems with rodents and no natural light or air-conditioning.

Staff liken it to Upstairs, Downstairs, the television drama series that explored class relations in Edwardian England.

The curator, who wished to remain anonymous, told the Guardian: “It’s almost become a running joke within the National Gallery. Security staff are being treated like second-class citizens.”

The insider said gallery employees – everyone from curators to marketing staff – used the hub, which was created in previously underused spaces between and beneath the gallery’s exhibition halls, while outsourced security staff were prevented from doing so.

While the hub has a heavily subsidised canteen and its own chef, the basement space is described as “dingy, dirty and dark”, with a kiosk offering little more than a KitKat and no cooked food.

“It wasn’t meant for people,” the curator said. “It was meant for storage.”

The National Gallery has reportedly told them that restricting the hub access is about avoiding overcrowding, but the security staff are still barred during weekends and holidays, when there are virtually no National Gallery employees using it.

The curator added that on any one day there were perhaps 60 guards on site, but barely a handful took their break at the same time. “So the argument that the hub’s overcrowded is probably pushing it a bit,” the curator said.

Security staff are represented by the PCS union, which believes they are being treated with “absolute contempt”, warning of the basement space: “Most dangerously, it is unventilated and accessible only by ducking under pipes.”

Security staff are also said to feel the gallery is putting the collection at risk in expecting an individual guard to cover as many as four rooms at once.

One observer said guards could only be in one room at a time and it was easy to distract them. Incidents in recent years have included activists from Just Stop Oil hurling tomato soup over Van Gogh’s Sunflowers and attacking Velázquez’s Rokeby Venus with hammers.

Kindness of strangers: Lost in the Thai rainforest, a fellow backpacker picked me up and carried me home

The Guardian Sun, 02 Aug 2026 15:00:26 GMT

For hours we hobbled back, until we were close enough for him to place me down and run for help

Read more in the kindness of strangers series

We had heard there was an incredible waterfall somewhere deep in the Thai rainforest. Seeking it out almost killed me.

In 2003 I was travelling solo through south-east Asia when I met Paul, an American with an easygoing, natural warmth. We were the only two people bunking at a youth hostel somewhere in southern Thailand and got chatting one morning. When the staff told us about a beautiful waterfall not far from where we were staying, we made plans to hike there together.

It was only meant to be an hour’s walk away. Thinking we would be back in time for lunch, we didn’t bother to take any food with us. Big mistake.

For four hours we walked through dense foliage, even climbing down vines in search of this supposed waterfall. At many points it occurred to us that we might be lost, but the naivety of youth propelled us forward. Eventually, the forest opened up to reveal a glistening pool of water with a waterfall at one end. We jumped in and laughed at how the trek had taken us four times as long as expected.

It was on the way back that things began to go wrong. Within minutes of setting off, I started tripping over my own feet. Then I became confused and unable to answer simple questions. In hindsight, I was clearly starving and dehydrated. But at the time I did not understand what was happening to me.

That was when Paul did something unexpected. He put my arm over his shoulder, lifted me up and started to carry me back through the forest. When he could go on no longer, we stopped while Paul dug through my bag, found some old sugar and salt sachets, and whipped me up a makeshift rehydration elixir. It gave me enough strength to walk on my own.

For hours we hobbled back, Paul leading the way and cheering me on. Close to the hostel, I slipped on a loose rock and badly twisted my ankle. Paul again picked me up and carried me until we were close enough for him to place me down and run for help. He returned a short while later on the back of a motorcycle, before I was transported the remaining distance home. Paul walked back alone.

Paul left the next day and I never saw him again. But I’ll always remember how a kind young man I had met only a few hours earlier wrapped his arms around me, picked me up and quite literally carried me home. Did he save my life that day? I would say so.

From making your day to changing your life, we want to hear about chance encounters that have stuck with you.

The Guardian Sun, 02 Aug 2026 13:58:43 GMT

New education secretary says it is ‘false trade-off’ by critics to suggest schools cannot pursue academic excellence alongside technical skills

Lucy Powell has said she wants to be an ambitious “tiger mum” for all young people, whatever their route through education, after the government was accused of dumbing down England’s schools with plans to create more vocational routes.

The new education secretary said secondary pupils should be able to pursue academic excellence as well as high-quality vocational training, and it was a “false trade-off” to suggest schools could not provide both.

In an interview with the Guardian, Powell said she did not have “lower ambition” for those children following technical routes, and her critics – including Michael Gove, the former Tory education secretary – should recognise that their approach had left too many behind.

Andy Burnham told schools across England this week to adapt their curriculums to the needs of local businesses, as part of a drive to make technical and vocational skills as valued as academic qualifications and help tackle the jobs crisis for young people.

Powell said: “I absolutely don’t want schools to dumb down. My kids might say I’m a tiger mum. You know, I’m a tiger mum for all our kids – every single child that’s in our education system achieving excellence, achieving what they can do.”

Powell said those arguing against a focus on vocational education were making a “false trade-off” by framing Labour’s plans as a choice between knowledge and skills. “What I’m not going to oversee is some kind of lower ambition for some kids. It’s about ambition for everybody.”

Most of the criticism of her approach has come from Tory politicians who oversaw the system for years. “They have to take some responsibility for creating … a system that has left over a million young people now not in education, training or employment. The current approach has left too many behind,” Powell said.

However, she acknowledged that headteachers were concerned about extra pressure on their budgets to provide vocational routes, saying she was “very conscious” of school funding, which took a hit during the austerity years. She insisted any specific new proposals would be fully funded.

With many teachers struggling, and strikes potentially looming, Powell said she wanted a constructive relationship with the unions, and the government was already making changes to help ease the pressure. “What I’ll say to teachers is ‘work with me’,” she said.

Powell has been under pressure since she took over the brief to row back on plans made by her predecessor, Bridget Phillipson, to overhaul the special educational needs and disabilities system (Send), in particular limiting education, health and care plans (EHCP) to pupils with the “most complex needs”.

Powell signalled that she would stick to the plans, while accepting that the issue was creating worry and anxiety for many parents. “We can reassure them, because this is about tilting the system so that you don’t have to fight tooth and nail. That you get much earlier help,” she said.

Pressed on Labour’s election pledge to recruit 6,500 teachers, which has since been watered down, she suggested the government was doing well against a lower target, and that a sharp drop in primary numbers reflected falling rolls in schools.

Asked about private schools, Powell took a less adversarial approach than her predecessor, saying it was up to parents to make their own decisions about where they sent their children. “I’m not here to worry about private schools. I’m here to worry about state schools,” she said.

Powell added that she would be spending a significant amount of time at the No 10 North outpost in her central Manchester constituency. The DfE’s third biggest office, housing 1,100 civil servants, is also based in the city.

She batted away suggestions she was unhappy not to have been appointed deputy prime minister by Burnham, saying they had agreed she would continue to play a central role in Labour’s political direction as education secretary.

There had been no purge of the Starmerites, she added, saying the new cabinet was representative of people from across the party, and that, in contrast, the last cabinet had been too narrow. “That was one of the issues for Keir towards the end. His government wasn’t necessarily one of all the traditions.”

Powell also criticised Starmer’s government for focusing too much on the Reform threat rather than Labour’s own plan for the country. “What most people wanted to know was not what we thought about other political parties, but what were we doing? What were we about? What has been refreshing over the last week or two, is being on the front foot. Every day you’re on the front foot is a day you’re winning.”

She insisted that despite multiple spending pledges in Burnham’s first fortnight in office, all policy announcements were funded, with the prime minister and his chancellor, John Healey, “quite prudent and careful” about this.

Australia’s Louise Hoskins, 76, wins historic Commonwealth Games gold medal

The Guardian Sun, 02 Aug 2026 13:19:35 GMT

Para bowler is oldest gold medallist in Games history

Hoskins: ‘I never thought I’d win at my age. Never give up’

Louise Hoskins has become the oldest gold medallist in Commonwealth Games history, claiming women’s para bowls pairs glory alongside Serena Bonnell.

“It is incredible. I’m still pinching myself,” said 76-year-old Hoskins, who was born during the 1950 Auckland Games and is the oldest competitor at the 2026 Games in Glasgow. “I never thought I’d ever get [a gold medal] at my age. Get out there and have a go, and never give up.”

Down 4-1 in the second set, Hoskins and Bonnell were headed for the lottery of a sudden-death tiebreaker with New Zealand in the pairs B6-B8 final. A sprinkle of magic dust from Bonnell was the difference, as she nudged the jack and delivered three points to Australia to tie the set and secure a 6-3, 4-4 win.

The New Zealand pair, Julie O’Connell and Teri Blackbourn, were world champions in 2023 and opened their Glasgow campaign with victory over Australia, dropping just one game en route to a rematch with the Queensland duo in the final.

Bonnell had a feeling she and Hoskins would be able to turn the tables with gold on the line. The 44-year-old, who won silver in Birmingham four years ago, revealed that Hoskins’ words of wisdom from the sidelines helped her when it mattered most.

“I had good weight on my first, crap line on my second and my coach took a time out,” Bonnell said. “[Louise] settled me down, supported me and that was enough for me to play the bowl and win the game,” she added on her fellow Jackaroo.

“I have been dreaming and visualising the fact that I was going to have to play big bowls and Louise led exceptionally well,” Bonnell added. “Thankfully I was able to play the bowl when I needed to.”

Hoskins was the contest’s dominant figure and was delighted for her partner to play the match-winning bowl. “The moment Serena released it I could see she had it,” Hoskins said. “It was amazing and just heading for the jack. You could see it. I knew it was there before it even came through.”

Hoskins has broken the record held by Scotland’s George Miller, who was 75 when he won Para Mixed Pairs B2-B3 gold at the Birmingham Games in 2022.

Chaos of border crossing gives way to limbo for Moroccans on Ceuta’s streets

The Guardian Sun, 02 Aug 2026 13:11:56 GMT

People among the more than 50,000 who entered Spanish enclave this week describe the journey and their prospects

Four days ago, Youssef El Abbas saw an opportunity to reclaim the life he had lost seven years earlier. News was circulating that about 400 people had swum from Morocco to the neighbouring Spanish enclave of Ceuta on the north African coast, approximately 12 miles (19km) across the strait of Gibraltar from mainland Spain.

Here was a chance for the 44-year-old Moroccan father of four to return to Spain, from which he had been deported when his residency expired after the loss of his job in Bilbao in 2019.

El Abbas took a taxi and headed to the city of Tétouan, south of the enclave. While en route, he saw Facebook posts and news reports claiming that the Moroccan authorities were allowing people to pass through their side of the border. That meant that unlike those who had crossed the previous night, he could simply travel overland before swimming for just five minutes across the border from Moroccan to Spanish territory to avoid the Spanish border controls.

He reached Tétouan to find the city completely overwhelmed. “Young men were running through the streets, flooding every corner,” he said. By the time a second taxi took El Abbas to Fnideq, the town bordering Ceuta, he realised that the usual blockades and checkpoints preventing people without European documents from even approaching the frontier had been removed.

“The Moroccan police were shouting at us: ‘Go, go, go! Run now, run into Spain,’” he said. “The night before, they were beating people. But that morning they were letting us through. Nothing made sense.”

Despite the crowds, El Abbas noticed the police were only letting Moroccans cross over. “All the sub-Saharan migrants were being pushed back by force.”

He reached the border at 2.45pm on Wednesday. By 3pm, after a short swim, he was standing on Spanish soil. Not everyone was so lucky.

“In just 10 minutes in the water, I saw four people floating dead in Moroccan waters,” he said. “People were pulling their bodies out.” They were among at least 72 people who drowned or were crushed trying to reach the Spanish territory.

El Abbas is just one of the 50,000 or so people to have crossed into Ceuta this week, in what Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, described as “a violation of Spain’s territorial integrity”.

Madrid has attributed the latest influx to “human-trafficking mafias” that have taken advantage of a decision by Spain’s supreme court, which recently ruled that those intercepted at sea while trying to enter Ceuta or Melilla – the other Spanish enclave on the north African coast – could not be summarily returned under special rules.

But there has also been speculation that the Moroccan authorities may have opened the border to signal their displeasure at Sánchez’s recent visit to Algeria, which supports efforts to free the disputed territory of Western Sahara from Moroccan occupation.

Morocco’s ambassador to Spain, Karima Benyaich Millán, said Rabat was not happy about the mass crossing, adding that it hoped those in Ceuta would return.

Moroccan government sources told the Europa Press news agency that the surge of people entering Ceuta was down to “criminal organisations” and insisted that Rabat’s cooperation with Spain remained “exemplary”.

In May 2021, Rabat loosened border controls – allowing 10,000 people to cross into Ceuta over the course of two days – during a diplomatic standoff triggered after Madrid allowed a Western Sahara independence leader to be treated for Covid-19 in Spain.

El Abbas said he had never stopped dreaming of returning to Spain, where he had worked mainly in the hospitality sector for 14 years. Since being deported to Morocco in 2019, he has lived apart from his wife and four daughters, who remain in the northern Spanish city of Bilbao, while scraping by with occasional work repairing mobile phones alongside his father.

“I never stopped thinking about coming back,” he said. “In Morocco, I was alive, but I wasn’t really living.”

Sign up to Headlines Europe

A digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week day

after newsletter promotion

The return has been bittersweet. When he swam ashore in Ceuta, a Spanish Guardia Civil officer extended a hand to pull him from the sea. But that gesture of aid eventually gave way to one of violence. Three days after arriving, the group of people he was with were surrounded by a military patrol and beaten.

“The same hand that helped me out of the water was the one that later hit me,” he said.

El Abbas’s story is hardly unique. Although more than 48,000 people had crossed back into Morocco by Friday night, hundreds are still sleeping in parks, public squares and on pavements, waiting for a chance to move on or simply to find somewhere to rest. It appears to be virtually impossible for migrants to leave Ceuta for mainland Spain.

Said, 17, from Casablanca, was sitting on a kerb a few hundred metres away. He, too, had joined the Ceuta-bound crowds when he heard that the border was open. But the jubilation had given way to reality and all he had was a bottle of water and the carton of yoghurt a local resident had given him.

The teenager said he was taken to a centre for unaccompanied minors after he crossed, but there were no places available, so he ended up back on the streets. According to a soldier who asked to remain anonymous, the current protocol for the authorities – including the military, the police and the Guardia Civil – is to treat unaccompanied minors as regular migrants and return them to Morocco.

Said and the other teenagers with him said no one would sell them food or allow them into shops and restaurants because they did not speak Spanish.

Three days after the mass influx, Ceuta is slowly trying to recover a sense of normality. By early evening on Saturday, cafe terraces were beginning to fill again and some businesses had reopened their doors. Many of the remaining arrivals are being tended to by Ceuta locals, who walk the streets handing out bottles of water, sandwiches, blankets and clothes. Others stop to ask if they need help or to offer to call a relative.

Such shows of solidarity have been threatened by the arrival of far-right politicians and a neo-Nazi group, all keen to use the humanitarian crisis for their own ends.

“They’re going to exploit our feelings to claim the credit and say they defended Ceuta,” said a local woman called Malika. “We don’t want them here. If they want to defend something, they should go somewhere else.”

Malika, who was born in Ceuta to a soldier who served in the Spanish army, rejected the notion that the city should be defined solely by the political confrontation that followed this week’s mass arrival. But she also acknowledged the pressure on a city of just over 80,000 people. “It would have been an impossible situation for any city,” she said.

Fatima Hamed Hossain, a member of Ceuta’s assembly, fears that the strain created by the crisis has deepened divisions within the city. “Everything we’ve lived through has created tensions between neighbours,” she said. “That’s exactly what feeds the far right.”

As a caravan of people returned back over the border, Said’s mind was on the future. His goal is simple: get a place in a protection centre, spend the next year learning Spanish and, once he turns 18, find work as a barber. What he fears most is ending up without legal documentation and seeing that plan collapse before it has even begun.

Leaving is not on his agenda, however. “All I need,” he said, “is a chance.”

Struggling to get through summer? Treat yourself like a beloved dog – and six other survival tips

The Guardian Sun, 02 Aug 2026 13:00:22 GMT

August usually sends me into an anxious funk, but I think I’ve worked out how to handle 2026’s terrifying heat and apocalyptic images

Unfortunately for hairdressers, “How’s your summer going?” is a loaded question this year. Even basking lizards and barbecue obsessives are wavering in their sun worship as cataclysmic wildfires engulf our nearest neighbours (and threaten the UK), Wales and parts of England experience drought, and farmers issue dire warnings about our food supply in the near future. Rescue centres are filling up with dehydrated hedgehogs and the Environment Agency is having to rescue fish. Lazy, joyful, sunscreen-scented days are giving way to stifling, existentially terrifying ones spent skulking in the dark (assuming you don’t need to be out in the extreme heat, as many workers do), sweatily scrolling through apocalyptic images.

Vanity Fair has decreed it’s a “sad-girl summer”, highlighting the female singer-songwriters soundtracking the myriad anxieties of an “undeniably cruel” 2026 season, but it’s not just the girlies who are sad – many of us are struggling and we still have August to survive. How?

I’m a veteran of sad-girl summers (possibly Sad summers – some people get seasonal affective disorder when it’s hot and bright). For years, July and August have sent me into an anxious, distressed funk, afflicted by brain shutdowns that leave me useless for days at a time. That means I’m ahead of the curve in finding little survival tactics, so here are some, if you find yourself struggling with what used to be the carefree, fun season.

Look at canine heatwave advice and apply it to yourself. Little walks in the coolest parts of the day, frozen treats, wet towels and top-ups of chilled water will all help maintain your mental equilibrium. Naps won’t hurt either.

Defer your engagement with the horrors – they’ll still be there in half an hour; they don’t need to be the first thing to hit your eyeballs. Immerse yourself in something – anything – engaging offline for a while. If your concentration is shot and you fear you will struggle not to scroll, the novelist Naomi Alderman is running a brilliant reading version of Couch to 5K on her Substack.

Distract yourself with something ultra-low stakes. Last year, I tried growing melons. My misshapen babies were inedibly disgusting, but tending them helped during my twitchiest hours. This summer’s project is “making elaborate salads that would cost £17 in London”. Every day, I craft a photogenic heap of fancy, fibremaxxing fodder, take a picture, save it on my phone in a folder called “lunch” (that I will delete in September), then feast. It’s daft, but it is the high point of many distressing, scratchy-brained days.

I am not saying weather apps are gaslighting us, but it can feel like that when you are in the grip of summer derangement. Watching a tantalising chance of rain in five days’ time fall from 90% to 40% to 20%, then disappear altogether, or temperatures hover stubbornly around the mid-30s is at best a waste of time, at worst, actively maddening. For a few weeks, switch off and experience weather in the way your ancestors did: as an awe-inspiring, often awful but occasionally wonderful thing that happens (possibly because you have displeased the gods).

It is often too hot to sleep at your normal bedtime and there’s a special quality to summer nights that never quite get dark or cold. Last night, I saw bats, a hedgehog and many foxes in my suburb, but I enjoy late wanders around big cities too. There is almost always something unhinged going down that affirms how the inside of my head feels.

Namely fruit. The blackberries are already ripe (yes, worrying), there are peaches so juicy you have to eat them over the sink, fat and fragrant green figs and chunks of crisp, sweet watermelon to be bought. Also, not every apricot I’ve tried has been a sour marble of disappointment and I’ve even eaten melons my French in-laws wouldn’t have drop-kicked off their dinner table in righteous fury. This glut of good fruit is one puny (and doubtless temporary) upside.

It’s sane and rational to feel angry, grief-stricken and frightened. Wouldn’t it be weirder if you didn’t?

Emma Beddington is a Guardian columnist

Readers reply: What is the true Breakfast of Champions?

The Guardian Sun, 02 Aug 2026 13:00:21 GMT

The long-running series in which readers answer other readers’ questions chews on how best to start the day – from porridge to champagne, beer and cheesecake …

Read this week’s new question: What do you wish you could buy in vending machines?

The Commonwealth Games opened in Glasgow earlier this week. As the athletes limber up and engage in protein-maxxing (or is it carb-maxxing?), getting ready to compete, it made me wonder: what is the best breakfast food, or combination of foods, to set you up in the morning? Not necessarily as a top-tier athlete, but simply as someone who is ready to go out there and win the day. Tom, Tunbridge Wells

Send new questions to nq@theguardian. com.

One that stops you feeling hungry until five minutes before lunch. yogainspain

Sauteed mushrooms with a hint of garlic in fromage frais served on a slice of lightly toasted, freshly baked authentic French baton spread with the very best Normandy butter. Delicious, and truly the breakfast of champignons. ThereisnoOwl

Last night’s leftover curry, with the sauce fully mixed into the rice so all remains moist, placed within arm’s reach of the bed. For real champions, washed down with brown ale. Jason90

Last night’s leftover takeaway curry and a bloody caesar. Kill or cure. unclestinky

Egg salad sandwich. Patti Powell, Little Rock, Arkansas

Steel-cut oatmeal. Everybody knows that. Jay Robinson, by email

A leader on a residential course for the national professional qualification for headship opened day one with the question: “What is the breakfast of champions?” The answer, apparently, is “feedback”. Twenty years on, it has stuck in my memory. Ben Greene, by email

Champagne. RBEtuta

Cheesecake. dfic1999

Breakfast isn’t really breakfast unless it’s turkey with all the trimmings. EddieChorepost

Wasn’t that the favourite saying of Suleiman the Magnificent? bricklayersoption

Only when he got Hungary. EddieChorepost

Microwaved poached egg (one glass, one teaspoon of water, 35 seconds) on bread, coffee. Puncture the yolk. Alkahest

No breakfast through the morning, then, around lunchtime, a high-fibre, high-protein first meal plus a couple of portions of fruit and some coffee. Leaves a clear head through the morning, then carries you through the afternoon and sets you up for an evening meal. Dorkalicious

Same as the lunch and dinner of champions … a bar of chocolate. adogsatonmypizza

For me, it will always be bircher-style muesli. I like to mix together a bag of frozen berries, a kilo of yoghurt and a few cups of oats in a big Tupperware and keep it in the fridge for breakfast all week. MsUnderstanding

A flatmate used to buy two kebabs on the way back from the pub, eat one straight away and keep the other for his breakfast. Salt, fat, carbs, spices – perfect hangover cure. Randomusername222

Lester Piggott, the 11-time champion jockey whose struggle with his weight was a feature of his career, breakfasted – so went the mythology – on a cigar and a cough. Not many calories there. NationOfSimian

A rollie and a large mug of black coffee. manicstteacher

A five-egg omelette cooked with finely diced peppers and onion, accompanied by sauerkraut, kimchi and kombucha. A glass of water and a cup of tea or coffee as preferred. Delicious, and keeps your gut happy. GrasmereGardens

Cold pizza and warm beer. (For sports hero wannabes the morning after.) DavidGervais

Black coffee, toast and salty butter. All the major food groups there (starch, fat, salt, caffeine). Might add a smear of honey or jam if I feel like pushing the boat out. SharonHoward

Pasta or rice with chicken or fish, or scrambled eggs on toast, according to the nutritionist of Spain’s football team. A little soy sauce is permitted. alexito

A mashed sardine mixed with finely chopped onion and balsamic vinegar on a buttered rice cake. Absolutely delicious, though one’s breath leaves a bit to be desired. PatDavison

A poached egg on toasted wholemeal with Marmite, seeds, sourdough with some roasted tomatoes drizzled with olive oil, followed by a large portion of mixed berries with Greek yoghurt, all washed down with sparkling water with half a lemon squeezed into it. Zenthewonderdog

Broth (miso and chipotle paste) and noodles, perhaps with frozen peas. Followed by pinot grigio. mathurin

A couple of six-minute boiled eggs, a bagel with salmon, cream cheese and capers, a bowl of Weetabix, OJ and coffee. Covers a lot of food groups and fills you up. Twenty-five years or so ago, when I used to drink, my answer was a pint of ice-cold Diet Coke: it used to work wonders in the morning and early afternoon. catchytitled

Salad, according to the recent article in the Guardian. TobermoryNightlife

Coffee, cigarette, spanakopita. Nepthsolem

“Sex, breakfast of champions!” is an old chestnut no one seems to have mentioned so far. exlangrandeflaneuse

Surely it depends on the champion. A champion sumo wrestler probably needs a different breakfast from a chess champion. Goldgreen

Chorizo, the cooked salami-style one, sliced lengthways into fairly thin rashers, cooked slowly so the spiced fat runs, eaten dunked into the yolk of an egg fried in the fat. Some buttered toast would be good here, too.

The waitress in Kurt Vonnegut’s novel Breakfast of Champions says “breakfast of champions” to every customer she serves a martini to. There must be something in that. adamcgf

Porridge made with water, plus a dollop of full-fat Greek yoghurt, sprinkled with a nutty granola or mixed seeds. Or both. Not enough to weigh you down, but keeps you going till lunch and great for the gut. Spockle

Scrambled egg, served with diced tomatoes on the side, lasts me till lunchtime without any initial over-full sensation. Some chives are a nice addition, if I have them. nigeljones

Longer term, the best strategy to win at life may be to skip conventional breakfasts completely. Athletes have all sorts of reasons for specialised diets, but there is increasing evidence that staying healthy into later life might mean restricting the hours we eat.

The scale of trials is small so far, but it appears that eating meals over eight to nine hours has advantages in reducing the incidence of dementia compared with the same food intake over 12 hours. The basic regime started with healthy foods and reducing intake by 500 calories a day, but adding a shorter eating period came out ahead.

The studies effectively meant eating meals between 10am and 6pm. The findings may well be linked to the fact that our metabolism responds more effectively to food around the middle of our waking day than it does at the extremes. For example: “The body releases the most insulin – the hormone that helps move sugar from blood into cells – from 12-6pm, and the lowest during sleep.” There’s a whole body of evidence that the more recent trends of extended snacking over 14 hours or more is one of the worst possible ways to organise your food intake – with a whole heap of factors that are probably contributing to that. leadballoon

But does it have to be in the morning? I felt best when my schedule supported intermittent fasting, but for me something like 7am to 4.30pm. I can’t sleep on a full stomach and love waking up ravenous. bitthebeat

My platonic ideal of breakfast consists of plain, high-protein Greek yoghurt, berries or other fruit and a sprinkle of muesli. The protein keeps me full, the muesli gives good mouthfeel and the berries are high in flavour and antioxidants. This breakfast never bores me (ooh, pomegranate pips today!). I have been eating this every workday for over 10 years. Perhaps thanks to all of the antioxidants, I’m not dead yet. Rebekah Zinn, Olympia, Washington

The true Breakfast of Champions is by Kurt Vonnegut Jr. Alternatively, good black Mexican coffee. Huevos rancheros with fried bananas and frijoles de olla. Buen día to you all! Gerardo Martinez Casas, Mérida, México

I’ve radically changed my eating patterns over the last six months and breakfast has changed more than anything else. First, I eat it much later, about 11. I’m usually up by six and just have coffee and then a walk. Somehow, this routine seems to suppress my appetite. I have 5% fat Greek yoghurt with chopped peanuts, cashews, walnuts, flax seeds, sunflower seeds and pumpkin seeds along with half a chopped banana, apple, satsuma, raspberries or strawberries and a few blackcurrants. It’s totally delicious and usually keeps me going till dinner at about 7. Mark Fletcher, by email

I had lurched from one unhappy breakfast to another through much of my life. My gut is not my strongest organ. So when one of my older mentors suggested steel-cut oats [coarse oatmeal], as a recent retiree, I decided to give it a try. The results are very successful. No indigestion an hour after breakfast. My gut is so much happier and so is my cardiovascular system. All kinds of odd cravings are now gone. It’s very affordable and local (there is an oat processing mill in our neighbourhood). I make my oats a week at a time in a rice cooker, with a handful of raisins, and heat up each day’s breakfast in the microwave. Fred Tepfer, Eugene, Oregon

Maybe nothing other than a cup of coffee if I was playing an important match or a big run. PeteTheBeat

Black. 50% vodka. Jason90

Every fibre of my being desires fibre for breakfast. Sagarmatha1953

I’m afraid the Breakfast of Champions is in a glass case in the department of ancient history. There was a place in Brighton, the Market Diner, which shovelled out a creation called the Gutbuster. This was long, long before the Ministry of Marketing, Advertising, Publicity and Foul Lies invented the “full English” and similar terms of nonexistent japery. It consisted of nearly everything on a decent caff menu, apart from perhaps Spam, on one plate.

It was so effective as a breakfast of champions that after successfully tucking one inside, if there was the slightest squeak from a notorious family of troublemaking Herberts, all that was required was to breathe Gutbuster halitosis on one of ’em to have the whole clan fleeing over the South Downs, shrieking in terror.

It wasn’t bad value, either: lovely caff, good people and not greedy. There’s probably a poncey version called The Nonpareil or some other nonsense lurking between Shoreham Harbour and Roedean, but nothing will ever equal the “Gutbuster”. bricklayersoption

Little Chef used to provide Olympic breakfasts (though possibly not at the behest of the IOC). EddieChorepost

Predictable, but porridge and toast will keep you going till lunch. Nothing fancy. Oats, 50/50 milk/water, salt, sugar or sweetener and dried or tinned fruit with local bakery-made wholegrain toast with butter and jam. Nothing overprocessed. You need fuel to keep you going. Olddogandgrump

Pure OJ, dish of mixed fruits, three Weetabix with whole milk and two poached eggs with a large, crispy rasher of bacon. Good coffee. DeborahGeller

Decades on from the US’s disastrous campaign in Afghanistan, Trump is making all the same mistakes

The Guardian Sun, 02 Aug 2026 11:31:49 GMT

The president has blundered into a ‘forever war’ with Iran he can’t win, but refuses to end. Such hubris has a long history

It’s five years this month since the chaotic retreat of US forces from Kabul. The Nato-backed invasion and occupation of Afghanistan, launched after the 11 September 2001 terrorist attacks on New York City and Washington DC, is now widely regarded as a failure. It cost the lives of more than 2,400 US and 450 British troops, and tens of thousands of civilians (the exact number is unknown). Although al-Qaida terrorists were routed, their Taliban hosts reimposed repressive, misogynistic Islamist rule after regaining power in 2021. Afghanistan became a byword for ill-considered western interventionism and nation-building. It was the archetypal “forever war”, a phrase first coined during Vietnam.

If this cautionary tale had any lasting value, it was as a deterrent to politicians and generals tempted to rashly embark on open-ended conflicts without just cause, defined, achievable aims, and an exit strategy. Dismayingly, the forever war lesson had to be learned all over again in Iraq, which the US and UK invaded in 2003 and departed, having caused huge harm for scant benefit, in 2011. “Never again!” was the passionate cry at the time and since. And yet, it seems, the same disastrous pattern is now repeating after Donald Trump’s incomprehensibly foolish decision to attack Iran. A war he termed a “little excursion” is entering its sixth month and has been escalating rapidly. It, too, has a forever feel.

That this nightmare is happening again defies all reason. How can it be? Immediate causes of the war aside, answers may be found in persistent US exaggerations and misconceptions about the level and extent of external threats, mixed up with political dishonesty, national hubris, naivety and misplaced idealism. Recalling the harrowing US experience in Afghanistan, Carter Malkasian, a National War College professor who served as a civilian adviser to US forces in Helmand and Kabul, suggests the basic premise for keeping troops in Afghanistan for 20 years – a belief the country would otherwise revert to being a safe haven for international terrorism – was fatally flawed.

“Nothing of the sort occurred. Over the past five years, not a single act of terrorism against the US was carried out by a group based in Afghanistan,” Malkasian wrote. “Washington spent roughly $1tn on the war. More than 775,000 American service members were deployed … all to defend against a threat that turned out to have been exaggerated.

“Five years on, the greatest danger is not that a terrorist safe haven might once again emerge in Afghanistan. A graver threat comes from the risk of collective forgetting.” In short, “fears of the moment” should not cloud memories of the dreadful long-term costs – human, financial, geopolitical – of endless forever war.

If the Afghan war was prosecuted on the basis of a false assumption, so much more so was the invasion of oil-rich Iraq. George W Bush’s claim in 2002 that Saddam Hussein’s regime possessed stockpiles of readily usable chemical and biological weapons and was seeking a nuclear bomb proved untrue. Untrue, too, was the claim from the then vice-president, Dick Cheney, that Iraq “aids and protects” al-Qaida. The subsequent occupation and insurgency became part of an even larger forever war – Bush’s “global war on terror”. According to Brown University’s Costs of War project, an estimated 940,000 people were killed in direct post-9/11 violence in Iraq, Afghanistan, Syria, Yemen and Pakistan between 2001 and 2023. Up to 3.8 million died indirectly in post-9/11 war zones.

It’s easy to second-guess decisions about war and peace taken under the pressure of horrific events. The disingenuous pursuit of political, military and commercial agendas, and the manipulation of intelligence and public opinion, is harder to excuse. Yet was any war ever launched without ulterior motives? The much-discussed new film of Homer’s epic poem, the Odyssey, concerns the aftermath of the 10-year-long Trojan war, which was ostensibly triggered by the abduction of the beautiful Helen of Sparta. Yet, prosaically, the war may have been more about fair trade than a fair maiden. The US maintained it fought the Vietnam war to support democracy and halt the spread of communism – the discredited “domino theory”. But it was also very much about US exceptionalism and global hegemony. In that sense, little has changed.

What else makes American politicians risk costly entanglements in foreign wars they can’t control and usually lose? Insecurity – meaning fear – is a common denominator. Like Bush before him, Trump and Israel’s leader, Benjamin Netanyahu, have greatly and knowingly exaggerated the immediacy and existential nature of the Iranian threat. Like Iraq in 2003, Iran possesses no nuclear weapons and there is zero firm evidence it is trying, or has recently tried, to acquire them. There is a recurring paradox here: it’s the spectacle of the world’s most powerful country once again fearfully tilting at shadows.

Trump’s overbearing hostility to weaker neighbours such as Venezuela, Cuba, Colombia, Panama and Greenland has a forever aspect, too. It is rooted in the foundational myth that the US has a unique mission – and right – to oversee the western hemisphere, a view it later extended to the rest of the world. Likewise, greed is forever. Abandoning altruistic ideas of democracy promotion, Trump seeks to exercise economic as well as geopolitical dominance. He has tried to monetise the wars in Ukraine and Gaza. His focus on the strait of Hormuz shows how security policy and financial and commercial interests invariably intersect.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Lack of effective UN mediation and peacekeeping, the hollowing out of US diplomacy, which has accelerated under Trump’s lickspittle secretary of state, Marco Rubio, and a stubborn refusal to accept the militarily inevitable all play a role in turning US-led conflicts into intractable quagmires. In Trump’s case, ego is also a factor. It seems he would rather kill thousands more civilians, risk committing war crimes, set the Middle East ablaze and destroy Republicans’ electoral chances than admit he was wrong over Iran. Such extreme behaviour illuminates another pernicious aspect of the forever war phenomenon. Its utter pointlessness is fundamentally immoral. In its sheer un-reason, it offends against the laws of God and man. War without end is the death of hope.

As he frantically twists and turns over Iran, it’s plain that Trump perceives the bottomless pit on the edge of which, thanks to him, the US totters – and has no idea how to avoid it. One day, he talks about talks. The next, he hits out with massive, murderous violence. Careless of their people’s suffering, implacable Iranian hardliners relish his dilemma and turn the screw, mounting widening regional militia attacks and global economy-spooking drone and missile strikes. Lost in a maze of denial, Trump tries in vain to bomb his way out of trouble while desperate for a deal that can somehow be sold as a victory.

Neither option is going to work. This abysmal Iranian catastrophe is already defining Trump’s presidency. The bloody stain, the blame and the shame, if not the war, will last forever.

Simon Tisdall is a Guardian foreign affairs commentator

Why Andy Burnham’s devolution pledge will be tricky to deliver

The Guardian Sun, 02 Aug 2026 11:19:32 GMT

Sharing income tax with England’s regional mayors could tackle inequality but many councils are ill-equipped for an enlarged role

On the road to Downing Street, Andy Burnham promised to transfer power from Westminster to every postcode in the country. After his first two weeks in office, the size and complexity of this project are becoming clearer.

With a date set for the autumn budget, the work of filling in the detail that will underpin his devolution plans begins – starting with his proposal to hand England’s regional mayors a share of income tax to support local economic development.

Despite its history as a patchwork of nations, the UK is among the most fiscally centralised countries in the developed world. The Centre for Cities estimates as little as 5% of tax revenue currently stays with mayors and local authorities. The rest goes straight to Whitehall and is allocated by central government. By contrast, 14% of tax stays local in France, and 22% in Japan.

For years British devolution has been a messy patchwork in which Westminster has largely clung on to its position as ringmaster; just ask the parties pushing for independence in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. But the system in England is the messiest of the lot.

Successive governments have followed a piecemeal approach. Under the Conservatives, the creation of dozens of ringfenced funding pots fostered a begging-bowl culture. They were also no match for the billions of pounds in central government grant funding cut under austerity.

Burnham allowing mayors to retain a share of locally generated tax revenues is, therefore, a good idea in principle. Many economists say the idea – first announced by Rachel Reeves earlier this year – would help to tackle Britain’s deep regional inequalities.

In practice, the Institute for Fiscal Studies estimates that between 6% and 9% of local income tax revenues would be sufficient to fully replace the so-called integrated settlements, or central government grants, the mayoral authorities currently receive.

But it will take time to introduce the plan and there are wrinkles to iron-out – not least how to avoid weaker local economies falling behind.

The danger is the current fastest-growing mayoral authorities are typically the country’s wealthiest.

London, and the runaway success story that is Greater Manchester, are in pole position. The West Midlands and South Yorkshire are in a slower lane. If the winners get to keep a rising share of income tax, the laggards would risk a self-fulfilling cycle of weak growth; limited scope for investment, and yet weaker growth.

The reforms will also take a long time to bear fruit for a prime minister in a hurry.

It will be 2028 before the income tax plan comes into full effect. Dozens of new mayoralties are also still in the process of being created – with a deadline of the end of that year to give people in places including Essex, Stoke-on-Trent and Warrington similar powers to the trailblazing mayoralties of London and Manchester.

Last month the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development gave devolution a ringing endorsement. But it also warned that the starting point in Britain makes it challenging. Several vital building blocks need to be put in place to make Burnham’s agenda a success.

First and foremost will be the challenge of repairing the damage caused by the Tory austerity years. English local government is a shadow of its pre-2010 self. Most places lack the staff and expertise to use their new money and powers well, at a time when many are struggling to do the basics such as collecting bins or filling potholes.

after newsletter promotion

Across England’s town halls, the workforce has plunged since 2009 from 2.2 million to about 1.1 million. While Greater Manchester and the West Midlands have established sophisticated analytical, policy and delivery teams – enabling them to make better use of the devolved powers – the OECD says many authorities have a shortage of resources and have limited technical expertise.

The risk of making bad spending decisions is high. The shenanigans in Tees Valley, Birmingham, and the multibillion-pound debts amassed in Woking, Warrington and Thurrock are a serious red flag. Labour inherited a broken local audit system, evidenced by the fact that just 1% of places published audited accounts for 2022-23 by the original deadline.

The loss of the Audit Commission (abolished by the Tories) and the death of local journalism has removed important checks and balances. Labour knows this, and has plans to strengthen the role of the new Local Audit Office, which has picked up some of the commission’s functions, and could lean on the National Audit Office.

While the public has greater trust in local government than in its Westminster representatives, surveys show that only about 35% of people report that their trust is high or moderately high, well below the OECD average of about 45%.

However, devolution could be transformative for the economy. Local leaders are best placed to understand how to support growth in their area.

According to the Centre for Cities, measures to integrate bus, tram and train networks in the six largest English cities outside London would better connect 1.2 million people to their nearest city centre, generating productivity gains worth an estimated £17bn. The OECD finds that countries with higher levels of tax and spending devolution tend to have higher wages.

At present, the UK’s second-tier cities significantly underperform their peers elsewhere in the G7. Among the bottom 20 big cities in the G7 for productivity, seven are British. Powering-up the UK’s regions would make a big difference.

There is no doubt that on the road to transfer power from Westminster to local leaders Burnham will encounter more than a few potholes. But the path is well worth pursuing.

Attack of the birthdayzillas: the people turning their big days into epic events – at huge cost to their guests

The Guardian Sun, 02 Aug 2026 11:00:20 GMT

First it was weddings. Now, going overboard on birthdays, planning murder-mystery breaks or mini-festivals with dress codes and branded merch, is the norm for many. Is this driven by monster egos, or a search for connection in a fractured age?

MikeFest takes place every year, over the August bank holiday weekend, in a large leafy garden on the Cornish coast. Birthday boy Michael’s nearest and dearest turn up in their sparkliest gear (as per the invitation) with tents tucked under their arms. Masks with his face printed on them are handed out, as are handheld fans and sippy cups branded with each guest’s name. Organised fun ensues, including a compulsory talent show. Michael always wins first place with his interpretive dance routine.

Michael is not turning 10; he is about to be 44. And he accepts the title of “birthdayzilla”, admitting that he’s guilt-tripped friends who were unable to make it and barred those who miss two festivals in a row from future events. But he’s quick to defend his fellow birthday fanatics. “It doesn’t feel like there’s much to celebrate these days, and it’s harder than ever to get people together. So yes, I’m militant about my birthday,” he says. “I just think: I’ve managed to build a life I like and a network of people I love, why not make a fuss about it? I don’t think expecting them to show up for me once a year is such a big ask.”

While you may still be on the waitlist for a ticket to MikeFest, I’m sure you’ve noticed the ballooning of birthday culture. Perhaps you were added to a group chat against your will, its title crowded with cake emojis. Maybe a save-the-date arrived on creamy card bearing only one name in cursive font. Adult birthday celebrations are getting bigger, splashier and heavier with meaning, now jostling with weddings for a place at the pinnacle of our social calendars. Since when did they become such a big deal?

Where once a slice of cake sufficed to ring in a new age, today it’s not unusual to throw a fully catered party, rope your friends into a series of activities or organise a group holiday abroad. Lauren, a 29-year-old from Edinburgh, has already run through her annual leave allowance. “I’ve been to eight 30ths this year and the most low-key was a dinner in a private room that still set me back £100,” she says. “I’ve been to a castle in Scotland for a murder mystery weekend; a house party where we all took part in a quizshow about the birthday girl; a weekend of live music in Marseille; and a night out involving a salsa lesson and karaoke. It is draining my bank account, but once you say yes to one friend’s birthday it feels very loaded to say no to another. And you start to feel you deserve payback, so you plan your own huge thing and become part of the problem.”

Lauren has witnessed first-hand how quickly a birthday can breed a tyrant. One of her friendships is hanging by a thread after an old schoolmate berated her for announcing she was pregnant during their “birthday month”. “There’s something to be said about the main-character energy of my generation – we are all the stars of our social profiles, and we all like a bit of attention – but I think we’re losing the plot,” she says. “Not all of these big birthdays are about optics, but a lot of them are, and that’s when the time and expense of being a guest starts to grate.”

Birthdays are highly emotive because they act as mirrors. As American historian Howard P Chudacoff wrote in his 1989 book How Old Are You?, they “provide a milestone by which individuals can compare their status, accomplishment and appearance with other people who are the same age. It’s kind of like a train: are you ahead of time, on time or behind time?” For some, they’re a day to get through as quietly as possible, while others see them as a life-affirming moment to gather all their people around them. There seems to be a gender divide: according to a YouGov poll, women are twice as likely as men to see a big birthday as a chance to celebrate. Michael (of MikeFest fame) wonders if this is linked to “the outdated sense that organising a party or openly asking for what you need” – namely, some company on your special day – “is inherently unmasculine”. But the clearest distinction runs along generational lines, with people in their 20s, 30s and 40s being much more likely to treat their birthday as a major event.

For this generation, the traditional milestones that once clustered around this time of life have become less attainable – and in some cases, desirable. The latest ONS data shows that the number of people getting married in England and Wales continues to fall year on year, and among those who do get married, the median age is at historic highs of 34.8 for men and 33 for women. Last year, the birthrate was at its lowest since 1977 and the average age of a first-time homeowner climbed to 34. There are many reasons, from political failings to the tectonic plates of our culture shifting beneath our feet, but the common denominator is financial squeeze.

Oyinda sent save-the-dates almost a year in advance for her 30th: four days in Mykonos that she wanted to treat “like a wedding”. Her guests arrived at a villa decorated with her childhood photos and were given personalised gift bags and a printed itinerary including a meal made by a private chef, a boat trip and several beach clubs, all of which she saved up to subsidise. “Growing up, I thought I’d have reached lots of milestones by 30, but for people my age things like getting married and buying a house require a lot of money,” she says. “We still want to lean into life experiences and be celebrated even when we may not achieve those things. I wanted to go all out for my 30th and be as extra as I could be, to celebrate how much I’ve grown as a person and the friends I’ve made over three decades.”

Krisha, who flew to the Dominican Republic for a week of hiking, safaris, horse riding and massages to mark a new friend’s birthday, feels similarly – why not “spend on a bucket-list experience” in a time when saving for a house deposit feels futile? She also flags the double standards when you’re rallying around one person versus a couple. “I find it interesting that when I tell people I flew across the world for a birthday party they say it’s insane, but when it’s for a wedding they don’t question it.”

Where people put their money is changing, but what about when you can’t afford it full stop? Polly from the Midlands felt backed into a corner by her friend’s many invitations, which came to feel like a referendum on their relationship. “She had several events planned for her 40th, ranging from a trip to Portugal to smaller pub gatherings. She wanted to stretch things out across the year, but it came with a lot of friend guilt for me,” Polly says. “I really struggled to tell her that I couldn’t afford that much. I had a lot of anxiety trying to think of my wording and excuse. I feel as if I’ve now been put in a different tier to her other friends who earn high salaries – I can always tell now that the ‘no pressure’ comments are targeted at me and I feel like the poor friend holding back the group.”

She and the birthday girl have known each other for a long time, but the different value they each place on birthdays has given Polly pause. “I love to see my friend having fun, celebrating herself and living her best life, but it’s quite excessive just for a birthday,” she says. “To me, age and numbers are arbitrary and I prefer to celebrate achievements or special occasions: engagements, weddings, promotions, babies. Personally, I’d always choose to keep things small. An evening laughing over wine, a perfectly picked card – those are more than enough.”

Although there’s evidence of pharaohs putting on feasts in ancient Egypt, the adult birthday party is a relatively recent phenomenon, picking up steam in the west around the 1900s as a way for wealthy people to show off their social standing. Anna Goldfarb, friendship expert and author of Modern Friendship: How to Nurture Our Most Valued Connections, says commercial venues have played a role in making showy celebrations mainstream. “Most of our grandparents would have spent their birthday with family at home, but in the 70s and 80s suburban businesses like cinemas and fast-food chains started offering kids’ parties as a way to drum up profit,” she says. “Those kids grew up with the idea that a birthday equals a big gathering where you get all this attention. Huge parts of pop culture, like MTV’s My Super Sweet 16, have only added to the feeling that you should get to be a prince or princess for a day.” Many cultures’ coming-of-age traditions have come to be associated with big parties, from bar- and batmitzvahs to quinceañeras.

Of course, adding social media to the mix has been like dousing a fire with petrol. We see how thousands of other people – including the ultra-rich and terminally attention-hungry – are celebrating themselves and our visions of a low-key picnic in the park start to wilt. The baseline of normal gets skewed by Dua Lipa dancing on a chartered yacht for her 30th, or Kris Jenner being serenaded by Bruno Mars at 70. Even for those of us who aren’t millionaires, the visibility of being online ups the ante on a day that can already feel like a litmus test for how loved we are.

“I have seen adults have full meltdowns, and they’re not bad people, they’ve just got these very set ideas of how the day should go,” says Tom, a photographer based in Brighton. “Recently I was hired to work a party and the person redid their entrance three times, because the crowd wasn’t screaming loudly enough. She actually grabbed a microphone to shout at her friends and family: ‘That will look shit on TikTok, do it again.’”

The behaviour of some birthday divas can cause lasting reputational damage. Oliver’s cousin wanted her garden party to look perfect, but her preoccupation with perception rubbed him up the wrong way. “She had quite a specific dress code: she wanted everyone to dress in an outfit inspired by her, because she’s had many wild fashion eras. But the week before the party she became this monster on WhatsApp, demanding to see pictures of everyone’s outfits and giving us notes,” he says.

“Things got worse the day before, when she sent this long message saying that the expense of hiring a marquee and decorations and huge floral arrangements was higher than she’d realised, and could we all bring £50 in cash to chip in. It was the tackiest thing, and it put people in a bad mood. But you wouldn’t know it from all the staged photos of us laughing and nursing the one watery cocktail we were handed. The whole thing just left a bad taste because it was like she cared more about pulling off this Pinterest board vision than actually spending time with us.”

Even when you’re not modelling your event on the Met Gala, a mismatch between expectation and reality still stings. Amina, who was raised in a family “that didn’t really do Christmas but always made a big deal of birthdays”, invited 100 people to a London park to play games and ring in her 30th. When the forecast said rain, she moved it indoors to a bar – and only 10 people showed up. “I didn’t want the people who were there to think I was ungrateful or a brat, but they could tell I was hurt. I don’t want to need other people’s validation to feel good on my birthday, but it made me spiral about why my friends jumped at the chance to flake out.”

On reflection, Amina realised that “some people just don’t register birthdays the way I do. I was really upset with one of my close friends who turned up hours late and couldn’t even remember my age. Then I recalled the time when I’d just got home from backpacking, had zero money in my account, and was sitting doing some work in a cafe. The waiter brought over chai and a samosa and said that same friend had called up and had it sent over. They’ve shown me care in other ways, so maybe it doesn’t make sense to judge our whole friendship on one day.”

Goldfarb believes that the weight we’re putting on birthdays now tracks with a wider sociological trend around how we relate to one another. “Friendships used to be based on favours and context – something that researchers call ‘social identity support’. Your friends were all people who lived nearby, knew your family and would come through for you in a pinch,” she says. “But now we tend to outsource favours: we call an Uber to pick us up from the airport or hire someone to look after our cat. Our friendships are based more around entertainment and pleasure, so the group trip or party becomes the focal point. Plus, we move around a lot more. We can have friends who know nothing about where we grew up or what we’re like at home, and we crave the context that deepens those bonds.”

This is why, even if you’re not usually the type to covet the limelight or love socialising in large groups, you may still feel the pull to have a birthday that brings all the threads of your life together. “I think people are having more elaborate events to recreate that feeling of interconnected community. To have the friend from school meet the colleague, or the cousin meet the partner, means being recognised for all the roles you play in your life. It makes you feel whole,” says Goldfarb.

This rings true for Kejal, who is treating her next birthday as a way to honour the circle she’s gathered around her. “Turning 40 feels different to other birthdays. At this age, I’m crystal clear about who gives me energy, and my friendships are a reflection of who I am,” she says. “What I want most is for the weekend to be about connection, not just a boozy dinner and a hangover. I want us to leave with core memories.”

We live in an age where we have less to call our own. Fewer of us have homes we can freely decorate in a style that represents us, and even smaller identity markers such as music and films are streamed, not physically held. Against this backdrop, it makes sense that people are treating their birthdays as an opportunity to express who they are. For Kejal, it’s “my chance to celebrate the achievements of the last 40 years, to have the people who’ve championed me in the room, and to say thank you, properly, in a way that is uniquely me”.

For all the tales of smiling extortion and tantrums over RSVPs, the majority of people going big on their birthdays are seeking the same thing: meaningful togetherness. Perhaps the only way to get all the people you love in one place these days is to promise them the time of their lives. Or, at the very least, second place in the talent show.
