Inside M&S’s swanky Oxford Street revamp, the blueprint for its £700m growth strategy

The Guardian Sun, 02 Aug 2026 11:00:20 GMT

As boss Stuart Machin unveils a new-look Pantheon the retailer has fashion and overseas challenges ahead

On a hot summer’s evening on London’s busy Oxford Street, a crowd of fashion influencers, models, journalists and the odd City analyst gathered for a first look at the upmarket revamp of Marks & Spencer’s landmark Pantheon store.

Some may have had to double-check they had the right address, such is the scale of the makeover at the 88-year-old outlet, which is intended as a blueprint for change across the retailer’s more than 200 large stores.

“We know we’ve got a big job modernising the store experience and modernising the online experience as well,” M&S’s chief executive, Stuart Machin, told the crowd.

He said a collection of “legacy old stores” – such as outlets in Newcastle or central London – had remained profitable so “most previous leadership just kept them open”.

But Machin has a bigger vision. He is an exacting, obsessive leader who loves to wade into the detail of store operations and warehouse refurbishments. He once admitted to disliking “all this talk about work-life balance”. Four years into the job, he is keen to leave his mark on the 142-year-old retail group.

After a tough year marred by a cyber-attack that knocked out M&S’s online trading for almost seven weeks and hit profits by more than £300m, Machin told shareholders at its recent annual meeting that the year ahead was “one of the most important in our history”. He went on to say: “The next three years are critical for M&S as we invest for growth.”

The Pantheon, which was built in the late 18th century, was an opera house and entertainment venue before its reconstruction for M&S in the 1930s. With the latest revamp now finished, the next big project for the retailer will be its Marble Arch store, at the other end of Oxford Street.

Machin said the group’s most profitable but rather low-ceilinged and labyrinthine outlet would be knocked down next year, a plan which has prompted outrage over the potential environmental impact.

The new, 10-storey building won planning permission only after a legal challenge and approval by the housing secretary, Angela Rayner, in 2024. It will include just two and a half floors of shop space – compared with five at present – topped by offices and a gym, and will stand at the eastern tip of the London mayor Sadiq Khan’s pedestrianisation of Oxford Street, which is due to be in place next year. .

The rebuild is expected to take four years, during which M&S will lease a temporary store across the road in the same block as Zara. Machin told those gathered at the Pantheon that “hopefully” he would still be chief executive when the Marble Arch rebuild was completed, adding: “So let’s see how we do.”

It is a question many shoppers and analysts may well be asking as Machin, backed by his retail veteran chair, Archie Norman, attempt to lead a turnaround of M&S that actually sticks and extends beyond a few high-profile outlets.

Several predecessors have come up with flashy, short-lived revival plans to combat competition from Primark, H&M, Zara and younger, online rivals. After losing momentum, M&S only briefly regained annual pre-tax profits of £1bn in 2008, having first reached that milestone in 1998.

Despite a global financial crisis, Brexit, the coronavirus pandemic and the cyber-attack, the retailer appears to be on the front foot – with strong food sales and fashion credentials to match.

Underlying profits fell to £671m last year, and Machin told the Guardian that climbing back to £1bn was not the aim. “Profit will be what it will be,” he said. “Our plan is for a growth business.”

While some shareholders may complain about lacklustre dividends, Machin said they would thank him in the long term. His plan involves £700m of investments in revitalising stores, modernising its supply chain and distribution system, and further improvements in products.

The group, which employs more than 65,000 people, has 227 full-line stores – containing food, clothing, homewares and beauty – after closing dozens of old and out-of-place outlets. More will shut over the next two years and a handful of new outlets are opening. It aims to have 200 full-line stores in the UK.

In contrast, M&S’s food arm is expanding, with 18 food-only stores opening this year as it heads for a target of 420, compared with 335 directly operated outlets now. Franchise partners run another 466 in the UK and more overseas.

A wave of new food stores and some cheaper groceries may have brought a broader range of shopper into M&S, but Machin said the retailer was “just at the starting blocks” with changes in fashion, home and beauty.

after newsletter promotion

The Pantheon store is “where we’re testing how we make shopping our ranges easier, more curated and more inspiring”, he said.

The fashion floors are now broken up into bright “rooms” for different brands and product types, – flanked by digital displays, green-tiled pillars and modern shelving.

On food, M&S is aiming to become a “true shopping-list retailer” as it aims to double sales. It is already the fastest-growing food retailer in the UK, with sales up 16% in the latest three-month tally from Worldpanel by Numerator. This has kept its market share at an all-time high of 4.1%, or 4.6% if sales via its online partner Ocado are included.

On clothing, Machin has said M&S had “finally dumped the frump” – grasping the No 1 spot on style perception from its Spanish rival Zara to add to its existing top position on value, according to Worldpanel.

M&S is regaining market share – now controlling more than 10% of the UK fashion (clothing and footwear) market – and driving for more. It has even had to buy in more smaller-sized womenswear and lingerie as consumers in their 40s, 30s and even 20s reappraise the brand.

With the help of its marketing director, Sharry Cramond, who is bringing the social media-fuelled interest to fashion that she first delivered on food, the brand is creating a buzz.

Senior industry insiders believe M&S is now “in a solid place”. One said it had “re-established itself and its credentials”, and another that it had “a lot more self-confidence”. “Clothing has finally got its mojo back,” according to one former senior executive.

But another former executive needled that despite Machin’s “quite high ego quotient”, massaged with appearances on social media with glamorous influencers such as the Chicken Shop Date comedian Amelia Dimoldenberg or the actor Gillian Anderson, there was more work to do.

“It has lost a massive amount of market share on womenswear which it will never recover,” he said.

Another industry insider said M&S, which once had a vast empire, was continuing to struggle overseas. Two decades after quitting the US, it still has a presence in 70 countries – but many operations are small. He added that the acquisition of a 50% stake in Ocado’s retail arm in 2019 was largely unprofitable, even if it had brought in a younger audience.

Machin said revamping the international business had been harder than he envisaged, but said its fashion revival was helping overseas too.

Perhaps his biggest challenge lies behind the scenes, with big warehouse projects in the next few years in south-west England and the Midlands. “Deadlines are realistic. We are not going from zero to 10 overnight,” he said.

Why we’re all obsessed with Jimothy the raccoon, the internet’s animal of the moment

The Guardian Sun, 02 Aug 2026 11:00:20 GMT

From Grumpy Cat to Moo Deng, viral animals have long united people online. Are they becoming our only source of collective enjoyment?

Anyone who enjoys memes (who doesn’t?) has surely by now accumulated a mental menagerie of internet-famous animals. Mine include: Grumpy Cat, the Ikea monkey, Moo Deng the pygmy hippo, Paul the oracle octopus and – my personal favourite – Roger the hot kangaroo (go on, look him up).

Now we have Jimothy, a raccoon with short spine syndrome. A familiar sight in his neighbourhood in Seattle for his unusually rounded appearance and scuttling movement, Jimothy went viral on Instagram two weeks ago and has since taken over the world. Within weeks of his debut, there has been fan art, merchandise, multiple tattoos, a stadium “theme night” and even a civic ceremony.

Even going by the internet’s longstanding enthusiasm for weird little guys, the scale and suddenness of his ascent has been striking. It’s easy to see why people, brands and even baseball teams have jumped on Jimothy: he’s cute, unproblematic and not at all political. Unlike with Taylor Swift’s wedding, say, or the Coldplay kiss cam couple – to name two recent shared, seismic cultural moments – Jimothy poses no ethical quandary. He’s just a funny- looking racoon. This places him in that rare, dwindling and highly prized category of “stuff that everyone can agree is good”.

Animals have served this purpose online for as long as there’s been social media, and indeed influenced its modern form and function.

It’s been 14 years since Ikea monkey was spotted; you can probably instantly picture him, pensive in his stylish shearling coat. Some of these viral animals’ meanings are still evolving (Doge the side-eyed shiba inu is now some kind of Musk-related currency? I admit I lost the thread there) while others effectively became celebrities: I dropped everything to cover Grumpy Cat’s passing in 2019.

You can tell the story of the internet, and with it the 21st century, through the animals it has rallied around. As a petfluencer pioneer, Grumpy Cat’s merchandising and brand deals were mind-boggling back in 2013; now everything can be monetised. Three years later, in May 2016, the online outpouring that greeted the fatal shooting of Harambe the gorilla at Cincinnati zoo in hindsight signalled a shift to a darker experience of the internet and society.

Now, animal content is not just a pillar of the internet but load-bearing infrastructure, with cute pictures and funny videos providing respite from an angry, anxiety inducing internet.

This is perhaps one reason why recent years have seen non-human main characters emerge at an astonishing pace, with social media monitoring not just the Jimothy situation but also Neil the seal in Tasmania and Punch the infant macaque in Japan. Having gone viral in February, Punch received a reported 2,500 cards for his first birthday this week. When Moo Deng recently turned three, she had a three-day celebration, mass sing-along and “hippo-friendly” cake.

Internet history shows we’ve always come together over animals, but increasingly they feel like our only common ground, because they’re depoliticised, uncomplicated and benign. It’s not just brands: people are hailing Jimothy as “the hero we need right now” (including in song).

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

The most heartening, human takeaway from Jimothy’s viral moment is that it suggests we really do desire more unity and connection; we just don’t feel comfortable doing so in public, or at scale, on anything other than the most innocuous topic. But as with so many of the nice things periodically enabled by the internet, we’re not even allowed that for long: late on Wednesday, the White House shared a meme showing Jimothy wearing a Maga cap. This is why we can’t have nice things.

This exposes the sad truth of Jimothy, our furry folk hero: he won’t break us out of our online silos. With algorithms distorting our shared reality, he may not even have travelled that far across them. Just now a friend, who spends as much time online as I do, sat down next to me and asked what I was writing about. He met my one-word answer with confusion and an immediate Google search: “Who’s ‘Jimothy’ – and how is he ‘bridging political divides’?”

If it were up to me, we’d have sex every other day, but it’s more like twice a week. Once Thomas has had time to replenish, I’ll say: “It’s been a few days …” But my desire is responsive and I’m not used to being the initiator.

Thomas’s libido has declined since we’ve been together, and I worry it will continue to. Our drives probably aren’t that different, but for me, sex is connection and reassurance. Gianni Infantino could face leadership challenge as Fifa council members rebel

The Guardian Sun, 02 Aug 2026 07:00:15 GMT

Council wants to trigger emergency general meeting

Members demand review of Balogun decision

Gianni Infantino is facing a rebellion from members of the Fifa council who are attempting to force an extraordinary general meeting (EGM) that could develop into a full-blown leadership challenge.

The Guardian has learned that moves to call an EGM were already under way before the emergence of Infantino’s abortive plan to sell off stakes in the World Cup, with council members demanding an independent review into the unprecedented decision to lift Folarin Balogun’s suspension during the World Cup, which involved multiple phone calls from Donald Trump.

The Fifa council is the world governing body’s main decision-making forum composed of 28 representatives of the six confederations, eight vice-presidents and Infantino. Under Fifa rules a motion from 50% or 19 of the 37 council members can trigger an EGM.

It is understood that the rebels had already reached double figures before it emerged that Infantino had secretly proposed to sell 20% of a new World Cup operating company to Thrive Capital, an investment company founded by Joshua Kushner, the younger brother of Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner.

The unhappy council members had been planning on calling for Infantino to resign if he refused to sanction an independent review of the Balogun affair, which led to the Norwegian FA filing an official complaint to the International Olympic Committee alleging Fifa had breached rules on political neutrality by bowing to pressure from Trump.

Fifa has insisted all along that it followed due process, with the decision taken independently by its ethics committee, but has yet to publish a written report on the hearing.

The rebels are likely to have been emboldened by Infantino’s U-turn over the World Cup sell-off debacle, with the plan abandoned in a statement from Fifa in the early hours of Saturday morning after Uefa, Concacaf – the North and Central American and Caribbean confederation – and the Asian Football Confederation denounced it.

Uefa and Concacaf both issued further statements condemning Infantino and calling for a thorough review of Fifa’s governance on Saturday, but it is unclear if they have sufficient support from the rest of the world to oust him.

The Confederation of African Football and the South American Conmebol remain fully behind Infantino, while the Qatar Football Association issued a statement yesterday backing him to stay as president.

Of the 37 council members 14 are from Europe and North America so support from Asia will be required to put real pressure on Infantino.

Sign up to Football Daily

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

after newsletter promotion

The Fifa council is not due to meet until November with the rebels attempting to move quickly to force an EGM, where Infantino would be asked to explain himself. A refusal to commission an external review into Balogun would lead to more active attempts to oust Infantino, with alternative presidential candidates already being sounded out.

Qatar’s stance has definitely ruled out a presidential bid from Paris Saint-Germain’s president, Nasser Al-Khelaifi, and much will depend on whether Victor Montagliani, the Canadian who is president of Concacaf, has the appetite to take on Infantino. A campaign from the AFC president, Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim al-Khalifa, who lost narrowly to Infantino in the 2016 Fifa election, would be difficult without his own confederation’s support.

Infantino has already secured more than 200 letters of support endorsing his re-election campaign, but they can be withdrawn and the deadline for other candidates to announce an intention to stand is not until 18 November.

Another potential vehicle for removing Infantino would be an emergency Fifa congress to trigger a vote of no confidence in the president, which can be called if letters are submitted by 43 associations.

I’m all for the nanny state – but we should abolish fines for holidays in term time

The Guardian Sun, 02 Aug 2026 07:00:14 GMT

Some parents are sticklers for the rules, yet mass civil disobedience by parents in England and Wales suggests many agree with me

Perhaps it’s my stage of parenthood, or the fact that I’ve been lying awake at night, but I think I have an idea that could secure the electoral future of the Labour party. All Andy Burnham needs to do to win a landslide at the next general election is abolish fines for parents who take their children on term-time holidays. More than 2 million – around a fifth – have taken their children out of school because they could not afford to travel during holidays, according to a national survey released this month. A record 459,288 fines were issued to parents last year.

This issue has recently become relevant to me because my son starts school in September, so this year will be the last in which we will be allowed to take term-time trips. Obviously, as I contemplate the preposterous costs for summer holidays, I have developed a new and vested interest in being able to get away with my family. It’s deeper than that, though: I didn’t get many childhood holidays, for financial and circumstantial reasons. As a result I feel very passionately that all small people need leisure time away. Without wanting to turn this into a big sob story, I was so desperate to go on holiday like my friends that I used to collect brochures from high street travel agents and spend hours poring over the different hotels, with kids’ clubs, beaches, swimming pools and waterslides that I could only dream of.

Living in a wealthy middle-class area has further radicalised me. I have heard enough parents casually admit that they simply incorporate the fine into their budget to understand that a two-tier system exists. Fines for term-time holidays discriminate unfairly against low-income and Send families, who for the aforementioned financial and circumstantial reasons (too expensive, too crowded for children with sensory or mobility issues) will struggle to take their children away at peak times or cover the fines for doing so in term time. Handing out fines also discriminates against people who work in certain professions, such as farmers, members of the military or people who work in the leisure and tourism industry, and those who have family living a great distance away.

Also, fines don’t even work. Taking your child out of school for a holiday is an ongoing act of mass civil disobedience on the part of the public in England and Wales (Scotland and Northern Ireland do not have automatic fines). Considering how law-abiding we generally are, I find this quite extraordinary. It implies there is a passionate and significant proportion of the public who believe in the importance and the value of a family holiday to the extent that they are willing to break the law to give their kids one. I also suspect many find the rules off-puttingly paternalistic (even as a socialist who loves the “nanny state”, I consider it a huge overreach).

Of course, there are inevitably people who get very exercised about everyone following the rules. These objectors think you should simply plan your holidays around the school calendar, and if you can’t afford to go anywhere, tough. I have met people in real life who have said this in conversation, and they are always the sorts who take their children on gastronomic cycling tours of the Dordogne every summer. In other words, they have a certain level of privilege and don’t seem able to make the imaginative leap to barely being able to scrape together enough cash for a few rainy days in a caravan near Prestatyn.

Don’t get me wrong: there are reasonable objections to my proposition. School attendance and its impact on education is an important issue – I fundamentally believe that. What I don’t believe is that schools should be such a high-pressure environment that one term-time holiday a year – which would still need to be authorised at the headteacher’s discretion – will always have a disastrous impact on learning. With school refusals at record highs and a crumbling Send system, term-time holidays are clearly not the most urgent cause of poor educational outcomes. The coalition government did much to damage the state education system. It also, incidentally, made the system for unauthorised absences at state schools much more punitive . Many of the politicians responsible were privately educated and went on to send their children to fee-paying schools where parents are free to take their kids on term-time holidays.

If I’ve managed to convince you, perhaps I will risk losing you when I say that I don’t believe these trips even necessarily need to be “educational”. On the few holidays I was taken on, we went to museums and old workhouses and castles and ruins, and yes, it’s beneficial to do that. It’s also good for children to see the worried frowns on their parents’ faces melt away – to socialise, to practise their swimming and eat new foods. Memories of fun and togetherness can last a lifetime, sustaining us through tough times. Value to taxpayers is often mentioned in these discussions, but the wellbeing and mental health benefits for children can be economic as well as holistic.

By all means, also look at other measures, such as penalising travel companies that engage in unreasonable profiteering, and staggering or shortening the summer holidays – and providing proper childcare during them. But this should be an open goal for Burnham. He says he cares about alleviating the cost of living pressures on families, allowing them to enjoy life. Abolishing fines would be one effective way of doing that, while correcting a source of social inequality. And it’s a vote winner.

‘This is where democracy beats totalitarianism’: Ukraine’s drone strike force takes the fight to Russia

The Guardian Sun, 02 Aug 2026 05:00:12 GMT

Exclusive: At a launch site in the Ukrainian countryside, members of the elite ‘Magyar’s Birds’ brigade are turning Russia’s vast size into a weakness

Sparrows were cheeping as the sun set over a field of tall yellow sunflowers when a moped-like growl suddenly disturbed the evening calm. The noise rose, dipped, and rose again. Lt Col Ray – a Ukrainian commander with the 414th aviation brigade – took cover in a leafy ditch.

Seconds later a Ukrainian drone roared into a mauve sky. It jerked upwards at a 45-degree angle, orange flames fizzing, and then motored serenely onwards. The flying object resembled a sleek grey biplane with a wooden propeller and tail. It left behind clouds of billowing black smoke and a whiff of gunpowder.

Four and a half years after Vladimir Putin sent tanks to seize Kyiv, the war in Ukraine has moved from the earth to the sky, turning into a battle of drones. This contest – unprecedented in the history of warfare – features technology, innovation and rapid development.

“We are making history here. This is where democracy beats totalitarianism. It’s like George Orwell. But this time Big Brother loses,” Ray said, as the drone vanished over the horizon, engine thrumming. Its destination was Crimea, a scenic Ukrainian peninsula of beaches and white chalk mountains, stolen by Russia in 2014, and militarised thereafter.

Next, two more long-range drones hurtled forward. They soared into the twilight, above a darkening steppe landscape. Each carried 50-100kg of explosives. Mission over, the Ukrainian soldiers packed briskly, winding up white cables with practised ease. Within 10 minutes the men were gone. They disappeared down a tree-lined and potholed track.

Far away from the frontline, other crews were crisscrossing Ukraine, releasing drones according to a precise evening schedule. Operators sitting in front of computer screens nudged them towards enemy targets. The model can fly more than 2,500km, far enough to pummel anywhere in European Russia, and much of Siberia as well.

The journey made by Ray’s trio of drones was shorter. After four hours, at about 1am, the first reached its endpoint: the holiday resort of Alushta on the southern coast of occupied Crimea. The drone weaved between grey apartment blocks and crashed into a 110kV electricity substation. Flames erupted, pricking the city’s inky blackness.

These remote strikes on 21 July were part of what Ukraine has nicknamed the Crimean “switch off”: a campaign to disconnect the region from its power and logistics networks. The same night, unmanned drones hit 13 electricity nodes. Several were located in the Russian-controlled parts of Zaporizhzhia and Kherson provinces, which the Kremlin says it has annexed.

Since 2022 Russia has carried out nightly attacks on Ukrainian cities and towns. It sends Iranian-designed Shaheds as well as ballistic and hypersonic missiles. After Donald Trump returned to the White House last year, these swarms grew. They rain down chaotically, killing families in their apartments and other civilians, in a calculated campaign of terror.

Once a recipient of western assistance, Ukraine has responded by developing its own military manufacturing base. After rapid growth, the country has become the world’s leading unmanned systems power. The drones hurled last week at Crimea were built in Kyiv by a defence technology startup. The firm’s representatives take part in operations.

Ray’s battalion – named after Kairos, the ancient Greek god of opportunity, luck and the fleeting moment – has carried out hundreds of deep strikes against Russia. Targets have included oil refineries, warehouses and munitions depots. It has also struck ports and harbours, as well as routes used for army logistics such as roads and railways.

In 2026 Ukrainian drones have struck Moscow and Putin’s home city of St Petersburg, embarrassing Russia’s president and bringing the war home to ordinary citizens who have previously ignored it. “I think Putin is afraid,” Ray suggested. “One of the justifications he gave for his war was to stop Ukraine from [potentially] bombing Moscow. It’s happening now as a direct consequence of his actions.”

Ray said he felt “revenge and justice” every time one of his drones ascended into the moonlit heavens, bound for enemy territory. “We didn’t start this war. We have no choice. We are fighting for our independence, for our people, for the memory of those who have died, and for our future. This is a contest between slaves and free people,” he said.

Secrecy surrounds Ukraine’s well-organised drone operation. An analytics department finds targets. Western partners provide some intelligence, but most is open source. Drone crews are given coordinates at the last minute. So far none of those who take part in launches have been injured or killed, despite attempts by Moscow to identify and blow up lift-off points.

One person involved said: “You are making change on a global scale. Trump wakes up and sees the results. At the same time it’s very solitary. You can’t tell anybody about what you do, even your wife, or boast: ‘Today we bombed Moscow.’ Only your commander understands.” They added: “It’s an important job. You feel the biggest satisfaction and a member of an elite.”

Kairos is a part of “Magyar’s Birds”, a brigade named after the call sign of its founder, Robert Brovdi, the head of Ukraine’s unmanned systems forces. In July Brovdi launched a campaign to destroy oil tankers and other vessels in the Sea of Azov and Black Sea. So far, more than 200 have been hit. The Russians were taken unawares, their boats unable to escape.

Since last week the brigade has been burning warehouses belonging to Wildberries, Russia’s equivalent of Amazon, obliterating at least nine of them. Ukraine says the company sells military products. The strikes have crippled small businesses and caused billions of roubles in damage. “The socio-psychological impact on society is greater than that of an oil refinery,” Brovdi said.

He said Ukrainian long-range drones had “significantly thinned out” Russia’s air defences. “We have already destroyed the majority of them,” he said. “With every air defence unit destroyed, the breach expands.” Three days earlier air defence units were flattened in the Russian port of Yeysk on the Azov Sea, he added, bringing the number of systems knocked out to 305.

Russia’s enormous size – once a strategic strength – has turned into a weakness. A panicked Kremlin has moved “a certain number” of air defences from the frontline to protect Moscow, Brovdi said. The commander said he wanted to stop Russia from using Crimea as a “springboard” to fire on Ukraine and to push out the nearly 1 million Russian residents or “colonisers” who settled on the peninsula after Putin’s 2014 takeover.

Crimea now has so little fuel that Russian military groups are sometimes unable to fill up and launch drones. There are also frequent power cuts.

One brigade member, call sign Schweik, predicted food shortages would happen soon: “The operation is endless. There will be a cascade effect. We will continue this pressure. They will be thinking about survival instead of assault operations.”

Schweik added: “The situation is humiliating for Russia. Crimea is symbolic. It was Putin’s first trophy and the place where the world order was broken. He created a kind of euphoria in Russia society, which in turn gave him permission to go and take more [Ukrainian] territory. Now everyone in the world understands that Russia is really weak.”

Not all Ukrainian drones reach their targets. According to Ray, about a third are brought down over occupied territory. He admitted losses in the skies above Russia were considerably higher. Nevertheless, Ukraine’s strategy – to pile pressure on the Russian economy – appears to be working. “Troops and resources must be exhausted, so that it becomes impossible for them to continue the war,” Brovdi said.

The commander acknowledged that Russian troops were still advancing in the eastern Donbas region, with battles in the city of Kostiantynivka. “Their gains to date do not justify the price they’re paying for them,” he said. He continued: “At this rate, with their intention to seize half of Ukraine, are they planning to fight for 100 years?”

Back in the countryside, Ray’s colleague “Panama” described the latest launch as a success. “It was 10 out of 10. With us it’s always like this,” he said, adding that he had been working with the current biplane-like model for a year and a half. “To begin with we used foreign drones. Sometimes things went wrong. Now we don’t have problems,” he reflected.

The only challenge came from the mosquitoes, which fill the air during summer evenings. “Over time we’ve become friends with them. They don’t annoy me any more. They are also inhabitants of free Ukraine. They can do whatever they want,” Panama said. “But if they irritate us we will launch them at the enemy. They can eat Russians.”

Betrayal: Trump, Putin and The New Age of Conquest by Luke Harding is published on 27 August by Guardian Faber. To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop. com. Delivery charges may apply.

Apparently, I’ve got ‘comfort creep’. I prefer to think of it as finally knowing what I like

The Guardian Sun, 02 Aug 2026 04:00:10 GMT

Routine isn’t a failure of imagination – it’s the reward for having done enough experimenting. So, yes, I’m going to my favourite restaurant again – and ordering my favourite dish

Feeling seen isn’t always a positive thing. “Comfort creep: do YOU have it?” Good Housekeeping asked, accusingly. I was certain that I did, even before knowing what it was. And that this was not good.

“Same holidays, same TV shows, same restaurants, same wine … If your life lacks excitement, it’s time for an anti-comfort crusade!” OK, guilty as charged, but hang on a second. When did the comfort zone become a horrific dystopia from which you must escape at all costs? Comfort? Ugh, the worst! Run, screaming, as fast as you can.

What about those of us who have comfort creep and don’t want to crusade against it, thanks? In today’s non-figuratively burning world, what’s wrong with battening down the hatches and refusing to budge from your comfort zone? After years of being ashamed, carrying it as a guilty secret, while trying to avoid the fuddy-duddy-sounding (but accurate) phrase “I know what I like”, I’m ready to admit I’m a routine queen. I’m in good company, too: the female cast members of Friends had the same meal, daily, for a decade.

In 2010, Courteney Cox told the Los Angeles Times: “Jennifer [Aniston], Lisa [Kudrow] and I ate lunch together every single day for 10 years. And we always had the same thing – a cobb salad. But it wasn’t really a cobb salad. It was a cobb salad that Jennifer doctored up with turkey bacon and garbanzo beans and I don’t know what. She just has a way with food, which really helps. Because if you’re going to eat the same salad every day for 10 years, it better be a good salad, right?”

Cox put her finger right on it there. It’s no coincidence that comfort creep is a mostly middle-aged occurrence and so can be billed as a miserable, joyless rut in which you’re stuck; proof you’ve given up, surrendered to the blah. It could, alternatively, be viewed as reaching a point where you have sampled much of what life has to offer and curated the choices down to a bespoke selection that suits you perfectly. Welcome to your good-salad days.

When I catch up with my closest friend, we invariably go to the same restaurant. That’s our place. After trying a few, we found one that was great. Even better (or worse, depending on your point of view), after sampling various menu options, we discovered something particularly delicious, so that’s what we both have. It’s not that we’re too set in our ways to take risks – it’s that we’ve already taken them. They were fine, but not as nice as the sea bass.

So now we’re regulars with a regular. The staff recognise us and vice versa; we’re at the exhilarating stage of being able to say – albeit slightly self-consciously – “the usual, please” when they come to take our order. It’s not quite “where everybody knows your name” territory, but it’s not far off. A reassuring, convivial little corner of the planet where we’re sure what’s what and that we will enjoy all of it. On a practical level, it also means we’re spared the boring bits of meeting up – deciding where to go and what to have when we get there. Tedious logistics are moot for ever more; let’s get on with the good stuff.

Similarly, there are a few TV shows I restart whenever I’m overwhelmed by events in real life. Comfort-watching, it’s called – and there it is, the C-word again, soothing billed sneeringly as unfavourable. I also have a favourite knife – my comfort knife, I suppose. If I’m chopping anything, that’s the knife I’m using, guaranteed. Maybe this sounds desperately sad to the kind of thrill-seeker who would grab randomly at the cutlery drawer, but why would I settle for the rest when I could have the best? I know what I like and what isn’t going to cut it.

It seems as though one person’s dull is another’s discerning – it just depends where you’re standing. More than enough about the times we’re living through is uncertain – I’m not sure about you, but I’ll take all the cosy, familiar comfort I can get.

Polly Hudson is a freelance writer

There can be no letup. Humiliated Infantino must stand down at Fifa or be removed

The Guardian Sat, 01 Aug 2026 15:00:55 GMT

Uefa’s call for a boycott and declaration of no-confidence must be the opening salvos in push to dethrone game’s global leader

There is no time to dance around the subject. Gianni Infantino must stand down as Fifa president or otherwise be legally removed. No fresh chances can be made available for an official who has demolished trust in football’s integrity and governance, trashing all remaining credibility of the body that oversees the world’s most-cherished sport.

Infantino was forced into a humiliating climbdown on Saturday morning when he accepted the failure of his plan to sell off portions of the World Cup to private investment. He resolved to resume dialogue about football’s growth “in the spirit of shared interest in our game”. But such a naked attempt to save his own skin cannot hold. Every day Infantino remains in power is a fresh stain on an institution whose reputation is on the floor.

The overreach involved in unilaterally launching the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) scheme – with its vision to place huge influence on football’s future in the palms of venture capitalists – would be enough to bring down most leaders. But Infantino’s rap sheet goes far beyond that. He has routinely made a mockery of Fifa’s own statutes and governance regulations, so nobody should be surprised that patience has finally snapped in corridors of power globally. Fifa’s “football unites the world” slogan has never looked more empty.

Article 10.3 of those regulations, which specifically pertains to the presidency, requires the incumbent to ensure “Fifa’s objectives, mission, strategic direction, policies and values are sustainably pursued, protected and implemented, and that a positive image of Fifa is fostered”. It stipulates “promoting friendly and peaceful relations within Fifa”, which is a nonsense given the degree to which federations and senior personnel have distanced themselves from Infantino in recent days.

The rules give no green light to the pursuit of multiple private projects that, most recently in lockstep with the current US administration or its tributaries, have been tabled with scant appetite for oversight or explanation.

Where to begin? The Folarin Balogun saga tipped many leading figures in football, particularly in Europe, towards the edge. There had already been widespread bafflement and disgust at Infantino’s presentation of the new Fifa peace prize to Donald Trump in December, with little background given about the process and highly contestable information provided about the US president’s qualifying achievements. Stakeholders were frustrated by a lack of consultation about the introduction of “hydration breaks”, which fundamentally toyed with the fabric of matches at this summer’s World Cup.

The bizarre expedited bidding process for the 2034 tournament, which resulted in Saudi Arabia’s candidature being waved through in December 2024, also brought widespread criticism. This list only covers the past 20 months of controversies inflicted by Infantino, capped on Friday by revelations that plans for a 64-team World Cup are in full swing.

When a scathing statement from Uefa on Saturday called for an end to “secret schemes on fast track timescales, cooked up by faceless individuals and of dubious benefit to the game”, it was not only referring to the FFE project and its casual sidelining of other decision makers within Fifa.

A critical mass has been reached. Uefa took a decisive lead in following more than a year of harsh words with strong, united action in pledging to boycott future Fifa tournaments if Infantino did not withdraw his plan. It undoubtedly influenced the outcome and the Uefa president, Aleksander Ceferin, secured an achievement that may define his own reign. But it will mean nothing if Infantino, who is understood to have deployed a major consultancy to smooth relations with federations in recent days, is given the oxygen to dangle fresh promises and turn heads back towards the status quo.

There is an acknowledgment within Uefa and beyond that the pace must not let up. Senior figures are adamant Infantino must not survive the current scandal. Some insiders feel a crucial next step will be for member associations, the overwhelming majority of whom had formally pledged their support for Infantino’s re-election next March, to recall those letters.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

after newsletter promotion

Doing so requires a request to Fifa but could, in sufficient numbers, be a de facto vote of no confidence in Infantino. Fifa had lobbied aggressively for those submissions but many FAs would now be red faced if their expression of fealty towards Infantino was more widely publicised.

Member associations have a duty not to shrink in staving off existential threats to their sport otherwise they, like Infantino, are doing it an egregious disservice. Backing away now would mean leaving the job half done at best.

Uefa have pledged to devise a new method for distributing Fifa’s wealth, delving into its multibillion cash reserves without “selling the family silver”. Behind the scenes it continues to work with other confederations in an effort to find credible candidates for Infantino’s replacement, with a view to running in the election should the Swiss hold on until then. The present crisis can be used to reshape football for the better but only if Infantino is not in situ to impose the final say.

The alternative is that Fifa, and by extension the game, continue lurching from one disaster to the next. It is no laughing matter when the public conversation around football centres on one man, his ego and brazen ventures.

In December Zvonimir Boban, a former sidekick to Infantino as Fifa’s deputy secretary general, told the Guardian that “the way is lost” after the peace prize award to Trump. Fifa will not find a route back until Infantino plays no further part in its operation.

Biohacker Bryan Johnson is keeping his girlfriend’s menstrual blood in his freezer

The Guardian Sat, 01 Aug 2026 12:00:51 GMT

The longevity influencer and his girlfriend, Kate Tolo, say they’re studying women’s health – a worthy goal, but perhaps some skepticism is in order

The tech entrepreneur Bryan Johnson has devoted his life to dodging death. The 48-year-old is obsessed with becoming the healthiest person in the world and is on a quixotic quest to reverse his biological age and live forever. As such, Johnson is disciplined about what he eats, takes dozens of supplements a day, and measures every single biomarker possible, boasting that he is “certainly the most biologically measured person ever”.

In short: good luck finding any ice cream in his freezer. But you know what you will find? His girlfriend’s menstrual blood. On Thursday, Johnson, a chronic oversharer, posted a photo of his 30-year-old girlfriend, Kate Tolo, on X with the caption: “Kate’s period blood is in my -80 °C freezer. Around 10 mL.”

This isn’t the first time Johnson has collected a loved one’s bodily fluids: a few years ago he boasted about infusing himself with a liter of his “blood boy’s” plasma. What in God’s name is a blood boy? Oh, that’s just what Johnson calls his son Talmage, who was 17 at the time. Johnson also donated a liter of his own blood to his own father.

This also isn’t the first time Johnson has taken it upon himself to share personal information about his loved ones on the internet. Last year, he posted data comparing his and his teenage son’s nocturnal erection metrics. “Nighttime erection data from my 19-year-old son ... and me,” he wrote on X, tagging Talmage. “His duration is two minutes longer than mine. Raise children to stand tall, be firm, and be upright.”

Once we’ve all taken a moment to recover from that, we can move on to the menstrual blood in the freezer. What is Johnson planning to do with it? Study it, apparently. “Menstrual blood is valuable and underutilized … It’s a non-invasive look into the uterus,” Johnson explained on X. Tolo and Johnson intend to examine the blood for everything from endocrine disruptors to microplastics. “I like that Kate is a science experiment with me,” he added.

OK. But does she like it? Well, she hasn’t said she doesn’t. Rather she replied to his post with a message saying: “Thanks for looking after me bby.”

Tolo hasn’t just given a one-off blood sample. Johnson has said that she is collecting “14 million data points on her menstrual cycle”, which he touts as a “world first for female health”. Her protocol involves “100+ tasks a day” and “50+ devices”, all of which is being monitored by a “12 person medical team”. Tolo has to take regular urine samples, swallow a temperature pill, and blow into a metabolism tracker. At exactly 9.42 pm, he writes, she has to “insert techno tampon device”. When the Independent asked for more information about the techno tampon, Johnson said: “We will be sharing more on that soon.”

Tolo has done some sharing of her own. In mid-July, she was featured in a Wall Street Journal piece titled: “Bryan Johnson’s girlfriend wants to share her body with the world,” where she explained that she’s doing all this data-tracking for the good of womankind. “I’m really doing it because I think that this is our path toward women being understood in the world and being seen,” Tolo told the Journal. On a personal level, Tolo has said she has polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome, and is hoping to find treatments that might help her symptoms. Helping her out with that is the famous techno tampon: the Journal’s piece features a photo of Tolo looking very intently at a small tampon-shaped device which will track her blood-flow variations.

As Johnson has said: “Women are not well understood medically.” It wasn’t until 1993, when US Congress passed a law requiring that women and minorities be included in clinical research, that we began to be properly represented in medical trials. Menstruation has also been understudied. Indeed, until 2023 there hadn’t been a published study testing period products like tampons using human blood. They’d used saline solution instead. This sort of “medical misogyny” has impacted the quality of care that women get, and resulted in women’s pain not being taken as seriously as men’s.

In many ways, then, Johnson and Tolo’s new women’s health initiative is to be applauded. It’s helping break down the stigma attached to menstruation, and it’s raising awareness about women’s health.

All that said, I think a smidgen of skepticism is warranted. It’s important to remember that Tolo (who has a background in fashion) and Johnson (whose background is in tech) are not exactly highly credentialled medical researchers. They own a company called Immortals that sells supplements. And guess what? According to the Journal: “The company is on the verge of launching products for women.” Which makes all of this feel a lot like a marketing campaign. I don’t know if the techno tampon will end up being a giant step forward for womankind, but it might well provide a healthy boost to the Immortals balance sheet.

Minnesota is implementing a first-in-the-nation law to ban apps and software that allow someone to “nudify” an image or video. Guess who isn’t excited about this? Musk’s AI company. xAI sued to block the new law on Monday, arguing that its definition of “intimate part” is too broad and the statute “imposes an overbroad, content-based ban on free speech”. A good time to remember that Musk is the world’s biggest free speech hypocrite and only seems to care about free speech when it enriches him.

The genocide scholar Omer Bartov has a powerful piece in the New York Times about how: “If the plans that are being elaborated for Gaza go forward, genocide may come to be seen by some nations as the legitimate and lucrative extension of politics by other means.”

Per a Politico poll: “Two-thirds of self-identified MAGA Trump voters say they would continue supporting a GOP candidate accused of sexual assault” by a former partner. That’s “13 percentage points higher than the share of Trump 2024 voters writ large, which include those who do not identify as MAGA”. These numbers don’t really make sense considering that 100% of Trump voters voted for a man accused of sexual misconduct by multiple women, and found liable for abuse in the E Jean Carroll case.

Seems like a very common theme in the party of family values! As for whether this will impact Miller’s career, see the poll above.

The map was apparently made with OpenAI tools.

Per the Washington Post, at least nine schools in three states (Florida, Georgia, Colorado) have bought drones “that can zoom through halls, smash windows and pepper-spray active shooters if teachers report a threat”. Nearly 400,000 students have experienced gun violence at school since the 1999 attack at Colorado’s Columbine High School. Instead of sparking gun reform, it’s spawned a multibillion-dollar security industry focused on campus shootings.

Resolutions like this are largely symbolic, so a possible pardon isn’t completely out of the question.

Dalton is getting a lot of buzz after an interviewer congratulated Damon on his biceps in the Odyssey and the actor explained that his double was a female stunt performer who had “the greatest arms I have ever seen”. I have investigated further and can confirm they are elite arms.

The Trump administration has slashed environmental research funding, meaning cash-strapped scientists are having to get creative. Enter an OnlyFans account called OnlyMarms, promising “unfiltered yellow-bellied marmot content from the Rockies!” While OnlyFans is known for risqué content, you’ll be glad to hear this is G-rated. “We’re not trying to sexualize marmots,” the marmot researcher Daniel Blumstein said. “Although I was just at an international conference and three people came up to me and said: ‘Oh, you have to have more pictures of Marmot feet.’” So far the site has only raised about $3,000, but let’s hope it builds marmentum.

Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist

The idealism of the Esperanto movement, a plague of flies and a clinic in a deep salt mine

The Guardian Sat, 01 Aug 2026 05:00:45 GMT

Need something brilliant to read this weekend? Here are six of our favourite pieces from the last seven days

double quotation markWho would have thought that life would unfold in this way? That ChatGPT would find an article that would lead to an email that would lead to all of this? Technology seems to be in alignment, in the same way that stars can be sometimes. There is a human touch to AI – look what happened.

Commonwealth Games builds to finale and the Tour de France Femmes – follow with us

The Guardian Fri, 31 Jul 2026 16:05:43 GMT

Here’s how to follow along with our coverage – the finest writing and up-to-the-minute reports

The penultimate day of action in Glasgow features a twist in the tale of the track as the mile returns for the first time since 1966, replacing the middle-distance blue-riband 1500m. Expectations are high in the men’s race as the Scottish duo of Jake Wightman and Josh Kerr vie for glory. Kerr has just lowered the world record for the event and said after his midweek heat: “How many times in my career am I going to be running to the line in front of a world-class pack feeling as good as I am in front of a home crowd?” Elsewhere, the boxing concludes today, with 14 gold medals up for grabs, plus action in track cycling. The netball competition reaches the semi-final stage. England, who beat South Africa in a comeback thriller on Thursday, will face New Zealand at 9am. In the later semi, Australia – four-time Commonwealth Games winners and reigning champions – meet Jamaica. John Ashdown, Billy Munday and Rob Smyth will keep the updates flowing. Sean Ingle reports from Glasgow.

Goodwood has certainly lived up to its glorious billing this past week and the final day of the high-summer meeting on the rolling South Downs has plenty of interest for racing’s cognoscenti. Consent can gain the upper hand once again during her continuing tussle with Santorini Star in the Qatar Lillie Langtry Stakes (3pm). Sir Mark Prescott’s star filly returns to the distance of her Prix de Royallieu victory at Longchamp in October. In the preceding contest over a mile and a half, William Haggas’s Al Aasy is seeking a third successive Glorious Stakes victory (2.25pm). There could be another successful title defence with Richard Spencer’s Two Tribes in the Stewards’ Cup (3.35pm). The Phil Cunningham-owned five-year-old is treading the same path as last year which yielded glory in the International Handicap at Ascot, too, where this year he came second. Greg Wood is at the track to liveblog all the action.

Pauline Ferrand-Prévot begins the Tour de France Femmes determined to repeat last year’s triumph, but the Frenchwoman faces a tough challenge in a field headed by her in-form Dutch rival Demi Vollering. Ferrand-Prévot, the Olympic mountain bike champion, returned to road racing two years ago with the Tour as her primary target, and rewarded that decision by becoming the first home winner of the race since 1989. She has carefully tailored her schedule to repeat the feat, finishing second at the Tour of Flanders and third at Paris-Roubaix before stepping away from competition after the Vuelta Femenina in May, where she finished 35th overall. Her Team Visma-Lease a Bike squad has been built around another bid for yellow and includes the triple stage winner Marianne Vos. However, Vollering is viewed as the pre-race favourite. The Dutchwoman has enjoyed a stellar season, winning the Giro d’Italia as well as several marquee one-day races, and arrives with perhaps the strongest form in the women’s peloton. Luke McLaughlin helms the stage one liveblog, with Jeremy Whittle reporting from Lausanne.

The final day of the 2026 Games sees 15 gold medals on offer and features the contest for netball gold, plus a compelling day of action at the Sir Chris Hoy Velodrome. In the women’s event, Great Britain’s Olympic medal-winning trio of Katy Marchant, Sophie Capewell (both England) and Emma Finucane (Wales) go head-to-head in the keirin. But the one to beat is New Zealand’s reigning Olympic and Commonwealth champion, Ellesse Andrews. The sprinter has been the dominant force over recent years, and became world champion in the event in 2023 in Glasgow. England’s Kadeena Cox has a strong chance of success in the Women’s C4-C5 4,000m individual pursuit, her signature event, which she won gold medals in at Rio 2016 and Tokyo 2020. In the bowling, Scotland’s Paul Foster and Alex Marshall are targeting a repeat of the pairs gold they claimed on home grass at Glasgow 2014. Rob Smyth and Daniel Gallan host the rolling blog, all the way to the closing ceremony.

The nine-stage route features nearly 19,000m of climbing, an individual time trial in Dijon and a potentially decisive summit finish on Mont Ventoux. It is the first time the legendary climb features in the women’s race. If that doesn’t decide the battle for the yellow, it could come down to the demanding final stage around Nice. Among those in contention are the Swiss rider Marlen Reusser, the Vuelta winner, Paula Blasi, and the former Tour champion Katarzyna Niewiadoma-Phinney, while the veterans Elisa Longo Borghini and Anna van der Breggen cannot be ruled out. Sunday’s second stage from Aigle via the Vaudois vineyards ends with back-to-back ascents before the finale: a bunch sprint on Quai du Mont-Blanc. Alex Reid saddles up for our liveblog.

‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Review: Can We Do Whatever a Spider Can?

The New York Times July 28, 2026

What to Watch

Advertisement

Supported by

The Spider-Man series is about growing up. Now its superhero has become an adult.

By Alissa Wilkinson

When you purchase a ticket for an independently reviewed film through our site, we earn an affiliate commission.

Spider-Man’s story has always been, on some level, about the terrifying experience of growing up. One morning, you discover your body is changing and doing things you can’t quite control, and you have to figure out what to do with that. As winningly played by Tom Holland, Peter Parker has been a kind, openhearted teenager who wants to do the right thing and is horrified that his powers often put everyone he loves in the path of danger. At the end of “Spider-Man: No Way Home,” he asked Doctor Strange to cast a spell that would cause the whole world — including the love of his life — to forget that he was Spider-Man, because it was the only way to save his universe from destruction.

“Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” directed by Destin Daniel Cretton from a screenplay by Chris McKenna and Erik Sommers, picks up where “No Way Home” left off. Peter lives alone now that his aunt May (Marisa Tomei) has died, and MJ (Zendaya) and Ned (Jacob Batalon) have gone to M. I. T. As years go by, Peter watches them from afar via Ned’s social media updates. Spider-Man is beloved by New Yorkers again, so he fights crime and chats on the phone with Detective Jean DeWolff (Liza Colón-Zayas), never revealing his identity as Peter Parker. Occasionally he crosses paths with Frank Castle, a. k. a. the Punisher (Jon Bernthal), with whom he has a testy relationship.

But a weird threat menaces the city, a vengeful entity seemingly jumping from person to person. It’s apparently seeking something that’s hidden at Damage Control, the organization that was created to do cleanup after the Battle of New York but turned a bit more authoritarian over time. The director of the organization, Bill Metzger (Tramell Tillman), explains that he’s not sure what the entity is after, but the goal of Damage Control is to harness destructive energy and turn it to something good. They’re hoping to just keep everyone safe, he says.

At the same time, Peter has his own issues with energy, because his arachnid hormone levels are spiking, giving him major headaches and the ability to shoot web fluid from his wrists instead of his suit. He wants nothing more than to tamp down his powers, to return to the abilities that he knows well. And it’s imperative he does this before the entity gets to MJ, who still doesn’t know who he is.

There is, of course, a lot more, some of which I can’t tell you; Sadie Sink has spent the last year dancing around questions about her role in this movie. “Brand New Day” is the fourth in this particular series of Spider-Man movies, and it feels like a cap on the growing-up arc that this iteration of the character has gone through. If “Homecoming” was about adolescence, and “Far From Home” was about growing through the loss of a mentor, and “No Way Home” was about taking responsibility for your actions (and also, college applications), then this is, in part, about deciding to accept your adult powers, even when they scare you.

It is not, unfortunately, nearly as fun as the previous few films, though that may just come with the territory. Much of the lighthearted comedy that made the other movies so amusing is gone, largely because Peter’s relationship to Ned and MJ has changed drastically, which means the bantering chemistry between Holland, Batalon and especially Zendaya is mostly absent. In its place is an emotional heaviness, which compounds in some of the film’s other plot threads. (Thankfully, Florence Pugh shows up a few times as Yelena Belova, and she is a pure delight.)

The film is also bogged down by the same thing that has caused late-stage Marvel Cinematic Universe films to sag: the weight of tying all of the stories together. For instance, if you’re not a walking encyclopedia of M. C. U. lore — or didn’t watch “Daredevil” Season 2 and “Daredevil: Born Again” Season 1 and the two-season “Punisher” TV show and the “Punisher: One Last Kill” Marvel TV special — you might not know who Frank Castle is or why he and Peter know each other, which seems like an awful lot to expect of your audience.

Spider-Man has been tied into the M. C. U. since he appeared in “Captain America: Civil War” (2016), thanks to a deal between Sony Pictures Entertainment and Walt Disney Studios (which owns Marvel Studios), and he’s in several “Avengers” movies. Although other M. C. U. characters crop up in the stand-alone Spider-Man movies, sometimes with substantial roles, the films have still mostly felt like character-driven features about Peter and his friends. Even “No Way Home,” with its many winking ties to other movies, was mostly about various generations of Spider-Mans (Spiders-Men?), not really the M. C. U.’s main arc.

This movie feels as if it’s carrying more franchise weight on its shoulders, and that leaves less room for emotional weight. It’s more scattered as a result, and while hardcore M. C. U. fans might be pleased, the rest of us are, demonstrably, getting kind of tired of having to do our homework.

Nothing can erase the enjoyment of witnessing Holland’s performance, which remains winsome and wonderfully kinetic even if you know that’s got to be a computer-generated Spidey a lot of the time. As he’s grown up onscreen, his audience has grown up with him. The question this film asks is one that has cropped up over and over throughout comic book cinema: What do we do with our specialness? For the most part, Peter has chosen to stay local and hidden, to undo the damage done when people know his powers. But now he has to either accept who he is and let himself be known again, or stay in the shadows and take the clean slate promised by the title.

Similarly, a slice of his audience has gone from teen to new adult in a world where creative powers — especially exceptional ones — are seen as something that might be taken from you and put to profitable use. Peter even considers whether there might be a way to create a device that puts everyone on a level playing field, and that doesn’t seem coincidental. If movies subconsciously tap the anxieties of their audiences, maybe this one is about the terrifying experience of growing up and discovering that everyone sees what makes you special and wants it for themselves.

Spider-Man: Brand New DayRated PG-13 for the usual cartoonish violence and sad feelings. Running time: 2 hours 25 minutes. In theaters.

What We Know About the Shooting at an In-N-Out Burger in Idaho

The New York Times August 02, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Gunfire brought panic to a shopping center in Twin Falls in what the authorities described as a chaotic scene. At least three people were killed.

By Bernard Mokam

A gunman opened fire Saturday afternoon at a recently opened In-N-Out Burger in Twin Falls, Idaho, sending a shopping center into chaos as people fled from stores and restaurants. At least three people were killed and seven injured, according to the authorities.

In a news conference on Sunday, the authorities named Chad Williams, 24, as the gunman and said that he had died from a self-inflicted gunshot wound. They offered no further description of Mr. Williams.

Chief Matthew Hicks, of the Twin Falls Police Department, said that Mr. Williams acted alone but possible motives were still being investigated.

The F. B. I. has set up a digital tip line for the public to submit images and videos related to the shooting.

Here’s what we know.

The Twin Falls Police Department said it received a call for an active shooter inside the restaurant around 2:30 p. m. Dispatchers could hear screaming and gunfire on the other end of the call, according to the authorities.

Local, state and federal law enforcement agencies responded to calls of shots fired at In-N-Out Burger shortly after.

Officers arrived at what Chief Hicks said on Saturday was “the most chaotic scene that many of them will ever have in their careers.”

The gunman fired into traffic near the restaurant but two bystanders, a private citizen and an off-duty police officer, exchanged fire with Mr. Williams, according to the authorities. The bystanders were not named by officials.

“These people are true heroes in our community, and their actions diverted the shooter and no doubt saved many lives,” said Sheriff Jack Johnson, of Twin Falls County.

During the police search for the shooter, an officer-involved shooting occurred, according to Chief Hicks. He did not specify with whom the officer engaged . No one was injured in that shooting, the authorities said, but the incident is being investigated.

The In-N-Out location opened on July 24 and was the first in Twin Falls. The shooting occurred in a busy commercial district, with stores such as Petco and Best Buy and restaurant chains like IHOP and Taco Bell.

The popular fast food restaurant drew large crowds at its opening, according to local news reports.

At least three people were killed and seven injured, according to the authorities.

Two people remained in critical condition and two others have been treated and released from the hospital, Chief Hicks said on Sunday.

The authorities did not identify the victims.

Lynsi Snyder, the president of In-N-Out Burger, confirmed that a female worker was among those killed.

“We lost one of our beautiful Associates tonight,” Ms. Snyder wrote on social media. “She was taking care of our most important asset — our Customers, and her life was taken by a disgusting human who doesn’t value the lives of others or his own.”

In interviews, bystanders depicted a harrowing scene.

Lane Koehn, 34, said he was driving home when he saw what appeared to be a young man firing a large rifle into traffic near an In-N-Out.

A bystander returned fire with his handgun, which encouraged the young shooter to find cover, Mr. Koehn said.

Mr. Koehn drove into the In-N-Out parking lot, he said, and assisted a group helping the restaurant employee who had been shot in the chest. A man applied pressure to her wound until the ambulance arrived, he added.

Inside the restaurant, Jaylyn Sanchez, 20, barricaded herself in the bathroom after she saw people rushing from the restaurant, “running out of there as fast as they could.”

When she felt the scene was clear, she exited the building, she said. But in the parking lot the gunman pointed his weapon at her. Ms. Sanchez immediately ducked behind a car.

She later rejoined her older brother, Dominic Gonzales, 29, who had been waiting in her truck with their two younger brothers, 5 and 6 years old.

Mr. Gonzales said he heard “pops” after Ms. Sanchez left the truck to enter the restaurant. He told his two younger brothers to get down, he said. They had been near the shopping center to see the new “Spider-Man” movie.

Bernard Mokam covers breaking news.

Spokane Wildfires Destroy Hundreds of Buildings as Thousands Evacuate

The New York Times August 02, 2026

North American Wildfires

Advertisement

Supported by

Firefighters were hopeful that improving weather conditions in Washington state could help their efforts, but worried that fire might spread to a canyon, where it could expand rapidly.

By Christina Morales and Bernard Mokam

Hundreds of structures were destroyed and thousands of people in Spokane County, Wash., remained under evacuation orders on Sunday as firefighters continued their efforts to knock back and control several blazes in the area.

Nearly 1,000 firefighters were combating at least three wildfires in Spokane, which is home to nearly 600,000 residents. More than 5,390 acres of land have been scorched and officials said there was no containment of the fires on Sunday afternoon.

Firefighters were racing to take advantage of weather conditions that had improved, but could worsen by Wednesday.

The National Weather Service said on Sunday that wind gusts would increase after noon and ease after midnight and that conditions would remain very dry, which could propel wildfires into residential areas. Officials said that the danger from fires was still elevated, but that winds were weaker than those on Saturday.

Officials have become increasingly concerned about the rapid spread of the wildfires and the significant risks they pose to populated communities in Spokane, one of the largest counties in Washington.

On Sunday, Gov. Bob Ferguson of Washington traveled to the area to speak with local officials, days after county officials urged residents in Level 3 evacuation zones — the highest level of evacuation order — to leave immediately. About 4,000 structures were at risk of burning.

Gov. Ferguson said that he spoke with President Trump and Secretary Markwayne Mullin of the Department of Homeland Security, to express “how dire the situation is in Spokane and across our state.”

More than a dozen other fires were also burning across Washington, but most of those were in less populated areas, affecting about 250,000 acres. About 4,000 firefighters were working across the state.

“The President is aware of the situation, and expressed his concern for the people of Washington during this difficult time,” Gov. Ferguson said in a social media post on X, where he added that he hoped for a quick approval for the state’s request for a federal emergency declaration.

Videos on social media showed billowing smoke and orange-colored skies as cars in slow-moving traffic tried to get away from the fires. Others showed scorched communities, homes and vehicles.

Benjamin Cossel, the spokesman for the California Interagency Incident Management Team 7, which began leading the firefighting effort on Sunday morning after coming in from Oregon on Saturday, called the Spokane wildfires the “No. 1 priority fire in the nation,” because of its proximity to many homes.

The Old Trails and Autumn Lane fires jumped the Spokane River on Saturday and were encroaching on a nearby canyon on Sunday, Mr. Cossel said, moving northwest away from the city of Spokane, but into the surrounding wilderness. If the fire continues into the canyon, which local residents call Look Out Mountain, it could grow exponentially.

“The possibility for things to go sideways if it gets established in that canyon is pretty high,” he said, adding that “there is nothing really there to stop it.”

On Sunday, several aircraft dropped retardant and water on the flames.

Washington has been experiencing a record-breaking wildfire season, largely because of drought and heat. More than 1,000 fires have burned this year, covering about 425,000 acres, according to the Washington Department of Natural Resources.

On Saturday, forecasters with the National Weather Service had issued their most urgent alert — “a particularly dangerous situation” red-flag warning — for large parts of eastern Washington and northeastern Oregon. It marked the first time such a warning was issued in Washington, officials said.

Gov. Bob Ferguson also declared a state of emergency across Washington, pointing to drought conditions, unusually high temperatures and strong winds.

Response resources from across the nation have been called on to combat this blaze, Mr. Cossel said, depleting already limited reserves.

“We have multiple large incidents across the nation,” Mr. Cossel said, “resources are absolutely tapped.”

Christina Morales is a national reporter for The Times.
