Connections: Sports Edition

Connections: Soccer Edition

Connections Coach

When Mary’s Underground in Sydney closed, it was a familiar tune for a scene hit by high costs and low attendance. Critics worry about a shrinking space for new talent.

Clearing out Mary’s Underground in Sydney. Credit... Matthew Abbott for The New York Times

Supported by

By Laura Chung

Reporting from Sydney, Australia

Jake Smyth and Kenny Graham stood in the green room of Mary’s Underground, a live music venue in Sydney, for the final time. The walls were covered in the names of artists who have performed at the venue over the past seven years.

“They want to leave their mark somewhere that they’ve played,” Mr. Smyth said of the 3,000 musicians who have passed through. The venue has hosted more than 1,000 shows since it opened in 2019, including the New Zealand-born pop star Lorde and the Australian punk rock band The Living End.

But faced with declining bar sales and increasing costs, the friends, who own other venues, closed Mary’s Underground on June 30.

“It’s definitely going to leave a hole in Sydney,” Mr. Smyth said, adding, “This is a tough day.”

It is a familiar story across the country, which was once known for producing generations of rock ’n’ roll royalty, from Midnight Oil to INXS. But with the steady closure of pubs, bars and small venues, the future of Australia’s once-mighty live music industry is now on shaky ground.

MoshPit Bar, a rock ’n’ roll dive bar in Sydney, announced this past week that it would also close, saying that “ever-increasing operating costs, combined with declining revenues, have made it financially impossible for us to continue.”

After the coronavirus pandemic, more than 1,300 live music venues closed across Australia, according to a 2024 report from the music rights body, APRA AMCOS. While more recent figures show the number of live music venues nearing prepandemic levels, it represents six years of stalled growth for the sector, said Nicholas Pickard, executive director of public affairs for the group.

He added that the figures did not represent the number of gigs occurring or people attending, both of which are declining. While 28 percent of Australians listened to live music at a pub or club in 2019, that number dropped to 25 percent in 2024, government data shows.

Part of that is because of a change in consumers’ spending habits — patrons are drinking less, splurging on concerts by big-name stars (like Taylor Swift or Oasis) instead, or buying tickets at the last minute, which creates uncertainty for venues. And everything has become more expensive, from rent and insurance to bands’ touring costs.

“That’s really the big question for the nation: How important is it to hear and see our own music?” Mr. Pickard said.

Australia’s once-thriving music festival scene has also suffered from rising costs and unpredictable weather, leading to the cancellation of events like Bluesfest and Splendour in the Grass, both of which were considered a rite of passage for many Australian teenagers.

The pressures have left music venue owners grappling with how to stay open. Some are relying on government grants, but fear this model is not sustainable.

Tam Boakes, the owner and operator of Jive, an alternative venue in Adelaide, said her business would not survive without support.

“I never applied for a grant in my life, pre-Covid,” she said. “Now, I can’t survive without them,.”

Ms. Boakes said she was working more than 70 hours a week: booking bands, promoting them, helping clean the venue, and managing the bar and staff, but the future was precarious.

“We’ve put so much in,” she said. “I don’t want to see this place go.”

The decline of these venues has consequences for Australia’s broader music industry, experts said.

Lachlan Goold, a music producer and senior lecturer in contemporary music at the University of the Sunshine Coast in Queensland, warned that without small and independent venues giving emerging talent a space to be heard, “I just don’t know where the new music will come from.”

The federal and local governments have provided millions in funding to keep the music industry going. While many in the industry are thankful, they are calling for tax breaks for people running venues and ticket levies with proceeds going toward supporting local artists — a similar program runs in Britain. (Olivia Dean, a chart-topping British performer, will donate 1.10 Australian dollars, or 76 U. S. cents, of every ticket sale to support local venues during her tour of Australia this year.)

Some venues have taken matters into their own hands. In Sydney, Live Music Venues Alliance, the main body for independent music venues in the state of New South Wales, partnered with 25 venues to create MyGigPass. The scheme, which receives funding from the local government, offers weekly deals, such as free entry or discounted tickets, to people 18 to 25.

In the first five months, 2,100 people signed up and more than 1,750 tickets were made available. Beau Neilson, who helped create the program and runs the music venue the Vanguard, said the scheme gave young people a “gateway into live music” and could ensure the future of the industry.

“People don’t just wake up after having no exposure, or no music and arts education, and suddenly realize that they love it,” she said.

Brian Ritchie, the bassist for the American alternative rock band Violent Femmes, said the decline of live music venues, the rise of streaming and increased costs made it difficult for emerging artists.

He pointed to his first tour of Australia in 1984, which the band did “on the smell of a greasy rag.”

“That’s not possible anymore,” said Mr. Ritchie, who was also the artistic director of Mona Foma, a Tasmanian art and music festival that ended in 2024 because of low attendance.

“Musicians need gigs, and they need to be repetitive,” he said. “Just imagine if you were a football player and you only played a match once every six months; you wouldn’t be skilled. And it’s the same thing for live music.”

Back at Mary’s Underground, Mr. Smyth and Mr. Graham reflected on the years and community they had built —the venue had hosted weddings and a wake, and one former chef even named his daughter “Mary.” Before the duo took over, it was The Basement, one of the country’s first jazz and blues clubs, with legends like Prince and Herbie Hancock performing. The friends hope the venue will find new owners who can honor its heritage.

And they remain determined to give musicians a stage, including at Liberty Hall, another music venue, which is doing well.

“It’s hard to play soothsayer on the future,” Mr. Smyth said. “We will just keep turning up every day and trying to do our best.”

Growing up in Canberra, Australia's capital, attending the annual music festival was a rite of passage. When I finally went, I was blown away by all the new bands I discovered — many of which are still on my playlists today. Over time, though, I’ve gotten less adventurous with my music. This story made me want to start hunting for new music again.

An earlier version of this article misspelled the acronym for a music rights body. It is APRA AMCOS, not AMPA AMCO.

We acknowledge mistakes in our reporting with corrections. If you spot an error, please let us know at corrections@nytimes. com. Learn more.

Laura Chung is a Sydney-based reporter and researcher for The Times, covering Australia, New Zealand and the Pacific.

Trump, Paul Weiss and the Capitulation of Big Law: 5 Takeaways

The New York Times August 02, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

The law firm Paul Weiss led the legal resistance against President Trump. Then it led a sudden retreat across the legal industry. A Times investigation examined how it caved to White House pressure.

By Michael S. Schmidt and Jessica Silver-Greenberg

When the law firm Paul Weiss reached a deal with the White House last year to resolve an executive order that threatened it with crippling sanctions, the legal and political worlds were stunned.

The firm had long been known for standing up to the government and championing progressive causes going back to the civil rights movement. During the first Trump administration, Brad Karp, then chairman, had fought the president in court on issues like separating migrant children from their parents. Partners at the firm had hosted a Biden fund-raiser and helped Vice President Kamala Harris with her debate prep.

So, when Mr. Karp quickly surrendered to the White House and made a deal to resolve an executive order widely seen as illegal, it seemed like a dramatic pivot. It was also consequential, foreshadowing how an array of institutions would bend to President Trump. Though four firms fought similar executive orders, eight others followed Paul Weiss’s example and cut deals, agreeing to perform a total of nearly $1 billion in free legal work for causes Mr. Trump supported.

The New York Times spent months trying to understand what had happened within the storied institution — conducting interviews, reviewing court records and obtaining internal emails and other documents. Here are five takeaways from The Times’s investigation.

Long before the executive order, a struggle within Paul Weiss pitted its stable of elite litigators against a rising crop of corporate lawyers singularly focused on the bottom line.

As the corporate lawyers rode a wave of private equity growth and raked in more and more profits, their influence grew. They pushed against the pro bono civil rights litigation that had been at the center of Paul Weiss’s culture.

So when Mr. Trump took aim at Paul Weiss, partly because of its activist history, a long-simmering identity crisis morphed into an existential one.

Looking to amp up Paul Weiss’s corporate practice, Mr. Karp made what would turn out to be a fateful decision. In 2016, he hired Scott Barshay, a bona fide rainmaker from a rival firm who had a dizzying record of generating lucrative legal work.

Mr. Barshay helped the rich firm become even richer. But that came at a cost. Behind the scenes, he was at times abrasive and led the effort to clamp down on social justice litigation, arguing it was bad for business because it could alienate clients.

In private meetings with the firm’s top leadership, Mr. Barshay also pushed to hire more aggressive lawyers, not soft, idealistic ones interested in social justice cases.

Mr. Barshay took aim at a rising star, Lex Korberg, Paul Weiss’s first openly transgender partner.

Mx. Korberg — who uses they/them pronouns — decided to leave Paul Weiss after Mr. Barshay pushed against their social justice work. What Mx. Korberg didn’t know was that Mr. Barshay had privately told other firm leaders that after they transitioned in 2021, he no longer wanted them dealing with his clients, arguing that a transgender lawyer could hurt business by making people uncomfortable.

To insulate the firm, Paul Weiss struck a secret $3.5 million deal in 2023, never previously revealed, under which Mx. Korberg agreed not to sue or disparage the firm.

A Paul Weiss spokeswoman, Laura Van Drie, said that Mx. Korberg had been “a highly valued partner” and that Mr. Barshay had been “happy” for Mx. Korberg “to work for his clients.”

Among the leadership of Paul Weiss, there was broad support to resolve the executive order. Even Karen Dunn, a top partner who had helped the Harris campaign, pushed to finalize the deal.

“Let’s get this done!!!!" Ms. Dunn wrote to Mr. Karp and other leaders in an email reviewed by The Times.

Mr. Karp presented the framework of the deal at a March meeting of the firm’s partners. He said that Paul Weiss would perform $40 million in free legal work for causes that both Mr. Trump and the firm championed.

The text of the agreement, reviewed by The Times, also said that the firm would show no political favoritism in choosing clients, that its pro bono work would represent “the full spectrum of political viewpoints,” and that it would hire “experts” agreed upon with the administration to review the firm’s hiring practices.

Still, Mr. Karp assured partners that the agreement would not affect the firm’s integrity.

In the days after the deal, as the storm of public criticism grew, Ms. Dunn pushed top leaders to bring a case against the administration that would telegraph Paul Weiss’s continued independence. She had been searching for a potential client, including speaking with an abortion rights group about a lawsuit. But Mr. Barshay and Mr. Karp objected, unwilling to risk invoking Mr. Trump’s rage again. Paul Weiss never brought the case.

The firm looked to appease the Trump administration in other ways, too. It cleansed its website for the Center to Combat Hate of any references to its lawsuits against the Proud Boys and Oath Keepers for their role in the Capitol riot of Jan. 6, 2021.

Ms. Van Drie, the Paul Weiss spokeswoman, said that “any assertion that our independence has been jeopardized is completely false.” She said that Paul Weiss’s pro bono work had continued to increase but did not provide any examples of work it had done opposing the second Trump administration.

Michael S. Schmidt is an investigative reporter for The Times covering Washington. His work focuses on tracking and explaining high-profile federal investigations.

Jessica Silver-Greenberg is a Times investigative reporter writing about big business with a focus on health care. She has been a reporter for more than a decade.

Moving Back Home After College? All Your Friends Are Doing It.

The New York Times August 02, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

More young adults are living with their parents. The development suggests that they face a weak job market, but also that fewer face stigma in returning to the roost.

By Noam Scheiber

When he hadn’t landed a job a few months after graduating from the University of California, Santa Cruz, two years ago, Tommy Balmat moved back to his childhood home in the San Francisco Bay Area. He figured looking for a job would be easier with fewer expenses to shoulder. And, perhaps no less important, he was still close with his parents, who were keen to have him back.

“I communicate with my parents about every thought that goes through my head,” said Mr. Balmat, who majored in literature and anthropology and had hoped for a job in book publishing. “They honestly really encouraged me to come back home if that’s what I wanted.”

Mr. Balmat is hardly the only recent graduate to have accepted such an invitation lately. Data from the economists Stefania Albanesi, Rania Gihleb and Ning Zhang show that the portion of college graduates ages 23 to 27 living with their parents has returned to the high it reached during the Covid-19 pandemic. More than one-quarter did so as of last year, from a low of about 18 percent in 2001, according to updates to the paper that are not yet online.

The fact that so many young adults are living at home reflects persistent weakness in the job market for recent graduates even as the overall economy remains fairly strong. The weakness may be growing as artificial intelligence affects white-collar jobs.

Still, some experts wonder if it is all bad news. College graduates may be moving home because they recognize the benefits of conducting a job search from the relative comfort of their childhood bedroom and, as in Mr. Balmat’s case, they’re no longer discouraged by social norms from taking advantage of that arrangement.

Smartphones and video calls have meant that going off to college no longer requires cutting the cord with one’s mother or father, making re-entry less jarring to both parent and child. And huge social disruptions like the Great Recession and the pandemic left many young adults with no alternatives, lessening the stigma.

“This recognition of broader influences doesn’t eliminate frustration with one’s current lot,” said Daniel Holland, a therapist in Bloomington, Minn., who works with many recent college graduates living with their parents. “But it has resulted in what I see as less shame and guilt regarding moving back home.”

It’s hard to deny that a shortage of good jobs has helped drive the great graduate homecoming even as other economic forces, like the high cost of housing, have also weighed on those just starting out.

Over the past decade, young adults with bachelor’s degrees have become more likely to live at home while those with only a high school diploma became slightly less likely to do so, Dr. Albanesi has found. Both groups face rising housing costs, but their economic trajectories have diverged. People with less education appear to have made strong gains since the pandemic, while the college-educated have stalled out.

The unemployment rate for recent college graduates has increased much more rapidly than the country’s overall unemployment rate over the past four years, to 5.6 percent in the first quarter of this year, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.

Even graduates in some traditionally lucrative fields have felt the effects. A chemical engineer who had graduated from McGill University in Montreal moved in with her parents in April and said she and many of her classmates had not found jobs in the field. The unemployment rate for chemical engineers who recently graduated more than doubled between 2022 and 2024, to 4.7 percent, while the rate for computer engineers more than tripled, to 7.8 percent, according to data from the bank.

Such challenges may be altering the profile of those who live at home after graduation — from the rudderless to the driven-but-thwarted.

Alison Yoho assumed that an economics degree from the University of Minnesota, along with solid internship experience, would put her in a strong position to line up a job right out of school. And she moved quickly to capitalize on these advantages. During the fall of her senior year, she prepared to apply for an early career program at a clean energy firm where she had worked the previous summer.

But, in a change from past years, the firm did not appear to solicit applications for the program. A few months before graduation in 2025, while having coffee with a former supervisor, she learned that the company had recently gone through layoffs. “That should have been the first clue it would be an uphill battle,” Ms. Yoho recalled.

She moved home to a suburb in the Twin Cities last August and got her first offer in October. She wasn’t thrilled about the job and felt confident enough to keep searching for a better fit, which materialized two months later.

The findings of Dr. Albanesi and her co-authors suggest that Ms. Yoho will be less likely to take an earnings hit by age 27 than others who struggle to find a job out of school because she could afford to be choosier during her search.

Other data suggest that recent graduates are opting to live at home while searching for a job even if they might be able to land a worse job sooner, perhaps because they feel more comfortable doing so. According to the New York Fed, the underemployment rate — the portion of college graduates taking jobs that don’t require a degree — has been relatively low in recent years.

Lawrence Katz, a labor economist at Harvard, cautioned that such data is inexact and difficult to interpret. But Dr. Katz acknowledged that shifting norms might help explain why more young people were living at home.

“Is there some cultural change in the way people are parenting?” he said. “You see kids today and the degree to which they’re interacting with parents, that’s completely different than the world of 50 years ago, 25 years ago.”

The sheer number of people moving home after graduation, and the sense that they are up against economic forces beyond their control, also appears to be normalizing the choice and weakening whatever taboo might have once existed.

Betsy Balmat, Tommy’s mother, said she had observed fewer and fewer recent college graduates living on their own, at least in the Bay Area, where rent is especially high. “I can say from my own social circle of people I work with and know that it is more common than not to have kids moving home,” said Ms. Balmat, an assistant school superintendent.

When Lily Dall’Era moved home to Sacramento last year after graduating from the University of Washington, she found it comforting that many high school friends were in a similar position. They even began meeting on weekends for group activities, like going on a run or to the farmers’ market.

“I don’t feel bad about moving home,” said Ms. Dall’Era, who majored in oceanography and is hoping to become a veterinarian. “All my other friends are doing it.”

The transition is rarely frictionless, of course. A recent graduate of Syracuse University said she was sharing a bunk bed with her younger sister and complained that her mother insisted on tracking her location on her phone, which made her feel like a teenager again.

Mr. Balmat said he felt a little pressure from his parents to get a lot of applications out the door, sometimes to the detriment of their quality. He was applying to jobs “just to say I had done it,” he recalled.

But, overall, the experience has been a positive one, he said, allowing him to save enough money to move in with a college friend in August. He does not appear to have suffered much stigma from living at home, and for several months even dated a woman he had met at a cafe where he worked part time to burn off anxious energy.

“We ended up bonding really hard — we’re both writers,” said Mr. Balmat, who hopes to publish a novel someday. “We were both really passionate about what we were doing, struggling to figure out how to turn it into money.”

When he invited his girlfriend over to hang out, the attention from his parents was sometimes embarrassing. “They would both drop in on us if we’re watching a movie on the couch, to be like, ‘Can I get anybody any snacks?’” But his girlfriend took it in stride. It turned out she had moved back home, too.

Noam Scheiber is a Times reporter covering white-collar workers, focusing on issues such as pay, artificial intelligence, unemployment and economic mobility.

An unsecured police dashboard was a rare window into how the authorities track foreigners by collecting and aggregating vast amounts of private data.

By Lily Kuo and Pei-Lin Wu

Most days, Marc Hofer, a cybersecurity researcher and journalist based in Amsterdam, trawls the internet for clues about how China surveils its citizens, a subject that has fascinated him since he worked there as a foreign correspondent.

Mr. Hofer, 46, was doing his usual scan earlier this year when he came across something called “Dynamic Control Platform for Overseas Personnel.” It was a futuristic dashboard — like something from the movie “Minority Report” — that appeared to track foreigners in the northern Chinese city of Zhangjiakou, a popular skiing spot that co-hosted the 2022 Winter Olympics.

The system’s dashboard said it tracked more than 700 foreign residents living in the city. In total, it had entries for nearly 12,000 people, which included fugitives, people from Hong Kong and Taiwan, as well as more than 300 foreign journalists. Some of them had not been to Zhangjiakou.

Suddenly, Mr. Hofer saw his own face — in a photograph taken by Chinese immigration officials for their records. Next to it was his passport number and the cellphone number he had used in China.

He was floored. “Whoever put that stuff in there had access to real data,” he recalled. He also noticed a list of users who had recently logged into the site — it included the names of police stations in Zhangjiakou and other cities.

China monitors its 1.4 billion people on an unparalleled scale, with the help of cameras, cellphone signals and national IDs. The database Mr. Hofer found offered a rare window into how extensively the Chinese authorities also surveil foreigners, displaying entries about people categorized by nationality, with their birth date, sex, marital status, address and occupation, and sometimes their religion.

It also included instances when they were captured on camera at traffic intersections, markets, shopping malls or other locations, including a mosque.

Chinese companies hoping to sell their surveillance platforms to the police often create demo web pages that use photos and information about people taken from social media. This was different, Mr. Hofer said: “This is more than some guys playing around, or a student, or a low-level project.”

That day, in January, he began downloading as much data as possible from the site. By May, it had been taken offline.

The New York Times found links between the platform and Origin Dynamic, a Beijing company that provides robotics, surveillance services and equipment to the police, according to public tender documents.

Origin Dynamic had filed a patent application in 2023 for a similar system, which it described as an “information interface for non-Chinese citizens” and was nearly identical to the Zhangjiakou platform in its design and functions. The company is owned in part by the city government of Yancheng in Jiangsu Province.

Origin Dynamic and the Zhangjiakou Public Security Bureau did not respond to requests for comment sent by email and fax.

Mr. Hofer, who shared the data he saved with The Times, believed that the dashboard had been designed for the Zhangjiakou Public Security Bureau, the city’s police department. It included information that only the Chinese authorities would have had access to, and the user log that Mr. Hofer saw listed eight police stations in Zhangjiakou and three from other cities.

It was not clear how, or if, the police have used the database in their work. But its existence illustrates how the Chinese authorities aggregate vast amounts of data from surveillance cameras, medical records, bills, facial-recognition tools and other sources to monitor and analyze the behavior of foreign residents. It had fields for places they frequented, hospital visits and gas payments, as well as flights and trains taken, including seat numbers.

For example, it logged the movements of a woman from Mongolia as she went from a residential compound in Zhangjiakou to shopping malls, restaurants and supermarkets. In some instances, the database indicated, she had been tracked using facial recognition.

Under Xi Jinping, the ruling Chinese Communist Party has overseen a drive to use big data in the name of public safety to stamp out dissent and prevent potential terrorist attacks.

Other countries employ similar kinds of surveillance systems, but in China, there is little protection against police overreach, according to Maya Wang, the deputy Asia director at Human Rights Watch.

“That kind of integration of data is really quite unprecedented and illustrates China’s lack of safeguards,” Ms. Wang said.

When Mr. Hofer first came across the platform’s login page, a username and password had already been filled in. The fact that a system with sensitive personal information on hundreds of people was accessible to anyone who could find it on the internet suggested a major lack of privacy protections.

Greg Walton, a cybersecurity researcher who has studied similar Chinese systems, said the exposure of this one was not an anomaly. It was a consequence of China’s “surveillance sprawl,” which is fueled by an expanding ecosystem of vendors, contractors and public security agencies, he said.

Mr. Walton, a senior investigator at the SecDev Group, a Canadian research firm, said that each new platform “increases the number of places where sensitive personal data can be misconfigured, copied or left externally discoverable.”

The Times verified that data in the entries for six people besides Mr. Hofer was accurate. A Times reporter who used to be based in Beijing was in it, listed in an entry that included the name of her child. Her name was misspelled, but her passport and other information were correct.

Work on the Zhangjiakou system appeared to have started in 2021, and changes were made to it as recently as April, according to Mr. Hofer, who has documented his findings in a Substack newsletter. Several fields in the database were empty or filled with dummy text, suggesting it was still under construction.

Residents were tracked on cameras in public locations, but the platform also pulled from sources not directly connected to the police. It had a list of foreigners and Chinese citizens who had visited the city’s Thaiwoo Ski Resort, including photos of them taken there, their full names and passport numbers.

The platform labeled people from Australia, Canada, New Zealand, the United Kingdom or the United States as being in the “Five Eyes Alliance.” That is a reference to the intelligence-sharing agreement between the five countries that Beijing frequently criticizes as promoting Cold War-style divisions.

It also highlighted residents from what it called “key countries” — a list that included Egypt, Iran, Israel, Morocco, Pakistan and Sudan.

Visitors from Hong Kong, home to widespread anti-Beijing protests in 2019, and Taiwan, a self-governing democracy that China claims as its own, had their own categories. The database also tracked international students, foreign spouses and “key persons,” a euphemism often used by the Chinese authorities to refer to activists or fugitives, or others deemed to be threats to social stability.

Many of the foreign students listed appeared to be from Pakistan and India and were studying at Hebei North University in Zhangjiakou. Profiles of the students included their religion, marital status, focus of study and times they had been captured on cameras at the school’s entrances.

The platform also claimed to be able to map a person’s relationship network. An illustration of the function showed the names of three Pakistani men in their 20s, linking them to one another after they were captured on camera together.

One set of entries that Mr. Hofer downloaded included names of residents who had been penalized under Chinese law. It showed one woman who had been fined 1,000 Chinese yuan (about $150) in 2021, for example, for not registering a change of address. Other examples included foreigners who had been cited for teaching without required licenses.

The information appeared to have been entered by an official at the Zhangjiakou police station named Zhang Jinglong, according to files downloaded by Mr. Hofer that listed him as a contributor.

An official by that name was profiled by the Zhangjiakou police in 2020. He was praised for monitoring discussions online and actively participating in them to “guide citizens to establish correct” views.

Last year, an artificial intelligence lab in the police bureau was named for him.

Screenshots of the platform were provided by Marc Hofer, the cybersecurity researcher.

Lily Kuo is a China correspondent for The Times, based in Taipei.

Pei-Lin Wu is a reporter and researcher covering Taiwan and China for The Times.

Fact-Checking Trump’s Recent Comments About Costs of Iran War

The New York Times August 01, 2026

War in the Middle East

Advertisement

Supported by

Fact Check

The president misleadingly blamed the Biden administration’s weapons transfers to Ukraine for current concerns over munitions stockpiles, among other claims about the Iran war.

By Linda Qiu

Reporting from Washington

As the United States’ war with Iran stretches into its sixth month, concerns over a depleted weapons arsenal, rising casualties and economic consequences have mounted.

President Trump has waved off those worries, even as he seeks a diplomatic solution to end the fighting and polls show Americans growing frustrated with the war. Instead, he has characterized the war in Ukraine as a greater drain on military resources, defended the death toll by comparing it with previous military engagements and celebrated single-day drops in oil prices.

Here’s a fact-check of some of his recent claims.

What Mr. Trump Said

“We have a lot of ammunition, different types. You know, Biden gave a lot to Ukraine and so we’re building that up, but we have a lot. We have a lot of the midlevel stuff, too; I mean, more than we could ever use, no matter what. But we have a lot. I’d like to have more, to be honest, but so much was given to Ukraine by Biden.”— in remarks on Monday

This is misleading. The New York Times and other news outlets have reported that the Iran war has drained the United States’ arsenal of munitions. But Mr. Trump dismissed those concerns, blaming the Biden administration’s military aid to Ukraine instead. The president has a point that the Biden administration sent vast amounts of equipment and munitions to Ukraine, reducing stockpile levels. But those transfers played just a small role in the current issues with the Pentagon’s arsenal, because the military uses different weapons in the war with Iran.

Exact figures for stockpiles and weapons used are not publicly disclosed. But according to a Pentagon fact sheet from January 2025, the Biden administration transferred more than 100 types of equipment to Ukraine since Russia invaded the country in February 2022. The vast majority of that equipment was related to ground combat and not critical to Mr. Trump’s war in Iran, said Mark F. Cancian, a retired Marine Corps colonel and expert in war funding and procurement at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, a Washington think tank.

For example, the Biden administration provided Ukraine with thousands of armored vehicles, trucks and tanks; anti-tank weapons like Javelin and TOW missiles; mortar systems, artillery and millions of rounds of ammunition.

In contrast, the war in Iran has been fought in the sky. The Trump administration and congressional officials as well as outside military experts have raised concerns of depleted inventories of other types of weapons. According to reporting by The Times and other news outlets and calculations from Colonel Cancian, the military has recently used:

1,200 Patriot missiles out of an inventory of 2,330

More than 1,000 Tomahawk cruise missiles out of 3,000

More than 1,100 Joint Air-to-Surface Standoff Missile, or JASSM, out of 4,400

40 to 70 Precision Strike Missiles out of 90

130 to 250 SM-3 missiles out of 410

90 to 370 SM-6 missiles out 1,160

190 to 290 Terminal High Altitude Area Defense, or THAAD, missiles out of 360

The United States only provided a few weapons and munitions on that list to Ukraine, such as 600 Patriot missiles. Other aerial equipment given include short-range air defense equipment, like more than 3,000 Stinger antiaircraft missiles.

On the other hand, The Wall Street Journal reported in August 2022 that some officials thought that after transfers to Ukraine, the level of 155-millimeter combat rounds in the United States’ arsenal was “uncomfortably low.” The Pentagon used a portion of funding provided by Congress in 2024 to replace some of the equipment given to Ukraine including Javelin and Stinger missiles, 155-millimeter ammunition and armored vehicles. These have not posed an issue in the Iran war.

A White House spokeswoman defended Mr. Trump’s characterization, citing billions of dollars in weapons transfers to Ukraine under the Biden administration and a recent executive order by Mr. Trump that makes it more difficult for weapons makers to use materials from adversarial nations like China and Russia.

What Mr. Trump Said

“Oil dropped very big today.”— in the Monday remarks

This needs context. It is true that oil prices dipped on Monday, when Mr. Trump spoke, as fighting between the United States and Iran paused. It was the largest single-day decline since late May. But oil prices still remain high and volatile compared with levels before the war.

The price of Brent crude, the global benchmark, fell by nearly 9 percent on Monday, closing at $88 a barrel. The price of West Texas intermediate crude, the U. S. benchmark, fell by more than 7 percent and closed at almost $83 a barrel.

But prices are subject to large fluctuations. The week before, prices rose to over $100 a barrel. And on Wednesday, prices rose again, briefly topping $91 a barrel. Before the war began in February, the price of Brent was $72 a barrel. So although Monday’s price was low compared with recent levels, it was still 20 percent higher than before the war began.

The White House spokeswoman said that Mr. Trump was right to cite the single-day drop and that prices would plummet to prewar levels as the United States reopens the Strait of Hormuz.

What Mr. Trump Said

This needs context. The death tolls cited in the chart Mr. Trump shared in July are largely accurate, though some are imprecise. More important, he is comparing more limited military incursions in his presidency to major wars that spanned decades throughout multiple administrations. His chart also omits dozens of other casualties that have occurred under his presidency beyond the two conflicts listed.

Mr. Trump’s chart cited 2,000 deaths in the war in Afghanistan and 4,600 in the Iraq war, compared with the Pentagon’s tally of 2,350 deaths in the first phase of the war in Afghanistan and 4,418 in Iraq.

Mr. Trump noted that 18 American service members had been killed in the war in Iran and none in the single-day military intervention in Venezuela in January. Those figures have been reported by the Pentagon. (More than 600 have been wounded in Iran and seven in Venezuela.)

Additionally, two U. S. Army soldiers were killed during counterterrorism operations in Syria in December 2025. The Pentagon also recorded more than 60 deaths from 2017 to 2020 in Afghanistan and military campaigns in other countries during the first Trump administration.

It is also worth pointing out that a number of more limited campaigns that occurred under Mr. Trump’s predecessors also had low death tolls. For example, a U. S.-led maritime operation called Operation Prosperity Guardian that began in 2023 aimed to deter attacks in the Red Sea by Houthi rebels and also led to zero combat deaths (though at least one died in a noncombat-related incident). Similarly, there were no combat deaths of American soldiers in the 1999 bombing of Kosovo (though two died in a helicopter crash).

A previous version of this article misidentified the name of a munition. It is a Patriot missile, not a Patriot cruise missile.

We acknowledge mistakes in our reporting with corrections. If you spot an error, please let us know at corrections@nytimes. com. Learn more.

Linda Qiu is a Times reporter who specializes in fact-checking statements made by politicians and public figures. She has been reporting and fact-checking public figures for nearly a decade.

Trump’s Polling Numbers Hit a New Low. Don’t Expect Him to Change Course.

The New York Times August 01, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

News Analysis

Barely a third of Americans approve of Mr. Trump’s handling of the job, putting him at historic depths for a second-term president at this stage of his tenure.

By Peter Baker

Peter Baker is the chief White House correspondent and reported from Washington.

After a spate of bad polls earlier this summer, President Trump simply declared that they were not true. “MY REAL POLL NUMBERS ARE THE HIGHEST THEY HAVE EVER BEEN,” he wrote on social media, using capital letters as if they would shout away any contrary data.

In fact, his real poll numbers are at or near the lowest they have ever been in some nonpartisan surveys. A flurry of new samples in recent days found that Mr. Trump is at the nadir of his presidency, with support from just around a third of Americans as a stalemated war in Iran and high gas prices take a political toll.

The latest surveys indicate that Mr. Trump is now all but the most unpopular second-term president at this stage of their tenure in the history of polling going back to the 1940s. The only exception is not one that would give Mr. Trump much solace: Richard M. Nixon had even less public support at this stage in his second term but at that point he was just days away from resigning over the Watergate scandal.

These kinds of poll numbers would throw a normal White House into panic mode, especially coming just three months before a midterm election. Someone might be fired. A speech might be written. A new set of policies might be devised. But Mr. Trump has never been a normal president, and he does not react to political circumstances in the same way his predecessors have. Through force of will and command over his MAGA base, he has traditionally played a weak hand strong.

“He’s always going to project strength regardless what the numbers are and he’ll say they’re fake anyway,” said Douglas Heye, a longtime Republican strategist, adding that he did not expect any switch in political strategy. “Short of him screaming and throwing something at a staffer, that’s it.”

It is, of course, hard to have a course correction if it is not entirely clear what the course was to begin with. The most impulsive president of modern times, Mr. Trump follows his instincts and can completely reverse himself by the day, or sometimes the hour.

It has worked well enough for him that he has dominated American politics for more than a decade. Even though he won a plurality in 2024, Mr. Trump has never won a majority of the popular vote in any of his three elections nor enjoyed support from a majority in Gallup polling at any point of either term. Yet he has governed as if he were a more popular president.

Still, the latest numbers are particularly bleak and have Republicans increasingly rattled as they dread a Democratic wave that could cost them the House and possibly even the Senate in November. Mr. Trump has the support of just 34 percent of Americans in CNN’s latest poll, matching his lowest point just after the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol. He had the approval of just 33 percent in a new AP-NORC survey, tying his lowest since 2017, and 32 percent in Quinnipiac University data, falling to an all-time low in that poll.

By comparison, at this stage of their second terms, Bill Clinton was at 64 percent, Ronald Reagan at 61 percent and Dwight D. Eisenhower at 58 percent, according to historical Gallup surveys. Those underwater included Barack Obama at 43 percent, Harry S. Truman at 39 percent and George W. Bush at 37 percent, all of whom went on to see their party lose seats in midterm elections months later. Nixon, on the verge of resignation as he faced impeachment, was at 24 percent at this point.

The challenge for Mr. Trump and Republicans is that the president is underwater on issues almost across the board, including areas where he historically had been stronger, like the economy and immigration. As for the war in Iran, it was already the only U. S. war in the history of polling that more Americans opposed from the very start — and what support there was has cratered even further, with voters now against it 2 to 1.

Moreover, the worry for Republicans is not just that voters disapprove of Mr. Trump’s handling of the presidency but strongly disapprove, suggesting that they would be more motivated than Trump loyalists to show up this fall.

“Those people are going to vote,” said Douglas B. Sosnik, who was Mr. Clinton’s White House political director and senior adviser. “And the non-MAGA Republicans are not motivated to turn out.”

Having said that, politics are not the same as they once were. The way that House lines are drawn these days means that there are fewer genuinely competitive districts, suggesting that even a strong Democratic wave may not generate as many new seats as it might have in the past. That was cemented even more so by a wave of mid-decade redistricting in recent months.

“It is true that Trump’s polling is at the bottom of any president in the run-up to a midterm election,” Mr. Sosnik said. But he added, “I think that politics has changed so much that you need to put some context to Trump’s disapproval and how it compares to other presidents and how this will impact the election results.”

“Most importantly,” he said, “the Republicans are far more insulated than in the past due to the structural changes in American politics driven by political polarization and education as the new fault line in American politics. There are simply far fewer competitive states and districts which will limit the size of the blue wave.”

Kristen Soltis Anderson, a Republican pollster, said that political polarization means that “job approval trades in a narrow band these days” compared with the past. “Job approval in the low 40s or even high 30s is not the political catastrophe it would have been two or three decades ago,” she said. “Presidents barely start out at 50 percent to begin with.”

“But,” she added, “low 30s, if accurate, means pieces of the coalition have started to break away. You’re not just cutting loose swing voters at that point.”

Mr. Trump has to count on the opposition squandering its advantage. “The best thing Republicans have going for them is that the Democratic Party is going through its own issues and does not have a crisp message besides ‘Trump is bad,’” she said. “However, if the environment truly stays this grim, that may be enough.”

The White House did not address the president’s polls in response to a request for comment but boasted of his record. “No other president in history has accomplished more for hard-working Americans than President Trump, who is working tirelessly to create jobs, cool inflation, increase housing affordability, and more,” said Davis Ingle, a White House spokesman. “The president has already made historic progress not only in America but around the world, and this is just the beginning as his agenda continues taking effect.”

Mr. Trump himself has made clear that he sees a different reality than most independent pollsters and political strategists of both parties — and distrusts results that are not favorable to him.

“Polls are very dishonest, just like a lot of reporters,” he told journalists during a news conference at the Group of 7 summit in France in June. A week later, he made his claim that his approval ratings were “THE HIGHEST THEY HAVE EVER BEEN” on his social media site.

Two days later, on June 26, he cited a survey conducted by his own pollsters putting his approval rating at 50 percent. Not satisfied with that, he then gave himself another 15 points. “Other Polls have my Approval Rating at 65%, and more!” he wrote. “Like Journalists, Honest Pollsters are very rare and hard to find!”

A couple weeks later, he seemed to invent another number, albeit even in his own rendering his public support was slipping. “59% Approval Rating,” he wrote on July 12, down six points from his previously asserted rating. “Prices coming down along with the lowering of oil and gas.” In neither case did he cite an actual poll with those numbers. And the price of oil has gone up since then.

Whether he believes such numbers or not, Mr. Trump has made a point of acting as if he were popular even when he is not. And because of his proven ability to punish Republican lawmakers in primaries, he has managed to keep his party in line most of the time.

In Washington, the question is whether that control is beginning to slip amid Republican resistance on Capitol Hill to his plan to give $1.8 billion in taxpayer money to his supporters who claim to have been mistreated by the Biden administration and his nomination of Todd Blanche as attorney general.

Political observers have counted Mr. Trump out before only to see him survive the kinds of controversies and poll numbers that would hobble other politicians. He seems unconcerned by the pleadings of Republicans who want him to end the Iran war and focus more on affordability. Instead, he is pursuing legacy projects like a new White House ballroom and a triumphal arch, no matter how much the polls suggest that voters are not as enthusiastic.

“He is YOLO,” said Mr. Heye, using the initials for You Only Live Once. “He’s not sitting there thinking, ‘Gosh, my powers are weakened because of this.’ It’s part of why he was re-elected and why he’s impervious to some scandals.”

Peter Baker is the chief White House correspondent for The Times. He is covering his sixth presidency and sometimes writes analytical pieces that place presidents and their administrations in a larger context and historical framework.

What You Need to Know About Installing Plug-In Solar Panels

The New York Times July 31, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

You can now buy panels that plug into electrical outlets, but there are some important safety issues to consider when picking and installing a system.

By Ivan Penn and Claire Brown

So you want to cut your electric bill and are eyeing the solar panels that can plug into any outlet in a home to produce your own power?

You may want to wait for a little while.

None of the systems available in the United States have yet received a crucial certification that deems them safe to use in single-family homes, condominiums and apartments. Experts who set safety standards expect to certify some panels soon.

“We really do love the idea of empowering consumers,” said Kenneth Boyce, vice president of engineering at UL Solutions, a company that tests, validates and sets standards for various products. “We’re really focused on keeping people safe.”

Plug-in or so-called balcony-solar systems have become popular in Germany in recent years. Ten American states have passed legislation making them legal, and many others are considering measures that would allow consumers to buy and install them.

Cost and simplicity have driven much of the excitement over the plug-in solar systems. Typically, homeowners do not need to hire installers to connect these solar panels, as they would for conventional rooftop systems that, in the United States, can cost as much as $36,000.

Plug-in systems can be as cheap as a few hundred dollars and typically top out at roughly $2,000.

You want to look for products that carry the “UL 3700” certification. It indicates that the product has been tested and meets the safety criteria set by UL Solutions.

Some systems produce so little electricity — under 400 watts — that they do not pose a safety risk, their makers claim.

But the prongs on larger systems could deliver a momentary shock risk after they are disconnected from the outlet. The UL 3700 standard requires the prongs to be “touch safe,” prompting some developer to encase them in plastic, similar to those found on electric vehicle chargers. Others have created equipment like protective sleeves.

Another potential problem has to do with home circuit breakers. Typically, a household circuit operates on a breaker based on how much electrical current an appliance requires.

When circuits are overloaded, breakers can trip to prevent fires and damage to the electrical equipment.

A plug-in solar system that lacks UL 3700 certification could mask how much electrical current is flowing on a particular circuit because the panels are supplying electricity. In that case, a breaker might not detect that the circuit is being overloaded by other appliances on the same circuit.

“The holy grail is to wait and make sure it is listed to UL 3700 certification,” said Bernadette Del Chiaro, a senior vice president at the Environmental Working Group, a nonprofit organization focused on health and safety. “It puts all the onus on the manufacturers to put in safety devices.”

Some products may claim to be UL certified or UL compliant because certain components of the system, such as inverters, meet existing or draft standards. However, UL Solutions has said it expects its certification to apply to entire systems, not just individual parts. Other organizations also certify these products, but certifications from UL Solutions tend to be coveted by industry players.

Theoretically, yes. A major selling point for these systems is that they are no more difficult to set up than a television or a Wi-Fi router. They are designed to be lightweight and renter friendly.

But some state lawmakers have considered mandating that qualified electricians install the systems. And the final UL 3700 safety certification may require an electrician’s help to install a special electrical outlet for plugging the panels into.

The panels are generally about the size of a window, and can be hung on balconies or placed in backyards — anywhere outdoors with six hours or more of full sun. South-facing areas are ideal because they tend to get the most sun.

If you rent your home, check your state’s law to see if there are any requirements about notifying your landlord. Vermont, for example, requires tenants to give their landlords 10 days’ notice before installing plug-in solar.

Ivan Penn is a reporter based in Los Angeles and covers the energy industry. His work has included reporting on clean energy, failures in the electric grid and the economics of utility services.

Claire Brown covers climate change for The Times and writes for the Climate Forward newsletter.

Plug-In Solar Panels Are Starting to Sprout in U. S. Backyards

The New York Times July 31, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

Ten U. S. states have legalized systems that can be plugged into standard wall outlets. The technology typically does not require permits or electricians.

By Ivan Penn and Claire Brown

Ivan Penn reported from Los Angeles, and Claire Brown from New York.

After watching a YouTube video about solar panels that can be plugged into a regular electrical outlet, Melani Jackson plopped four panels in the backyard of her Salt Lake City home.

In the six months since, she has lowered her electricity bill by about $77 in total. While that’s not a large sum, she is happy to have banked those savings, which required little effort on her part.

“I just really appreciated the idea of being able to do something to cut even just a few dollars off my energy bill plus just become a little bit more environmentally friendly,” Ms. Jackson, 35, said.

Millions of Americans worried about rising energy costs might soon follow in her footsteps as states start allowing homeowners and renters to plug in solar panels on balconies, in backyards and other places. Plug-in systems are much smaller and cheaper than rooftop build-outs — some costing just a few hundred dollars a panel. Permits are not required in the states that allow their use, and people can often install them on their own.

Utah became the first state to legalize plug-in solar systems last year. Nine others, including New Jersey, Virginia and Colorado, have joined it, and lawmakers in California, Massachusetts, New York, Pennsylvania and several other states are considering doing so.

Colorado enacted one of the broadest plug-in solar laws this year. The sponsor of the bill, State Representative Lesley Smith, a Democrat, said she had first seen the technology during a trip to Germany, which has pioneered its use. When she discussed plug-in solar systems at a town hall, she said, “everyone started clapping.”

Home solar panels have, of course, been around for many years. But conventional rooftop systems can cost as much as $36,000, and in many American cities and towns it can take months to obtain the required permits. Such systems have also lost financial appeal in recent years because states, at the urging of electric utility companies, have reduced the bill credits that homeowners can earn from the excess electricity their panels send to the grid.

Plug-in systems get around many of the hassles of conventional rooftop solar. But despite the enthusiasm for the technology, no plug-in solar system has yet been certified as safe to use in the United States. States that have passed laws allowing the systems to be sold require them to be certified by organizations like UL Solutions, a company that tests, validates and sets standards for various products.

The result is a gap growing between enthusiasm for plug-in solar and the availability of a product that has been proven safe.

UL Solutions soon expects to certify at least one of the plug-in solar systems for use in the United States, said Kenneth Boyce, the company’s vice president of engineering. He warned that people should avoid uncertified products, because they could cause electrical shocks or damage electrical equipment and start fires.

For now, some Americans are exploiting a murky certification landscape and shopping online for plug-in systems for their homes, condominiums and apartments.

In the San Francisco Bay Area, Alex Ottoboni, who lives in a condominium, bought two panels even though he knew that California had not yet passed a plug-in solar law. Hanging from his balcony, the panels generate enough electricity to save him $5 to $7 a month on a bill that typically runs about $400 but has reached as high as $680 in winter.

“I don’t like having to be reliant on my utility,” said Mr. Ottoboni, 32, who works in software. He added that his electricity service was not reliable and “just getting more expensive every year.”

The average residential electricity rate in the United States in April was up 7 percent from a year earlier, according to the Energy Information Administration. But rates have been steadily rising for several years, and most industry experts expect costs to continue increasing. Utility companies are spending to upgrade their systems to keep up with electricity demand from data centers and to make up for maintenance that was deferred over the past several decades.

Energy experts say power bills this summer could rise as much as 10.5 percent. The National Energy Assistance Directors Association, which represents state governments in securing federal money, warned last month that one in six U. S. households had fallen behind on its electric bills this year.

A handful of companies have begun catering to people like Mr. Ottoboni and Ms. Jackson.

Bright Saver, a California nonprofit group, recently began selling plug-in solar kits at cost, meaning the organization makes no profit on the sales. Its goal is to expand access to solar systems and push other companies to drive down their prices. Its two-panel, 360-watt system is roughly big enough to power a refrigerator and sells for $414.17.

Those systems are too small to pose any safety risks, said Cora Stryker, a co-founder of the organization. Even so, the laws in Maine, New York and Vermont require certification of those systems because of the more stringent policies in those states.

“We know people want these — they want them now,” Ms. Stryker said. “Electricity prices are skyrocketing, and people are really worried about climate change.”

EcoFlow and Craftstrom sell larger systems for $1,300 to $2,600. EcoFlow ships to addresses in Utah and Maryland, which have passed laws allowing plug-in solar, and Craftstrom sells to all 50 states, capitalizing on certification standards. Both companies have said they plan to seek full certification from UL Solutions.

Stephan Scherer, founder and chief executive of Craftstrom, said sales had increased 50 percent in the past year as state lawmakers passed legislation for plug-in solar systems. The company is on track to sell thousands of units a year, he said.

Plug-in solar systems route the direct current generated by one or a few panels to an inverter, which converts it to alternating current. The inverter, in turn, is plugged into a wall socket through which it transmits energy to appliances, lightbulbs or anything else that is using electricity.

Germany first allowed residents to install plug-in solar in October 2024. Some 800,000 people registered their systems in the first three months, and buyers can now pick them up at IKEA in that country. But the American electrical system is different enough from Germany’s that panels sold there cannot be used here.

Utility executives in the United States have expressed concerns that electricity produced by the systems might feed back into the power grid, posing a danger to linemen working on power lines that they believed were not carrying electricity.

Pedro J. Pizarro, president and chief executive of Edison International, the parent company of the utility Southern California Edison, said that he supported the idea of the plug-in solar technology but that his company opposed legislation introduced in the California Legislature to legalize such systems. He said the bill did not go far enough in protecting utility workers.

“It has to be safe, not only for consumers but for our workers,” Mr. Pizarro said. “It shouldn’t receive unfair subsidies. Beyond that, though, we’re all for it.”

But companies that sell plug-in systems argue that safety risks are minimal or nonexistent. Mr. Scherer of Craftstrom said his company’s systems would not shock electrical workers because they shut off automatically within one second of a power disruption or grid outage.

Mr. Boyce of UL Solutions said his company would certify panels only if they did not pose a risk to consumers or utility workers.

Backers of plug-in solar technology say that the safety issues will soon be resolved and that more states ought to legalize it to help people with rising energy costs.

“Politicians all over the country are wringing their hands, wanting to do something about energy affordability,” said Bernadette Del Chiaro, a senior vice president at the Environmental Working Group, a nonprofit organization focused on health and safety. “Here is an immediate answer.”

Ivan Penn is a reporter based in Los Angeles and covers the energy industry. His work has included reporting on clean energy, failures in the electric grid and the economics of utility services.

Claire Brown covers climate change for The Times and writes for the Climate Forward newsletter.

The FCC Is Coming for Robot Vacuums. How Soon Will It Be a Problem?

Wired July 30, 2026

This week, the US Federal Communications Commission banned the import of foreign-made advanced mobile robots. Humanoid and quadruped robots are specifically named, indicating the true target is robotic versions of people and animals, but something else happens to be an “advanced mobile robot”: robot vacuums.

So what does this ban mean? Though it's effective immediately, nothing changes for now. Robot vacuums won't get removed from the market, and your current robot vacuum won't stop working. The ban will instead stop new models from getting FCC approval to be sold in the United States. The vacuums available now won't be affected, but new models likely won't make it to the US if they're manufactured outside the country. And, unfortunately, a lot of great robot vacuum brands aren't based in the States.

Here's everything to know about what will happen next.

The FCC updated its Covered List this week to include foreign-made advanced mobile robots, which include robot vacuums. The Covered List, which comes from Section 2 of the Secure and Trusted Communications Networks Act of 2019, is a “list of communications equipment and services that are deemed to pose an unacceptable risk to the national security of the United States or the security and safety of United States persons.”

It may feel like overkill for just a robot vacuum, but the definition of an advanced robotic device from the National Security Determination, an interagency body of the Executive Branch, clearly includes them. That definition includes the following highlights:

The National Security Determination said that connected vehicles, vehicles on rail lines, aircraft, and unmanned underwater vehicles are not included in the ban, along with stationary robots. But foreign-made robot vacuums, along with similar robots like robotic pool cleaners and automated lawn mowers, look to be on the chopping block.

The announcement comes after the FCC labeled all of these devices a security risk, since, according to the National Security Determination, “the networked capabilities of advanced robotic systems create extensive vulnerabilities and vectors for attacks that can manipulate the data and physical operation of the advanced robotic system.”

The concern is primarily with the cameras and sensors built into these devices—some even have microphones built into the base station for voice commands. It is a security risk to bring any device into your home that has a camera and the ability to connect to the internet—especially if your Wi-Fi isn't secure. But it's interesting to see the ban stop at robot vacuums and not, say, smart speakers or devices with always-on cameras. The FCC documentation actually lists live cameras as an example, as well as an example of a humanoid robot being hacked, but no example for robot vacuums.

For the most part, it looks like robot vacuums just got unlucky. They're using the same sensors as other robots but aren't streaming live feeds of their surroundings. They do map your home, but that map isn't useful for anything besides knowing where the couch is and which rooms have carpet or hard floors. I wouldn't call these the most dangerous device with a camera in my home by any means, but it seems the government disagrees. This is not the only thing that's been banned lately, either—in May, the FCC also banned foreign-made routers, so we might continue to see bans for various household technology products roll out as the year goes on.

For now, you can shop robot vacuums (and other, similar automated home cleaning robots) as you normally would. FCC approval has already been given to all the robots on the market, so we can expect changes to take place in the future rather than immediately.

I reached out to the makers of my top robot vacuum picks, Shark and Eufy, along with popular robot makers Dreame and Roborock. Shark and Dreame didn't respond, and Roborock declined to comment. Eufy replied with the following statement:

“We are aware of the FCC’s recent update. Based on our current understanding, the new rule does not affect the continued availability, use, or support of products we currently sell in the United States. Those products remain available and will continue to receive updates and customer support.”

So don't worry about getting rid of your robot vacuum if you already have one you love. If you're in the market for a new model, I'd recommend shopping the newest models from brands that could be affected, like Dreame and Eufy, in case future models are blocked from arriving in the States.

It will also be interesting to see which companies avoid the ban—Shark is based in the US, for example, but it's unclear where the company's robot manufacturing is located. Matic is another US-based brand that could potentially evade the ban. But the buying options will be much, much more limited as time goes on.

The ban is disappointing news with IFA Berlin starting September 4, where we often see new robot vacuums announced. I'm not sure anything we'll see there this year will reach the US. A reduced market also isn't good for consumers—having fewer options never helps a category and might ultimately raise prices on less powerful vacuums because of limited supply. Only time will tell what the fallout will be.
